trg: This is the fruit of rashness! Mark'd you not How that the guilty kindred of the queen Look'd pale when they did hear of Clarence' death? O, they did urge it still unto the king! God will revenge it. But come, let us in, To comfort Edward with our company.

src: This is the fruit of rashness! Mark'd you not How that the guilty kindred of the queen Look'd pale when they did hear of Clarence' death? O, they did urge it still unto the king! God will revenge it. But come, let us in, To comfort Edward with our company.
trg: We wait upon your grace.

src: We wait upon your grace.
trg: Tell me, good grandam, is our father dead?

src: Tell me, good grandam, is our father dead?
trg: No, boy.

src: No, boy.
trg: Why do you wring your hands, and beat your breast, And cry 'O Clarence, my unhappy son!'

src: Why do you wring your hands, and beat your breast, And cry 'O Clarence, my unhappy son!'
trg: Why do you look on us, and shake your head, And call us wretches, orphans, castaways If that our noble father be alive?

src: Why do you look on us, and shake your head, And call us wretches, orphans, castaways If that our noble father be alive?
trg: My pretty cousins, you mistake me much; I do lament the sickness of the king. As loath to lose him, not your father's death; It were lost sorrow to wail one that's lost.

src: My pretty cousins, you mistake me much; I do lament the sickness of the king. As loath to lose him, not your father's death; It were lost sorrow to wail one that's lost.
trg: Then, grandam, you conclude that he is dead. The king my uncle is to blame for this: God will revenge it; whom I will importune With daily prayers all to that effect.

src: Then, grandam, you conclude that he is dead. The king my uncle is to blame for this: God will revenge it; whom I will importune With daily prayers all to that effect.
trg: And so will I.

src: And so will I.
trg: Peace, children, peace! the king doth love you well: Incapable and shallow innocents, You cannot guess who caused your father's death.

src: Peace, children, peace! the king doth love you well: Incapable and shallow innocents, You cannot guess who caused your father's death.
trg: Grandam, we can; for my good uncle Gloucester Told me, the king, provoked by the queen, Devised impeachments to imprison him : And when my uncle told me so, he wept, And hugg'd me in his arm, and kindly kiss'd my cheek; Bade me rely on him as on my father, And he would love me dearly as his child.

src: Grandam, we can; for my good uncle Gloucester Told me, the king, provoked by the queen, Devised impeachments to imprison him : And when my uncle told me so, he wept, And hugg'd me in his arm, and kindly kiss'd my cheek; Bade me rely on him as on my father, And he would love me dearly as his child.
trg: Oh, that deceit should steal such gentle shapes, And with a virtuous vizard hide foul guile! He is my son; yea, and therein my shame; Yet from my dugs he drew not this deceit.

src: Oh, that deceit should steal such gentle shapes, And with a virtuous vizard hide foul guile! He is my son; yea, and therein my shame; Yet from my dugs he drew not this deceit.
trg: Think you my uncle did dissemble, grandam?

src: Think you my uncle did dissemble, grandam?
trg: Ay, boy.

src: Ay, boy.
trg: I cannot think it. Hark! what noise is this?

src: I cannot think it. Hark! what noise is this?
trg: Oh, who shall hinder me to wail and weep, To chide my fortune, and torment myself? I'll join with black despair against my soul, And to myself become an enemy.

src: Oh, who shall hinder me to wail and weep, To chide my fortune, and torment myself? I'll join with black despair against my soul, And to myself become an enemy.
trg: What means this scene of rude impatience?

src: What means this scene of rude impatience?
trg: To make an act of tragic violence: Edward, my lord, your son, our king, is dead. Why grow the branches now the root is wither'd? Why wither not the leaves the sap being gone? If you will live, lament; if die, be brief, That our swift-winged souls may catch the king's; Or, like obedient subjects, follow him To his new kingdom of perpetual rest.

src: To make an act of tragic violence: Edward, my lord, your son, our king, is dead. Why grow the branches now the root is wither'd? Why wither not the leaves the sap being gone? If you will live, lament; if die, be brief, That our swift-winged souls may catch the king's; Or, like obedient subjects, follow him To his new kingdom of perpetual rest.
trg: Ah, so much interest have I in thy sorrow As I had title in thy noble husband! I have bewept a worthy husband's death, And lived by looking on his images: But now two mirrors of his princely semblance Are crack'd in pieces by malignant death, And I for comfort have but one false glass, Which grieves me when I see my shame in him. Thou art a widow; yet thou art a mother, And hast the comfort of thy children left thee: But death hath snatch'd my husband from mine arms, And pluck'd two crutches from my feeble limbs, Edward and Clarence. O, what cause have I, Thine being but a moiety of my grief, To overgo thy plaints and drown thy cries!

src: Ah, so much interest have I in thy sorrow As I had title in thy noble husband! I have bewept a worthy husband's death, And lived by looking on his images: But now two mirrors of his princely semblance Are crack'd in pieces by malignant death, And I for comfort have but one false glass, Which grieves me when I see my shame in him. Thou art a widow; yet thou art a mother, And hast the comfort of thy children left thee: But death hath snatch'd my husband from mine arms, And pluck'd two crutches from my feeble limbs, Edward and Clarence. O, what cause have I, Thine being but a moiety of my grief, To overgo thy plaints and drown thy cries!
trg: Good aunt, you wept not for our father's death; How can we aid you with our kindred tears?

src: Good aunt, you wept not for our father's death; How can we aid you with our kindred tears?
trg: Our fatherless distress was left unmoan'd; Your widow-dolour likewise be unwept!

src: Our fatherless distress was left unmoan'd; Your widow-dolour likewise be unwept!
trg: Give me no help in lamentation; I am not barren to bring forth complaints All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes, That I, being govern'd by the watery moon, May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world! Oh for my husband, for my dear lord Edward!

src: Give me no help in lamentation; I am not barren to bring forth complaints All springs reduce their currents to mine eyes, That I, being govern'd by the watery moon, May send forth plenteous tears to drown the world! Oh for my husband, for my dear lord Edward!
trg: Oh for our father, for our dear lord Clarence!

src: Oh for our father, for our dear lord Clarence!
trg: Alas for both, both mine, Edward and Clarence!

src: Alas for both, both mine, Edward and Clarence!
trg: What stay had I but Edward? and he's gone.

src: What stay had I but Edward? and he's gone.
trg: What stay had we but Clarence? and he's gone.

src: What stay had we but Clarence? and he's gone.
trg: What stays had I but they? and they are gone.

src: What stays had I but they? and they are gone.
trg: Was never widow had so dear a loss!

src: Was never widow had so dear a loss!
trg: Were never orphans had so dear a loss!

src: Were never orphans had so dear a loss!
trg: Was never mother had so dear a loss! Alas, I am the mother of these moans! Their woes are parcell'd, mine are general. She for an Edward weeps, and so do I; I for a Clarence weep, so doth not she: These babes for Clarence weep and so do I; I for an Edward weep, so do not they: Alas, you three, on me, threefold distress'd, Pour all your tears! I am your sorrow's nurse, And I will pamper it with lamentations.

src: Was never mother had so dear a loss! Alas, I am the mother of these moans! Their woes are parcell'd, mine are general. She for an Edward weeps, and so do I; I for a Clarence weep, so doth not she: These babes for Clarence weep and so do I; I for an Edward weep, so do not they: Alas, you three, on me, threefold distress'd, Pour all your tears! I am your sorrow's nurse, And I will pamper it with lamentations.
trg: Comfort, dear mother: God is much displeased That you take with unthankfulness, his doing: In common worldly things, 'tis call'd ungrateful, With dull unwilligness to repay a debt Which with a bounteous hand was kindly lent; Much more to be thus opposite with heaven, For it requires the royal debt it lent you.

src: Comfort, dear mother: God is much displeased That you take with unthankfulness, his doing: In common worldly things, 'tis call'd ungrateful, With dull unwilligness to repay a debt Which with a bounteous hand was kindly lent; Much more to be thus opposite with heaven, For it requires the royal debt it lent you.
trg: Madam, bethink you, like a careful mother, Of the young prince your son: send straight for him Let him be crown'd; in him your comfort lives: Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward's grave, And plant your joys in living Edward's throne.

src: Madam, bethink you, like a careful mother, Of the young prince your son: send straight for him Let him be crown'd; in him your comfort lives: Drown desperate sorrow in dead Edward's grave, And plant your joys in living Edward's throne.
trg: Madam, have comfort: all of us have cause To wail the dimming of our shining star; But none can cure their harms by wailing them. Madam, my mother, I do cry you mercy; I did not see your grace: humbly on my knee I crave your blessing.

src: Madam, have comfort: all of us have cause To wail the dimming of our shining star; But none can cure their harms by wailing them. Madam, my mother, I do cry you mercy; I did not see your grace: humbly on my knee I crave your blessing.
trg: God bless thee; and put meekness in thy mind, Love, charity, obedience, and true duty!

src: God bless thee; and put meekness in thy mind, Love, charity, obedience, and true duty!

trg: You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers, That bear this mutual heavy load of moan, Now cheer each other in each other's love Though we have spent our harvest of this king, We are to reap the harvest of his son. The broken rancour of your high-swoln hearts, But lately splinter'd, knit, and join'd together, Must gently be preserved, cherish'd, and kept: Me seemeth good, that, with some little train, Forthwith from Ludlow the young prince be fetch'd Hither to London, to be crown'd our king.

src: You cloudy princes and heart-sorrowing peers, That bear this mutual heavy load of moan, Now cheer each other in each other's love Though we have spent our harvest of this king, We are to reap the harvest of his son. The broken rancour of your high-swoln hearts, But lately splinter'd, knit, and join'd together, Must gently be preserved, cherish'd, and kept: Me seemeth good, that, with some little train, Forthwith from Ludlow the young prince be fetch'd Hither to London, to be crown'd our king.
trg: Why with some little train, my Lord of Buckingham?

src: Why with some little train, my Lord of Buckingham?
trg: Marry, my lord, lest, by a multitude, The new-heal'd wound of malice should break out, Which would be so much the more dangerous By how much the estate is green and yet ungovern'd: Where every horse bears his commanding rein, And may direct his course as please himself, As well the fear of harm, as harm apparent, In my opinion, ought to be prevented.

src: Marry, my lord, lest, by a multitude, The new-heal'd wound of malice should break out, Which would be so much the more dangerous By how much the estate is green and yet ungovern'd: Where every horse bears his commanding rein, And may direct his course as please himself, As well the fear of harm, as harm apparent, In my opinion, ought to be prevented.
trg: I hope the king made peace with all of us And the compact is firm and true in me.

src: I hope the king made peace with all of us And the compact is firm and true in me.
trg: And so in me; and so, I think, in all: Yet, since it is but green, it should be put To no apparent likelihood of breach, Which haply by much company might be urged: Therefore I say with noble Buckingham, That it is meet so few should fetch the prince.

src: And so in me; and so, I think, in all: Yet, since it is but green, it should be put To no apparent likelihood of breach, Which haply by much company might be urged: Therefore I say with noble Buckingham, That it is meet so few should fetch the prince.
trg: And so say I.

src: And so say I.
trg: Then be it so; and go we to determine Who they shall be that straight shall post to Ludlow. Madam, and you, my mother, will you go To give your censures in this weighty business?

src: Then be it so; and go we to determine Who they shall be that straight shall post to Ludlow. Madam, and you, my mother, will you go To give your censures in this weighty business?
trg: With all our harts.

src: With all our harts.
trg: My lord, whoever journeys to the Prince, For God's sake, let not us two be behind; For, by the way, I'll sort occasion, As index to the story we late talk'd of, To part the queen's proud kindred from the king.

src: My lord, whoever journeys to the Prince, For God's sake, let not us two be behind; For, by the way, I'll sort occasion, As index to the story we late talk'd of, To part the queen's proud kindred from the king.
trg: My other self, my counsel's consistory, My oracle, my prophet! My dear cousin, I, like a child, will go by thy direction. Towards Ludlow then, for we'll not stay behind.

src: My other self, my counsel's consistory, My oracle, my prophet! My dear cousin, I, like a child, will go by thy direction. Towards Ludlow then, for we'll not stay behind.
trg: Neighbour, well met: whither away so fast?

src: Neighbour, well met: whither away so fast?
trg: I promise you, I scarcely know myself: Hear you the news abroad?

src: I promise you, I scarcely know myself: Hear you the news abroad?
trg: Ay, that the king is dead.

src: Ay, that the king is dead.
trg: Bad news, by'r lady; seldom comes the better: I fear, I fear 'twill prove a troublous world.

src: Bad news, by'r lady; seldom comes the better: I fear, I fear 'twill prove a troublous world.
trg: Neighbours, God speed!

src: Neighbours, God speed!
trg: Give you good morrow, sir.

src: Give you good morrow, sir.
trg: Doth this news hold of good King Edward's death?

src: Doth this news hold of good King Edward's death?
trg: Ay, sir, it is too true; God help the while!

src: Ay, sir, it is too true; God help the while!
trg: Then, masters, look to see a troublous world.

src: Then, masters, look to see a troublous world.
trg: No, no; by God's good grace his son shall reign.

src: No, no; by God's good grace his son shall reign.
trg: Woe to the land that's govern'd by a child!

src: Woe to the land that's govern'd by a child!
trg: In him there is a hope of government, That in his nonage council under him, And in his full and ripen'd years himself, No doubt, shall then and till then govern well.

src: In him there is a hope of government, That in his nonage council under him, And in his full and ripen'd years himself, No doubt, shall then and till then govern well.
trg: So stood the state when Henry the Sixth Was crown'd in Paris but at nine months old.

src: So stood the state when Henry the Sixth Was crown'd in Paris but at nine months old.
trg: Stood the state so? No, no, good friends, God wot; For then this land was famously enrich'd With politic grave counsel; then the king Had virtuous uncles to protect his grace.

src: Stood the state so? No, no, good friends, God wot; For then this land was famously enrich'd With politic grave counsel; then the king Had virtuous uncles to protect his grace.
trg: Why, so hath this, both by the father and mother.

src: Why, so hath this, both by the father and mother.
trg: Better it were they all came by the father, Or by the father there were none at all; For emulation now, who shall be nearest, Will touch us all too near, if God prevent not. O, full of danger is the Duke of Gloucester! And the queen's sons and brothers haught and proud: And were they to be ruled, and not to rule, This sickly land might solace as before.

src: Better it were they all came by the father, Or by the father there were none at all; For emulation now, who shall be nearest, Will touch us all too near, if God prevent not. O, full of danger is the Duke of Gloucester! And the queen's sons and brothers haught and proud: And were they to be ruled, and not to rule, This sickly land might solace as before.
trg: Come, come, we fear the worst; all shall be well.

src: Come, come, we fear the worst; all shall be well.
trg: When clouds appear, wise men put on their cloaks; When great leaves fall, the winter is at hand; When the sun sets, who doth not look for night? Untimely storms make men expect a dearth. All may be well; but, if God sort it so, 'Tis more than we deserve, or I expect.

src: When clouds appear, wise men put on their cloaks; When great leaves fall, the winter is at hand; When the sun sets, who doth not look for night? Untimely storms make men expect a dearth. All may be well; but, if God sort it so, 'Tis more than we deserve, or I expect.
trg: Truly, the souls of men are full of dread: Ye cannot reason almost with a man That looks not heavily and full of fear.

src: Truly, the souls of men are full of dread: Ye cannot reason almost with a man That looks not heavily and full of fear.
trg: Before the times of change, still is it so: By a divine instinct men's minds mistrust Ensuing dangers; as by proof, we see The waters swell before a boisterous storm. But leave it all to God. whither away?

src: Before the times of change, still is it so: By a divine instinct men's minds mistrust Ensuing dangers; as by proof, we see The waters swell before a boisterous storm. But leave it all to God. whither away?
trg: Marry, we were sent for to the justices.

src: Marry, we were sent for to the justices.
trg: And so was I: I'll bear you company.

src: And so was I: I'll bear you company.
trg: Last night, I hear, they lay at Northampton; At Stony-Stratford will they be to-night: To-morrow, or next day, they will be here.

src: Last night, I hear, they lay at Northampton; At Stony-Stratford will they be to-night: To-morrow, or next day, they will be here.
trg: I long with all my heart to see the prince: I hope he is much grown since last I saw him.

src: I long with all my heart to see the prince: I hope he is much grown since last I saw him.
trg: But I hear, no; they say my son of York Hath almost overta'en him in his growth.

src: But I hear, no; they say my son of York Hath almost overta'en him in his growth.
trg: Ay, mother; but I would not have it so.

src: Ay, mother; but I would not have it so.
trg: Why, my young cousin, it is good to grow.

src: Why, my young cousin, it is good to grow.
trg: Grandam, one night, as we did sit at supper, My uncle Rivers talk'd how I did grow More than my brother: 'Ay,' quoth my uncle Gloucester, 'Small herbs have grace, great weeds do grow apace:' And since, methinks, I would not grow so fast, Because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.

src: Grandam, one night, as we did sit at supper, My uncle Rivers talk'd how I did grow More than my brother: 'Ay,' quoth my uncle Gloucester, 'Small herbs have grace, great weeds do grow apace:' And since, methinks, I would not grow so fast, Because sweet flowers are slow and weeds make haste.
trg: Good faith, good faith, the saying did not hold In him that did object the same to thee; He was the wretched'st thing when he was young, So long a-growing and so leisurely, That, if this rule were true, he should be gracious.

src: Good faith, good faith, the saying did not hold In him that did object the same to thee; He was the wretched'st thing when he was young, So long a-growing and so leisurely, That, if this rule were true, he should be gracious.
trg: Why, madam, so, no doubt, he is.

src: Why, madam, so, no doubt, he is.
trg: I hope he is; but yet let mothers doubt.

src: I hope he is; but yet let mothers doubt.
trg: Now, by my troth, if I had been remember'd, I could have given my uncle's grace a flout, To touch his growth nearer than he touch'd mine.

src: Now, by my troth, if I had been remember'd, I could have given my uncle's grace a flout, To touch his growth nearer than he touch'd mine.
trg: How, my pretty York? I pray thee, let me hear it.

src: How, my pretty York? I pray thee, let me hear it.
trg: Marry, they say my uncle grew so fast That he could gnaw a crust at two hours old 'Twas full two years ere I could get a tooth. Grandam, this would have been a biting jest.

src: Marry, they say my uncle grew so fast That he could gnaw a crust at two hours old 'Twas full two years ere I could get a tooth. Grandam, this would have been a biting jest.
trg: I pray thee, pretty York, who told thee this?

src: I pray thee, pretty York, who told thee this?
trg: Grandam, his nurse.

src: Grandam, his nurse.
trg: His nurse! why, she was dead ere thou wert born.

src: His nurse! why, she was dead ere thou wert born.
trg: If 'twere not she, I cannot tell who told me.

src: If 'twere not she, I cannot tell who told me.
trg: A parlous boy: go to, you are too shrewd.

src: A parlous boy: go to, you are too shrewd.
trg: Good madam, be not angry with the child.

src: Good madam, be not angry with the child.
trg: Pitchers have ears.

src: Pitchers have ears.
trg: Here comes a messenger. What news?

src: Here comes a messenger. What news?
trg: Such news, my lord, as grieves me to unfold.

src: Such news, my lord, as grieves me to unfold.
trg: How fares the prince?

src: How fares the prince?
trg: Well, madam, and in health.

src: Well, madam, and in health.
trg: What is thy news then?

src: What is thy news then?
trg: Lord Rivers and Lord Grey are sent to Pomfret, With them Sir Thomas Vaughan, prisoners.

src: Lord Rivers and Lord Grey are sent to Pomfret, With them Sir Thomas Vaughan, prisoners.
trg: Who hath committed them?

src: Who hath committed them?
trg: The mighty dukes Gloucester and Buckingham.

src: The mighty dukes Gloucester and Buckingham.
trg: For what offence?

src: For what offence?
trg: The sum of all I can, I have disclosed; Why or for what these nobles were committed Is all unknown to me, my gracious lady.

src: The sum of all I can, I have disclosed; Why or for what these nobles were committed Is all unknown to me, my gracious lady.
trg: Ay me, I see the downfall of our house! The tiger now hath seized the gentle hind; Insulting tyranny begins to jet Upon the innocent and aweless throne: Welcome, destruction, death, and massacre! I see, as in a map, the end of all.

src: Ay me, I see the downfall of our house! The tiger now hath seized the gentle hind; Insulting tyranny begins to jet Upon the innocent and aweless throne: Welcome, destruction, death, and massacre! I see, as in a map, the end of all.
trg: Accursed and unquiet wrangling days, How many of you have mine eyes beheld! My husband lost his life to get the crown; And often up and down my sons were toss'd, For me to joy and weep their gain and loss: And being seated, and domestic broils Clean over-blown, themselves, the conquerors. Make war upon themselves; blood against blood, Self against self: O, preposterous And frantic outrage, end thy damned spleen; Or let me die, to look on death no more!

src: Accursed and unquiet wrangling days, How many of you have mine eyes beheld! My husband lost his life to get the crown; And often up and down my sons were toss'd, For me to joy and weep their gain and loss: And being seated, and domestic broils Clean over-blown, themselves, the conquerors. Make war upon themselves; blood against blood, Self against self: O, preposterous And frantic outrage, end thy damned spleen; Or let me die, to look on death no more!
trg: Come, come, my boy; we will to sanctuary. Madam, farewell.

src: Come, come, my boy; we will to sanctuary. Madam, farewell.
trg: I'll go along with you.

src: I'll go along with you.
trg: You have no cause.

src: You have no cause.
trg: My gracious lady, go; And thither bear your treasure and your goods. For my part, I'll resign unto your grace The seal I keep: and so betide to me As well I tender you and all of yours! Come, I'll conduct you to the sanctuary.

src: My gracious lady, go; And thither bear your treasure and your goods. For my part, I'll resign unto your grace The seal I keep: and so betide to me As well I tender you and all of yours! Come, I'll conduct you to the sanctuary.
trg: Welcome, sweet prince, to London, to your chamber.

src: Welcome, sweet prince, to London, to your chamber.
trg: Welcome, dear cousin, my thoughts' sovereign The weary way hath made you melancholy.

src: Welcome, dear cousin, my thoughts' sovereign The weary way hath made you melancholy.
trg: No, uncle; but our crosses on the way Have made it tedious, wearisome, and heavy I want more uncles here to welcome me.

src: No, uncle; but our crosses on the way Have made it tedious, wearisome, and heavy I want more uncles here to welcome me.
trg: Sweet prince, the untainted virtue of your years Hath not yet dived into the world's deceit Nor more can you distinguish of a man Than of his outward show; which, God he knows, Seldom or never jumpeth with the heart. Those uncles which you want were dangerous; Your grace attended to their sugar'd words, But look'd not on the poison of their hearts : God keep you from them, and from such false friends!

src: Sweet prince, the untainted virtue of your years Hath not yet dived into the world's deceit Nor more can you distinguish of a man Than of his outward show; which, God he knows, Seldom or never jumpeth with the heart. Those uncles which you want were dangerous; Your grace attended to their sugar'd words, But look'd not on the poison of their hearts : God keep you from them, and from such false friends!
trg: God keep me from false friends! but they were none.

src: God keep me from false friends! but they were none.
trg: My lord, the mayor of London comes to greet you.

src: My lord, the mayor of London comes to greet you.
trg: God bless your grace with health and happy days!

src: God bless your grace with health and happy days!
trg: I thank you, good my lord; and thank you all. I thought my mother, and my brother York, Would long ere this have met us on the way Fie, what a slug is Hastings, that he comes not To tell us whether they will come or no!

src: I thank you, good my lord; and thank you all. I thought my mother, and my brother York, Would long ere this have met us on the way Fie, what a slug is Hastings, that he comes not To tell us whether they will come or no!
trg: And, in good time, here comes the sweating lord.

src: And, in good time, here comes the sweating lord.
trg: Welcome, my lord: what, will our mother come?

src: Welcome, my lord: what, will our mother come?
trg: On what occasion, God he knows, not I, The queen your mother, and your brother York, Have taken sanctuary: the tender prince Would fain have come with me to meet your grace, But by his mother was perforce withheld.

src: On what occasion, God he knows, not I, The queen your mother, and your brother York, Have taken sanctuary: the tender prince Would fain have come with me to meet your grace, But by his mother was perforce withheld.
trg: Fie, what an indirect and peevish course Is this of hers! Lord cardinal, will your grace Persuade the queen to send the Duke of York Unto his princely brother presently? If she deny, Lord Hastings, go with him, And from her jealous arms pluck him perforce.

src: Fie, what an indirect and peevish course Is this of hers! Lord cardinal, will your grace Persuade the queen to send the Duke of York Unto his princely brother presently? If she deny, Lord Hastings, go with him, And from her jealous arms pluck him perforce.
trg: My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak oratory Can from his mother win the Duke of York, Anon expect him here; but if she be obdurate To mild entreaties, God in heaven forbid We should infringe the holy privilege Of blessed sanctuary! not for all this land Would I be guilty of so deep a sin.

src: My Lord of Buckingham, if my weak oratory Can from his mother win the Duke of York, Anon expect him here; but if she be obdurate To mild entreaties, God in heaven forbid We should infringe the holy privilege Of blessed sanctuary! not for all this land Would I be guilty of so deep a sin.
trg: You are too senseless--obstinate, my lord, Too ceremonious and traditional Weigh it but with the grossness of this age, You break not sanctuary in seizing him. The benefit thereof is always granted To those whose dealings have deserved the place, And those who have the wit to claim the place: This prince hath neither claim'd it nor deserved it; And therefore, in mine opinion, cannot have it: Then, taking him from thence that is not there, You break no privilege nor charter there. Oft have I heard of sanctuary men; But sanctuary children ne'er till now.

src: You are too senseless--obstinate, my lord, Too ceremonious and traditional Weigh it but with the grossness of this age, You break not sanctuary in seizing him. The benefit thereof is always granted To those whose dealings have deserved the place, And those who have the wit to claim the place: This prince hath neither claim'd it nor deserved it; And therefore, in mine opinion, cannot have it: Then, taking him from thence that is not there, You break no privilege nor charter there. Oft have I heard of sanctuary men; But sanctuary children ne'er till now.
trg: My lord, you shall o'er-rule my mind for once. Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?

src: My lord, you shall o'er-rule my mind for once. Come on, Lord Hastings, will you go with me?
trg: I go, my lord.

src: I go, my lord.
trg: Good lords, make all the speedy haste you may. Say, uncle Gloucester, if our brother come, Where shall we sojourn till our coronation?

src: Good lords, make all the speedy haste you may. Say, uncle Gloucester, if our brother come, Where shall we sojourn till our coronation?
trg: Where it seems best unto your royal self. If I may counsel you, some day or two Your highness shall repose you at the Tower: Then where you please, and shall be thought most fit For your best health and recreation.

src: Where it seems best unto your royal self. If I may counsel you, some day or two Your highness shall repose you at the Tower: Then where you please, and shall be thought most fit For your best health and recreation.
trg: I do not like the Tower, of any place. Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?

src: I do not like the Tower, of any place. Did Julius Caesar build that place, my lord?
trg: He did, my gracious lord, begin that place; Which, since, succeeding ages have re-edified.

src: He did, my gracious lord, begin that place; Which, since, succeeding ages have re-edified.
trg: Is it upon record, or else reported Successively from age to age, he built it?

src: Is it upon record, or else reported Successively from age to age, he built it?
trg: Upon record, my gracious lord.

src: Upon record, my gracious lord.
trg: But say, my lord, it were not register'd, Methinks the truth should live from age to age, As 'twere retail'd to all posterity, Even to the general all-ending day.

src: But say, my lord, it were not register'd, Methinks the truth should live from age to age, As 'twere retail'd to all posterity, Even to the general all-ending day.

trg: What say you, uncle?

src: What say you, uncle?
trg: I say, without characters, fame lives long. Thus, like the formal vice, Iniquity, I moralize two meanings in one word.

src: I say, without characters, fame lives long. Thus, like the formal vice, Iniquity, I moralize two meanings in one word.
trg: That Julius Caesar was a famous man; With what his valour did enrich his wit, His wit set down to make his valour live Death makes no conquest of this conqueror; For now he lives in fame, though not in life. I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham,--

src: That Julius Caesar was a famous man; With what his valour did enrich his wit, His wit set down to make his valour live Death makes no conquest of this conqueror; For now he lives in fame, though not in life. I'll tell you what, my cousin Buckingham,--
trg: What, my gracious lord?

src: What, my gracious lord?
trg: An if I live until I be a man, I'll win our ancient right in France again, Or die a soldier, as I lived a king.

src: An if I live until I be a man, I'll win our ancient right in France again, Or die a soldier, as I lived a king.

trg: Now, in good time, here comes the Duke of York.

src: Now, in good time, here comes the Duke of York.
trg: Richard of York! how fares our loving brother?

src: Richard of York! how fares our loving brother?
trg: Well, my dread lord; so must I call you now.

src: Well, my dread lord; so must I call you now.
trg: Ay, brother, to our grief, as it is yours: Too late he died that might have kept that title, Which by his death hath lost much majesty.

src: Ay, brother, to our grief, as it is yours: Too late he died that might have kept that title, Which by his death hath lost much majesty.
trg: How fares our cousin, noble Lord of York?

src: How fares our cousin, noble Lord of York?
trg: I thank you, gentle uncle. O, my lord, You said that idle weeds are fast in growth The prince my brother hath outgrown me far.

src: I thank you, gentle uncle. O, my lord, You said that idle weeds are fast in growth The prince my brother hath outgrown me far.
trg: He hath, my lord.

src: He hath, my lord.
trg: And therefore is he idle?

src: And therefore is he idle?
trg: O, my fair cousin, I must not say so.

src: O, my fair cousin, I must not say so.
trg: Then is he more beholding to you than I.

src: Then is he more beholding to you than I.
trg: He may command me as my sovereign; But you have power in me as in a kinsman.

src: He may command me as my sovereign; But you have power in me as in a kinsman.
trg: I pray you, uncle, give me this dagger.

src: I pray you, uncle, give me this dagger.
trg: My dagger, little cousin? with all my heart.

src: My dagger, little cousin? with all my heart.
trg: A beggar, brother?

src: A beggar, brother?
trg: Of my kind uncle, that I know will give; And being but a toy, which is no grief to give.

src: Of my kind uncle, that I know will give; And being but a toy, which is no grief to give.
trg: A greater gift than that I'll give my cousin.

src: A greater gift than that I'll give my cousin.
trg: A greater gift! O, that's the sword to it.

src: A greater gift! O, that's the sword to it.
trg: A gentle cousin, were it light enough.

src: A gentle cousin, were it light enough.
trg: O, then, I see, you will part but with light gifts; In weightier things you'll say a beggar nay.

src: O, then, I see, you will part but with light gifts; In weightier things you'll say a beggar nay.
trg: It is too heavy for your grace to wear.

src: It is too heavy for your grace to wear.
trg: I weigh it lightly, were it heavier.

src: I weigh it lightly, were it heavier.
trg: What, would you have my weapon, little lord?

src: What, would you have my weapon, little lord?
trg: I would, that I might thank you as you call me.

src: I would, that I might thank you as you call me.
trg: How?

src: How?
trg: Little.

src: Little.
trg: My Lord of York will still be cross in talk: Uncle, your grace knows how to bear with him.

src: My Lord of York will still be cross in talk: Uncle, your grace knows how to bear with him.
trg: You mean, to bear me, not to bear with me: Uncle, my brother mocks both you and me; Because that I am little, like an ape, He thinks that you should bear me on your shoulders.

src: You mean, to bear me, not to bear with me: Uncle, my brother mocks both you and me; Because that I am little, like an ape, He thinks that you should bear me on your shoulders.
trg: With what a sharp-provided wit he reasons! To mitigate the scorn he gives his uncle, He prettily and aptly taunts himself: So cunning and so young is wonderful.

src: With what a sharp-provided wit he reasons! To mitigate the scorn he gives his uncle, He prettily and aptly taunts himself: So cunning and so young is wonderful.
trg: My lord, will't please you pass along? Myself and my good cousin Buckingham Will to your mother, to entreat of her To meet you at the Tower and welcome you.

src: My lord, will't please you pass along? Myself and my good cousin Buckingham Will to your mother, to entreat of her To meet you at the Tower and welcome you.
trg: What, will you go unto the Tower, my lord?

src: What, will you go unto the Tower, my lord?
trg: My lord protector needs will have it so.

src: My lord protector needs will have it so.
trg: I shall not sleep in quiet at the Tower.

src: I shall not sleep in quiet at the Tower.
trg: Why, what should you fear?

src: Why, what should you fear?
trg: Marry, my uncle Clarence' angry ghost: My grandam told me he was murdered there.

src: Marry, my uncle Clarence' angry ghost: My grandam told me he was murdered there.
trg: I fear no uncles dead.

src: I fear no uncles dead.
trg: Nor none that live, I hope.

src: Nor none that live, I hope.
trg: An if they live, I hope I need not fear. But come, my lord; and with a heavy heart, Thinking on them, go I unto the Tower.

src: An if they live, I hope I need not fear. But come, my lord; and with a heavy heart, Thinking on them, go I unto the Tower.
trg: Think you, my lord, this little prating York Was not incensed by his subtle mother To taunt and scorn you thus opprobriously?

src: Think you, my lord, this little prating York Was not incensed by his subtle mother To taunt and scorn you thus opprobriously?
trg: No doubt, no doubt; O, 'tis a parlous boy; Bold, quick, ingenious, forward, capable He is all the mother's, from the top to toe.

src: No doubt, no doubt; O, 'tis a parlous boy; Bold, quick, ingenious, forward, capable He is all the mother's, from the top to toe.
trg: Well, let them rest. Come hither, Catesby. Thou art sworn as deeply to effect what we intend As closely to conceal what we impart: Thou know'st our reasons urged upon the way; What think'st thou? is it not an easy matter To make William Lord Hastings of our mind, For the instalment of this noble duke In the seat royal of this famous isle?

src: Well, let them rest. Come hither, Catesby. Thou art sworn as deeply to effect what we intend As closely to conceal what we impart: Thou know'st our reasons urged upon the way; What think'st thou? is it not an easy matter To make William Lord Hastings of our mind, For the instalment of this noble duke In the seat royal of this famous isle?
trg: He for his father's sake so loves the prince, That he will not be won to aught against him.

src: He for his father's sake so loves the prince, That he will not be won to aught against him.
trg: What think'st thou, then, of Stanley? what will he?

src: What think'st thou, then, of Stanley? what will he?
trg: He will do all in all as Hastings doth.

src: He will do all in all as Hastings doth.
trg: Well, then, no more but this: go, gentle Catesby, And, as it were far off sound thou Lord Hastings, How doth he stand affected to our purpose; And summon him to-morrow to the Tower, To sit about the coronation. If thou dost find him tractable to us, Encourage him, and show him all our reasons: If he be leaden, icy-cold, unwilling, Be thou so too; and so break off your talk, And give us notice of his inclination: For we to-morrow hold divided councils, Wherein thyself shalt highly be employ'd.

src: Well, then, no more but this: go, gentle Catesby, And, as it were far off sound thou Lord Hastings, How doth he stand affected to our purpose; And summon him to-morrow to the Tower, To sit about the coronation. If thou dost find him tractable to us, Encourage him, and show him all our reasons: If he be leaden, icy-cold, unwilling, Be thou so too; and so break off your talk, And give us notice of his inclination: For we to-morrow hold divided councils, Wherein thyself shalt highly be employ'd.
trg: Commend me to Lord William: tell him, Catesby, His ancient knot of dangerous adversaries To-morrow are let blood at Pomfret-castle; And bid my friend, for joy of this good news, Give mistress Shore one gentle kiss the more.

src: Commend me to Lord William: tell him, Catesby, His ancient knot of dangerous adversaries To-morrow are let blood at Pomfret-castle; And bid my friend, for joy of this good news, Give mistress Shore one gentle kiss the more.
trg: Good Catesby, go, effect this business soundly.

src: Good Catesby, go, effect this business soundly.
trg: My good lords both, with all the heed I may.

src: My good lords both, with all the heed I may.
trg: Shall we hear from you, Catesby, ere we sleep?

src: Shall we hear from you, Catesby, ere we sleep?
trg: You shall, my lord.

src: You shall, my lord.
trg: At Crosby Place, there shall you find us both.

src: At Crosby Place, there shall you find us both.
trg: Now, my lord, what shall we do, if we perceive Lord Hastings will not yield to our complots?

src: Now, my lord, what shall we do, if we perceive Lord Hastings will not yield to our complots?
trg: Chop off his head, man; somewhat we will do: And, look, when I am king, claim thou of me The earldom of Hereford, and the moveables Whereof the king my brother stood possess'd.

src: Chop off his head, man; somewhat we will do: And, look, when I am king, claim thou of me The earldom of Hereford, and the moveables Whereof the king my brother stood possess'd.
trg: I'll claim that promise at your grace's hands.

src: I'll claim that promise at your grace's hands.
trg: And look to have it yielded with all willingness. Come, let us sup betimes, that afterwards We may digest our complots in some form.

src: And look to have it yielded with all willingness. Come, let us sup betimes, that afterwards We may digest our complots in some form.
trg: What, ho! my lord!

src: What, ho! my lord!

trg: A messenger from the Lord Stanley.

src: A messenger from the Lord Stanley.
trg: What is't o'clock?

src: What is't o'clock?
trg: Upon the stroke of four.

src: Upon the stroke of four.
trg: Cannot thy master sleep these tedious nights?

src: Cannot thy master sleep these tedious nights?
trg: So it should seem by that I have to say. First, he commends him to your noble lordship.

src: So it should seem by that I have to say. First, he commends him to your noble lordship.
trg: And then?

src: And then?
trg: And then he sends you word He dreamt to-night the boar had razed his helm: Besides, he says there are two councils held; And that may be determined at the one which may make you and him to rue at the other. Therefore he sends to know your lordship's pleasure, If presently you will take horse with him, And with all speed post with him toward the north, To shun the danger that his soul divines.

src: And then he sends you word He dreamt to-night the boar had razed his helm: Besides, he says there are two councils held; And that may be determined at the one which may make you and him to rue at the other. Therefore he sends to know your lordship's pleasure, If presently you will take horse with him, And with all speed post with him toward the north, To shun the danger that his soul divines.
trg: Go, fellow, go, return unto thy lord; Bid him not fear the separated councils His honour and myself are at the one, And at the other is my servant Catesby Where nothing can proceed that toucheth us Whereof I shall not have intelligence. Tell him his fears are shallow, wanting instance: And for his dreams, I wonder he is so fond To trust the mockery of unquiet slumbers To fly the boar before the boar pursues, Were to incense the boar to follow us And make pursuit where he did mean no chase. Go, bid thy master rise and come to me And we will both together to the Tower, Where, he shall see, the boar will use us kindly.

src: Go, fellow, go, return unto thy lord; Bid him not fear the separated councils His honour and myself are at the one, And at the other is my servant Catesby Where nothing can proceed that toucheth us Whereof I shall not have intelligence. Tell him his fears are shallow, wanting instance: And for his dreams, I wonder he is so fond To trust the mockery of unquiet slumbers To fly the boar before the boar pursues, Were to incense the boar to follow us And make pursuit where he did mean no chase. Go, bid thy master rise and come to me And we will both together to the Tower, Where, he shall see, the boar will use us kindly.
trg: My gracious lord, I'll tell him what you say.

src: My gracious lord, I'll tell him what you say.
trg: Many good morrows to my noble lord!

src: Many good morrows to my noble lord!
trg: Good morrow, Catesby; you are early stirring What news, what news, in this our tottering state?

src: Good morrow, Catesby; you are early stirring What news, what news, in this our tottering state?
trg: It is a reeling world, indeed, my lord; And I believe twill never stand upright Tim Richard wear the garland of the realm.

src: It is a reeling world, indeed, my lord; And I believe twill never stand upright Tim Richard wear the garland of the realm.
trg: How! wear the garland! dost thou mean the crown?

src: How! wear the garland! dost thou mean the crown?
trg: Ay, my good lord.

src: Ay, my good lord.
trg: I'll have this crown of mine cut from my shoulders Ere I will see the crown so foul misplaced. But canst thou guess that he doth aim at it?

src: I'll have this crown of mine cut from my shoulders Ere I will see the crown so foul misplaced. But canst thou guess that he doth aim at it?
trg: Ay, on my life; and hopes to find forward Upon his party for the gain thereof: And thereupon he sends you this good news, That this same very day your enemies, The kindred of the queen, must die at Pomfret.

src: Ay, on my life; and hopes to find forward Upon his party for the gain thereof: And thereupon he sends you this good news, That this same very day your enemies, The kindred of the queen, must die at Pomfret.
trg: Indeed, I am no mourner for that news, Because they have been still mine enemies: But, that I'll give my voice on Richard's side, To bar my master's heirs in true descent, God knows I will not do it, to the death.

src: Indeed, I am no mourner for that news, Because they have been still mine enemies: But, that I'll give my voice on Richard's side, To bar my master's heirs in true descent, God knows I will not do it, to the death.
trg: God keep your lordship in that gracious mind!

src: God keep your lordship in that gracious mind!
trg: But I shall laugh at this a twelve-month hence, That they who brought me in my master's hate I live to look upon their tragedy. I tell thee, Catesby--

src: But I shall laugh at this a twelve-month hence, That they who brought me in my master's hate I live to look upon their tragedy. I tell thee, Catesby--
trg: What, my lord?

src: What, my lord?
trg: Ere a fortnight make me elder, I'll send some packing that yet think not on it.

src: Ere a fortnight make me elder, I'll send some packing that yet think not on it.
trg: 'Tis a vile thing to die, my gracious lord, When men are unprepared and look not for it.

src: 'Tis a vile thing to die, my gracious lord, When men are unprepared and look not for it.
trg: O monstrous, monstrous! and so falls it out With Rivers, Vaughan, Grey: and so 'twill do With some men else, who think themselves as safe As thou and I; who, as thou know'st, are dear To princely Richard and to Buckingham.

src: O monstrous, monstrous! and so falls it out With Rivers, Vaughan, Grey: and so 'twill do With some men else, who think themselves as safe As thou and I; who, as thou know'st, are dear To princely Richard and to Buckingham.
trg: The princes both make high account of you; For they account his head upon the bridge.

src: The princes both make high account of you; For they account his head upon the bridge.
trg: I know they do; and I have well deserved it. Come on, come on; where is your boar-spear, man? Fear you the boar, and go so unprovided?

src: I know they do; and I have well deserved it. Come on, come on; where is your boar-spear, man? Fear you the boar, and go so unprovided?
trg: My lord, good morrow; good morrow, Catesby: You may jest on, but, by the holy rood, I do not like these several councils, I.

src: My lord, good morrow; good morrow, Catesby: You may jest on, but, by the holy rood, I do not like these several councils, I.
trg: My lord, I hold my life as dear as you do yours; And never in my life, I do protest, Was it more precious to me than 'tis now: Think you, but that I know our state secure, I would be so triumphant as I am?

src: My lord, I hold my life as dear as you do yours; And never in my life, I do protest, Was it more precious to me than 'tis now: Think you, but that I know our state secure, I would be so triumphant as I am?
trg: The lords at Pomfret, when they rode from London, Were jocund, and supposed their state was sure, And they indeed had no cause to mistrust; But yet, you see how soon the day o'ercast. This sudden stag of rancour I misdoubt: Pray God, I say, I prove a needless coward! What, shall we toward the Tower? the day is spent.

src: The lords at Pomfret, when they rode from London, Were jocund, and supposed their state was sure, And they indeed had no cause to mistrust; But yet, you see how soon the day o'ercast. This sudden stag of rancour I misdoubt: Pray God, I say, I prove a needless coward! What, shall we toward the Tower? the day is spent.
trg: Come, come, have with you. Wot you what, my lord? To-day the lords you talk of are beheaded.

src: Come, come, have with you. Wot you what, my lord? To-day the lords you talk of are beheaded.
trg: They, for their truth, might better wear their heads Than some that have accused them wear their hats. But come, my lord, let us away.

src: They, for their truth, might better wear their heads Than some that have accused them wear their hats. But come, my lord, let us away.
trg: Go on before; I'll talk with this good fellow. How now, sirrah! how goes the world with thee?

src: Go on before; I'll talk with this good fellow. How now, sirrah! how goes the world with thee?
trg: The better that your lordship please to ask.

src: The better that your lordship please to ask.
trg: I tell thee, man, 'tis better with me now Than when I met thee last where now we meet: Then was I going prisoner to the Tower, By the suggestion of the queen's allies; But now, I tell thee--keep it to thyself-- This day those enemies are put to death, And I in better state than e'er I was.

src: I tell thee, man, 'tis better with me now Than when I met thee last where now we meet: Then was I going prisoner to the Tower, By the suggestion of the queen's allies; But now, I tell thee--keep it to thyself-- This day those enemies are put to death, And I in better state than e'er I was.
trg: God hold it, to your honour's good content!

src: God hold it, to your honour's good content!
trg: Gramercy, fellow: there, drink that for me.

src: Gramercy, fellow: there, drink that for me.
trg: God save your lordship!

src: God save your lordship!
trg: Well met, my lord; I am glad to see your honour.

src: Well met, my lord; I am glad to see your honour.
trg: I thank thee, good Sir John, with all my heart. I am in your debt for your last exercise; Come the next Sabbath, and I will content you.

src: I thank thee, good Sir John, with all my heart. I am in your debt for your last exercise; Come the next Sabbath, and I will content you.
trg: What, talking with a priest, lord chamberlain? Your friends at Pomfret, they do need the priest; Your honour hath no shriving work in hand.

src: What, talking with a priest, lord chamberlain? Your friends at Pomfret, they do need the priest; Your honour hath no shriving work in hand.
trg: Good faith, and when I met this holy man, Those men you talk of came into my mind. What, go you toward the Tower?

src: Good faith, and when I met this holy man, Those men you talk of came into my mind. What, go you toward the Tower?
trg: I do, my lord; but long I shall not stay I shall return before your lordship thence.

src: I do, my lord; but long I shall not stay I shall return before your lordship thence.
trg: 'Tis like enough, for I stay dinner there.

src: 'Tis like enough, for I stay dinner there.

trg: I'll wait upon your lordship.

src: I'll wait upon your lordship.
trg: Come, bring forth the prisoners.

src: Come, bring forth the prisoners.
trg: Sir Richard Ratcliff, let me tell thee this: To-day shalt thou behold a subject die For truth, for duty, and for loyalty.

src: Sir Richard Ratcliff, let me tell thee this: To-day shalt thou behold a subject die For truth, for duty, and for loyalty.
trg: God keep the prince from all the pack of you! A knot you are of damned blood-suckers!

src: God keep the prince from all the pack of you! A knot you are of damned blood-suckers!
trg: You live that shall cry woe for this after.

src: You live that shall cry woe for this after.
trg: Dispatch; the limit of your lives is out.

src: Dispatch; the limit of your lives is out.
trg: O Pomfret, Pomfret! O thou bloody prison, Fatal and ominous to noble peers! Within the guilty closure of thy walls Richard the second here was hack'd to death; And, for more slander to thy dismal seat, We give thee up our guiltless blood to drink.

src: O Pomfret, Pomfret! O thou bloody prison, Fatal and ominous to noble peers! Within the guilty closure of thy walls Richard the second here was hack'd to death; And, for more slander to thy dismal seat, We give thee up our guiltless blood to drink.
trg: Now Margaret's curse is fall'n upon our heads, For standing by when Richard stabb'd her son.

src: Now Margaret's curse is fall'n upon our heads, For standing by when Richard stabb'd her son.
trg: Then cursed she Hastings, then cursed she Buckingham, Then cursed she Richard. O, remember, God To hear her prayers for them, as now for us And for my sister and her princely sons, Be satisfied, dear God, with our true blood, Which, as thou know'st, unjustly must be spilt.

src: Then cursed she Hastings, then cursed she Buckingham, Then cursed she Richard. O, remember, God To hear her prayers for them, as now for us And for my sister and her princely sons, Be satisfied, dear God, with our true blood, Which, as thou know'st, unjustly must be spilt.
trg: Make haste; the hour of death is expiate.

src: Make haste; the hour of death is expiate.
trg: Come, Grey, come, Vaughan, let us all embrace: And take our leave, until we meet in heaven.

src: Come, Grey, come, Vaughan, let us all embrace: And take our leave, until we meet in heaven.
trg: My lords, at once: the cause why we are met Is, to determine of the coronation. In God's name, speak: when is the royal day?

src: My lords, at once: the cause why we are met Is, to determine of the coronation. In God's name, speak: when is the royal day?
trg: Are all things fitting for that royal time?

src: Are all things fitting for that royal time?
trg: It is, and wants but nomination.

src: It is, and wants but nomination.
trg: To-morrow, then, I judge a happy day.

src: To-morrow, then, I judge a happy day.
trg: Who knows the lord protector's mind herein? Who is most inward with the royal duke?

src: Who knows the lord protector's mind herein? Who is most inward with the royal duke?
trg: Your grace, we think, should soonest know his mind.

src: Your grace, we think, should soonest know his mind.
trg: Who, I, my lord I we know each other's faces, But for our hearts, he knows no more of mine, Than I of yours; Nor I no more of his, than you of mine. Lord Hastings, you and he are near in love.

src: Who, I, my lord I we know each other's faces, But for our hearts, he knows no more of mine, Than I of yours; Nor I no more of his, than you of mine. Lord Hastings, you and he are near in love.
trg: I thank his grace, I know he loves me well; But, for his purpose in the coronation. I have not sounded him, nor he deliver'd His gracious pleasure any way therein: But you, my noble lords, may name the time; And in the duke's behalf I'll give my voice, Which, I presume, he'll take in gentle part.

src: I thank his grace, I know he loves me well; But, for his purpose in the coronation. I have not sounded him, nor he deliver'd His gracious pleasure any way therein: But you, my noble lords, may name the time; And in the duke's behalf I'll give my voice, Which, I presume, he'll take in gentle part.
trg: Now in good time, here comes the duke himself.

src: Now in good time, here comes the duke himself.
trg: My noble lords and cousins all, good morrow. I have been long a sleeper; but, I hope, My absence doth neglect no great designs, Which by my presence might have been concluded.

src: My noble lords and cousins all, good morrow. I have been long a sleeper; but, I hope, My absence doth neglect no great designs, Which by my presence might have been concluded.
trg: Had not you come upon your cue, my lord William Lord Hastings had pronounced your part,-- I mean, your voice,--for crowning of the king.

src: Had not you come upon your cue, my lord William Lord Hastings had pronounced your part,-- I mean, your voice,--for crowning of the king.
trg: Than my Lord Hastings no man might be bolder; His lordship knows me well, and loves me well.

src: Than my Lord Hastings no man might be bolder; His lordship knows me well, and loves me well.
trg: I thank your grace.

src: I thank your grace.
trg: My lord of Ely!

src: My lord of Ely!
trg: My lord?

src: My lord?
trg: When I was last in Holborn, I saw good strawberries in your garden there I do beseech you send for some of them.

src: When I was last in Holborn, I saw good strawberries in your garden there I do beseech you send for some of them.
trg: Marry, and will, my lord, with all my heart.

src: Marry, and will, my lord, with all my heart.
trg: Cousin of Buckingham, a word with you. Catesby hath sounded Hastings in our business, And finds the testy gentleman so hot, As he will lose his head ere give consent His master's son, as worshipful as he terms it, Shall lose the royalty of England's throne.

src: Cousin of Buckingham, a word with you. Catesby hath sounded Hastings in our business, And finds the testy gentleman so hot, As he will lose his head ere give consent His master's son, as worshipful as he terms it, Shall lose the royalty of England's throne.
trg: Withdraw you hence, my lord, I'll follow you.

src: Withdraw you hence, my lord, I'll follow you.
trg: We have not yet set down this day of triumph. To-morrow, in mine opinion, is too sudden; For I myself am not so well provided As else I would be, were the day prolong'd.

src: We have not yet set down this day of triumph. To-morrow, in mine opinion, is too sudden; For I myself am not so well provided As else I would be, were the day prolong'd.
trg: Where is my lord protector? I have sent for these strawberries.

src: Where is my lord protector? I have sent for these strawberries.
trg: His grace looks cheerfully and smooth to-day; There's some conceit or other likes him well, When he doth bid good morrow with such a spirit. I think there's never a man in Christendom That can less hide his love or hate than he; For by his face straight shall you know his heart.

src: His grace looks cheerfully and smooth to-day; There's some conceit or other likes him well, When he doth bid good morrow with such a spirit. I think there's never a man in Christendom That can less hide his love or hate than he; For by his face straight shall you know his heart.
trg: What of his heart perceive you in his face By any likelihood he show'd to-day?

src: What of his heart perceive you in his face By any likelihood he show'd to-day?
trg: Marry, that with no man here he is offended; For, were he, he had shown it in his looks.

src: Marry, that with no man here he is offended; For, were he, he had shown it in his looks.
trg: I pray God he be not, I say.

src: I pray God he be not, I say.
trg: I pray you all, tell me what they deserve That do conspire my death with devilish plots Of damned witchcraft, and that have prevail'd Upon my body with their hellish charms?

src: I pray you all, tell me what they deserve That do conspire my death with devilish plots Of damned witchcraft, and that have prevail'd Upon my body with their hellish charms?
trg: The tender love I bear your grace, my lord, Makes me most forward in this noble presence To doom the offenders, whatsoever they be I say, my lord, they have deserved death.

src: The tender love I bear your grace, my lord, Makes me most forward in this noble presence To doom the offenders, whatsoever they be I say, my lord, they have deserved death.
trg: Then be your eyes the witness of this ill: See how I am bewitch'd; behold mine arm Is, like a blasted sapling, wither'd up: And this is Edward's wife, that monstrous witch, Consorted with that harlot strumpet Shore, That by their witchcraft thus have marked me.

src: Then be your eyes the witness of this ill: See how I am bewitch'd; behold mine arm Is, like a blasted sapling, wither'd up: And this is Edward's wife, that monstrous witch, Consorted with that harlot strumpet Shore, That by their witchcraft thus have marked me.
trg: If they have done this thing, my gracious lord--

src: If they have done this thing, my gracious lord--
trg: If I thou protector of this damned strumpet-- Tellest thou me of 'ifs'?  Thou art a traitor: Off with his head! Now, by Saint Paul I swear, I will not dine until I see the same. Lovel and Ratcliff, look that it be done: The rest, that love me, rise and follow me.

src: If I thou protector of this damned strumpet-- Tellest thou me of 'ifs'?  Thou art a traitor: Off with his head! Now, by Saint Paul I swear, I will not dine until I see the same. Lovel and Ratcliff, look that it be done: The rest, that love me, rise and follow me.
trg: Woe, woe for England! not a whit for me; For I, too fond, might have prevented this. Stanley did dream the boar did raze his helm; But I disdain'd it, and did scorn to fly: Three times to-day my foot-cloth horse did stumble, And startled, when he look'd upon the Tower, As loath to bear me to the slaughter-house. O, now I want the priest that spake to me: I now repent I told the pursuivant As 'twere triumphing at mine enemies, How they at Pomfret bloodily were butcher'd, And I myself secure in grace and favour. O Margaret, Margaret, now thy heavy curse Is lighted on poor Hastings' wretched head!

src: Woe, woe for England! not a whit for me; For I, too fond, might have prevented this. Stanley did dream the boar did raze his helm; But I disdain'd it, and did scorn to fly: Three times to-day my foot-cloth horse did stumble, And startled, when he look'd upon the Tower, As loath to bear me to the slaughter-house. O, now I want the priest that spake to me: I now repent I told the pursuivant As 'twere triumphing at mine enemies, How they at Pomfret bloodily were butcher'd, And I myself secure in grace and favour. O Margaret, Margaret, now thy heavy curse Is lighted on poor Hastings' wretched head!
trg: Dispatch, my lord; the duke would be at dinner: Make a short shrift; he longs to see your head.

src: Dispatch, my lord; the duke would be at dinner: Make a short shrift; he longs to see your head.

trg: So dear I loved the man, that I must weep. I took him for the plainest harmless creature That breathed upon this earth a Christian; Made him my book wherein my soul recorded The history of all her secret thoughts: So smooth he daub'd his vice with show of virtue, That, his apparent open guilt omitted, I mean, his conversation with Shore's wife, He lived from all attainder of suspect.

trg: What, think You we are Turks or infidels? Or that we would, against the form of law, Proceed thus rashly to the villain's death, But that the extreme peril of the case, The peace of England and our persons' safety, Enforced us to this execution?

trg: Now, fair befall you! he deserved his death; And you my good lords, both have well proceeded, To warn false traitors from the like attempts. I never look'd for better at his hands, After he once fell in with Mistress Shore.

trg: Yet had not we determined he should die, Until your lordship came to see his death; Which now the loving haste of these our friends, Somewhat against our meaning, have prevented: Because, my lord, we would have had you heard The traitor speak, and timorously confess The manner and the purpose of his treason; That you might well have signified the same Unto the citizens, who haply may Misconstrue us in him and wail his death.

trg: Go, after, after, cousin Buckingham. The mayor towards Guildhall hies him in all post: There, at your meet'st advantage of the time, Infer the bastardy of Edward's children: Tell them how Edward put to death a citizen, Only for saying he would make his son Heir to the crown; meaning indeed his house, Which, by the sign thereof was termed so. Moreover, urge his hateful luxury And bestial appetite in change of lust; Which stretched to their servants, daughters, wives, Even where his lustful eye or savage heart, Without control, listed to make his prey. Nay, for a need, thus far come near my person: Tell them, when that my mother went with child Of that unsatiate Edward, noble York My princely father then had wars in France And, by just computation of the time, Found that the issue was not his begot; Which well appeared in his lineaments, Being nothing like the noble duke my father: But touch this sparingly, as 'twere far off, Because you know, my lord, my mother lives.

trg: This is the indictment of the good Lord Hastings; Which in a set hand fairly is engross'd, That it may be this day read over in Paul's. And mark how well the sequel hangs together: Eleven hours I spent to write it over, For yesternight by Catesby was it brought me; The precedent was full as long a-doing: And yet within these five hours lived Lord Hastings, Untainted, unexamined, free, at liberty Here's a good world the while! Why who's so gross, That seeth not this palpable device? Yet who's so blind, but says he sees it not? Bad is the world; and all will come to nought, When such bad dealings must be seen in thought.

trg: I did; with his contract with Lady Lucy, And his contract by deputy in France; The insatiate greediness of his desires, And his enforcement of the city wives; His tyranny for trifles; his own bastardy, As being got, your father then in France, His resemblance, being not like the duke; Withal I did infer your lineaments, Being the right idea of your father, Both in your form and nobleness of mind; Laid open all your victories in Scotland, Your dicipline in war, wisdom in peace, Your bounty, virtue, fair humility: Indeed, left nothing fitting for the purpose Untouch'd, or slightly handled, in discourse And when mine oratory grew to an end I bid them that did love their country's good Cry 'God save Richard, England's royal king!'

trg: Ah! and did they so?

src: Ah! and did they so?
trg: No, so God help me, they spake not a word; But, like dumb statues or breathing stones, Gazed each on other, and look'd deadly pale. Which when I saw, I reprehended them; And ask'd the mayor what meant this wilful silence: His answer was, the people were not wont To be spoke to but by the recorder. Then he was urged to tell my tale again, 'Thus saith the duke, thus hath the duke inferr'd;' But nothing spake in warrant from himself. When he had done, some followers of mine own, At the lower end of the hall, hurl'd up their caps, And some ten voices cried 'God save King Richard!' And thus I took the vantage of those few, 'Thanks, gentle citizens and friends,' quoth I; 'This general applause and loving shout Argues your wisdoms and your love to Richard:' And even here brake off, and came away.

trg: Ah, ha, my lord, this prince is not an Edward! He is not lolling on a lewd day-bed, But on his knees at meditation; Not dallying with a brace of courtezans, But meditating with two deep divines; Not sleeping, to engross his idle body, But praying, to enrich his watchful soul: Happy were England, would this gracious prince Take on himself the sovereignty thereof: But, sure, I fear, we shall ne'er win him to it.

trg: See, where he stands between two clergymen!

src: See, where he stands between two clergymen!
trg: Two props of virtue for a Christian prince, To stay him from the fall of vanity: And, see, a book of prayer in his hand, True ornaments to know a holy man. Famous Plantagenet, most gracious prince, Lend favourable ears to our request; And pardon us the interruption Of thy devotion and right Christian zeal.

trg: My lord, there needs no such apology: I rather do beseech you pardon me, Who, earnest in the service of my God, Neglect the visitation of my friends. But, leaving this, what is your grace's pleasure?

trg: Even that, I hope, which pleaseth God above, And all good men of this ungovern'd isle.

src: Even that, I hope, which pleaseth God above, And all good men of this ungovern'd isle.
trg: I do suspect I have done some offence That seems disgracious in the city's eyes, And that you come to reprehend my ignorance.

src: I do suspect I have done some offence That seems disgracious in the city's eyes, And that you come to reprehend my ignorance.
trg: You have, my lord: would it might please your grace, At our entreaties, to amend that fault!

src: You have, my lord: would it might please your grace, At our entreaties, to amend that fault!
trg: Else wherefore breathe I in a Christian land?

src: Else wherefore breathe I in a Christian land?
trg: Then know, it is your fault that you resign The supreme seat, the throne majestical, The scepter'd office of your ancestors, Your state of fortune and your due of birth, The lineal glory of your royal house, To the corruption of a blemished stock: Whilst, in the mildness of your sleepy thoughts, Which here we waken to our country's good, This noble isle doth want her proper limbs; Her face defaced with scars of infamy, Her royal stock graft with ignoble plants, And almost shoulder'd in the swallowing gulf Of blind forgetfulness and dark oblivion. Which to recure, we heartily solicit Your gracious self to take on you the charge And kingly government of this your land, Not as protector, steward, substitute, Or lowly factor for another's gain; But as successively from blood to blood, Your right of birth, your empery, your own. For this, consorted with the citizens, Your very worshipful and loving friends, And by their vehement instigation, In this just suit come I to move your grace.

trg: I know not whether to depart in silence, Or bitterly to speak in your reproof. Best fitteth my degree or your condition If not to answer, you might haply think Tongue-tied ambition, not replying, yielded To bear the golden yoke of sovereignty, Which fondly you would here impose on me; If to reprove you for this suit of yours, So season'd with your faithful love to me. Then, on the other side, I cheque'd my friends. Therefore, to speak, and to avoid the first, And then, in speaking, not to incur the last, Definitively thus I answer you. Your love deserves my thanks; but my desert Unmeritable shuns your high request. First if all obstacles were cut away, And that my path were even to the crown, As my ripe revenue and due by birth Yet so much is my poverty of spirit, So mighty and so many my defects, As I had rather hide me from my greatness, Being a bark to brook no mighty sea, Than in my greatness covet to be hid, And in the vapour of my glory smother'd. But, God be thank'd, there's no need of me, And much I need to help you, if need were; The royal tree hath left us royal fruit, Which, mellow'd by the stealing hours of time, Will well become the seat of majesty, And make, no doubt, us happy by his reign. On him I lay what you would lay on me, The right and fortune of his happy stars; Which God defend that I should wring from him!

trg: My lord, this argues conscience in your grace; But the respects thereof are nice and trivial, All circumstances well considered. You say that Edward is your brother's son: So say we too, but not by Edward's wife; For first he was contract to Lady Lucy-- Your mother lives a witness to that vow-- And afterward by substitute betroth'd To Bona, sister to the King of France. These both put by a poor petitioner, A care-crazed mother of a many children, A beauty-waning and distressed widow, Even in the afternoon of her best days, Made prize and purchase of his lustful eye, Seduced the pitch and height of all his thoughts To base declension and loathed bigamy By her, in his unlawful bed, he got This Edward, whom our manners term the prince. More bitterly could I expostulate, Save that, for reverence to some alive, I give a sparing limit to my tongue. Then, good my lord, take to your royal self This proffer'd benefit of dignity; If non to bless us and the land withal, Yet to draw forth your noble ancestry From the corruption of abusing times, Unto a lineal true-derived course.

trg: If you refuse it,--as, in love and zeal, Loath to depose the child, Your brother's son; As well we know your tenderness of heart And gentle, kind, effeminate remorse, Which we have noted in you to your kin, And egally indeed to all estates,-- Yet whether you accept our suit or no, Your brother's son shall never reign our king; But we will plant some other in the throne, To the disgrace and downfall of your house: And in this resolution here we leave you.-- Come, citizens: 'zounds! I'll entreat no more.

trg: Would you enforce me to a world of care? Well, call them again. I am not made of stone, But penetrable to your. kind entreats, Albeit against my conscience and my soul. Cousin of Buckingham, and you sage, grave men, Since you will buckle fortune on my back, To bear her burthen, whether I will or no, I must have patience to endure the load: But if black scandal or foul-faced reproach Attend the sequel of your imposition, Your mere enforcement shall acquittance me From all the impure blots and stains thereof; For God he knows, and you may partly see, How far I am from the desire thereof.

trg: No! why?  When he that is my husband now Came to me, as I follow'd Henry's corse, When scarce the blood was well wash'd from his hands Which issued from my other angel husband And that dead saint which then I weeping follow'd; O, when, I say, I look'd on Richard's face, This was my wish: 'Be thou,' quoth I, ' accursed, For making me, so young, so old a widow! And, when thou wed'st, let sorrow haunt thy bed; And be thy wife--if any be so mad-- As miserable by the life of thee As thou hast made me by my dear lord's death! Lo, ere I can repeat this curse again, Even in so short a space, my woman's heart Grossly grew captive to his honey words And proved the subject of my own soul's curse, Which ever since hath kept my eyes from rest; For never yet one hour in his bed Have I enjoy'd the golden dew of sleep, But have been waked by his timorous dreams. Besides, he hates me for my father Warwick; And will, no doubt, shortly be rid of me.

I say again, give out That Anne my wife is sick and like to die: About it; for it stands me much upon, To stop all hopes whose growth may damage me. trg: The tyrannous and bloody deed is done. The most arch of piteous massacre That ever yet this land was guilty of. Dighton and Forrest, whom I did suborn To do this ruthless piece of butchery, Although they were flesh'd villains, bloody dogs, Melting with tenderness and kind compassion Wept like two children in their deaths' sad stories. 'Lo, thus' quoth Dighton, 'lay those tender babes:' 'Thus, thus,' quoth Forrest, 'girdling one another Within their innocent alabaster arms: Their lips were four red roses on a stalk, Which in their summer beauty kiss'd each other. A book of prayers on their pillow lay; Which once,' quoth Forrest, 'almost changed my mind; But O! the devil'--there the villain stopp'd Whilst Dighton thus told on: 'We smothered The most replenished sweet work of nature, That from the prime creation e'er she framed.' Thus both are gone with conscience and remorse; They could not speak; and so I left them both, To bring this tidings to the bloody king. And here he comes. All hail, my sovereign liege!

Now, for I know the Breton Richmond aims At young Elizabeth, my brother's daughter, And, by that knot, looks proudly o'er the crown, To her I go, a jolly thriving wooer.

trg: If ancient sorrow be most reverend, Give mine the benefit of seniory, And let my woes frown on the upper hand. trg: Thou hadst a Clarence too, and Richard kill'd him. From forth the kennel of thy womb hath crept A hell-hound that doth hunt us all to death: That dog, that had his teeth before his eyes, To worry lambs and lap their gentle blood, That foul defacer of God's handiwork, That excellent grand tyrant of the earth, That reigns in galled eyes of weeping souls, Thy womb let loose, to chase us to our graves. O upright, just, and true-disposing God, How do I thank thee, that this carnal cur Preys on the issue of his mother's body, And makes her pew-fellow with others' moan!

trg: Bear with me; I am hungry for revenge, And now I cloy me with beholding it. Thy Edward he is dead, that stabb'd my Edward: Thy other Edward dead, to quit my Edward; Young York he is but boot, because both they Match not the high perfection of my loss: Thy Clarence he is dead that kill'd my Edward; And the beholders of this tragic play, The adulterate Hastings, Rivers, Vaughan, Grey, Untimely smother'd in their dusky graves. Richard yet lives, hell's black intelligencer, Only reserved their factor, to buy souls And send them thither: but at hand, at hand, Ensues his piteous and unpitied end: Earth gapes, hell burns, fiends roar, saints pray. To have him suddenly convey'd away. Cancel his bond of life, dear God, I prey, That I may live to say, The dog is dead!
