trg: Say thou wilt course; thy greyhounds are as swift As breathed stags, ay, fleeter than the roe.

src: Say thou wilt course; thy greyhounds are as swift As breathed stags, ay, fleeter than the roe.
trg: Dost thou love pictures? we will fetch thee straight Adonis painted by a running brook, And Cytherea all in sedges hid, Which seem to move and wanton with her breath, Even as the waving sedges play with wind.

src: Dost thou love pictures? we will fetch thee straight Adonis painted by a running brook, And Cytherea all in sedges hid, Which seem to move and wanton with her breath, Even as the waving sedges play with wind.
trg: We'll show thee Io as she was a maid, And how she was beguiled and surprised, As lively painted as the deed was done.

src: We'll show thee Io as she was a maid, And how she was beguiled and surprised, As lively painted as the deed was done.
trg: Or Daphne roaming through a thorny wood, Scratching her legs that one shall swear she bleeds, And at that sight shall sad Apollo weep, So workmanly the blood and tears are drawn.

src: Or Daphne roaming through a thorny wood, Scratching her legs that one shall swear she bleeds, And at that sight shall sad Apollo weep, So workmanly the blood and tears are drawn.
trg: Thou art a lord, and nothing but a lord: Thou hast a lady far more beautiful Than any woman in this waning age.

src: Thou art a lord, and nothing but a lord: Thou hast a lady far more beautiful Than any woman in this waning age.
trg: And till the tears that she hath shed for thee Like envious floods o'er-run her lovely face, She was the fairest creature in the world; And yet she is inferior to none.

src: And till the tears that she hath shed for thee Like envious floods o'er-run her lovely face, She was the fairest creature in the world; And yet she is inferior to none.
trg: Am I a lord? and have I such a lady? Or do I dream? or have I dream'd till now? I do not sleep: I see, I hear, I speak; I smell sweet savours and I feel soft things: Upon my life, I am a lord indeed And not a tinker nor Christophero Sly. Well, bring our lady hither to our sight; And once again, a pot o' the smallest ale.

src: Am I a lord? and have I such a lady? Or do I dream? or have I dream'd till now? I do not sleep: I see, I hear, I speak; I smell sweet savours and I feel soft things: Upon my life, I am a lord indeed And not a tinker nor Christophero Sly. Well, bring our lady hither to our sight; And once again, a pot o' the smallest ale.
trg: Will't please your mightiness to wash your hands? O, how we joy to see your wit restored! O, that once more you knew but what you are! These fifteen years you have been in a dream; Or when you waked, so waked as if you slept.

src: Will't please your mightiness to wash your hands? O, how we joy to see your wit restored! O, that once more you knew but what you are! These fifteen years you have been in a dream; Or when you waked, so waked as if you slept.
trg: These fifteen years! by my fay, a goodly nap. But did I never speak of all that time?

src: These fifteen years! by my fay, a goodly nap. But did I never speak of all that time?
trg: O, yes, my lord, but very idle words: For though you lay here in this goodly chamber, Yet would you say ye were beaten out of door; And rail upon the hostess of the house; And say you would present her at the leet, Because she brought stone jugs and no seal'd quarts: Sometimes you would call out for Cicely Hacket.

src: O, yes, my lord, but very idle words: For though you lay here in this goodly chamber, Yet would you say ye were beaten out of door; And rail upon the hostess of the house; And say you would present her at the leet, Because she brought stone jugs and no seal'd quarts: Sometimes you would call out for Cicely Hacket.
trg: Ay, the woman's maid of the house.

src: Ay, the woman's maid of the house.
trg: Why, sir, you know no house nor no such maid, Nor no such men as you have reckon'd up, As Stephen Sly and did John Naps of Greece And Peter Turph and Henry Pimpernell And twenty more such names and men as these Which never were nor no man ever saw.

src: Why, sir, you know no house nor no such maid, Nor no such men as you have reckon'd up, As Stephen Sly and did John Naps of Greece And Peter Turph and Henry Pimpernell And twenty more such names and men as these Which never were nor no man ever saw.
trg: Now Lord be thanked for my good amends!

src: Now Lord be thanked for my good amends!
trg: Amen.

src: Amen.
trg: I thank thee: thou shalt not lose by it.

src: I thank thee: thou shalt not lose by it.
trg: How fares my noble lord?

src: How fares my noble lord?
trg: Marry, I fare well for here is cheer enough. Where is my wife?

src: Marry, I fare well for here is cheer enough. Where is my wife?
trg: Here, noble lord: what is thy will with her?

src: Here, noble lord: what is thy will with her?
trg: Are you my wife and will not call me husband? My men should call me 'lord:' I am your goodman.

src: Are you my wife and will not call me husband? My men should call me 'lord:' I am your goodman.
trg: My husband and my lord, my lord and husband; I am your wife in all obedience.

src: My husband and my lord, my lord and husband; I am your wife in all obedience.
trg: I know it well. What must I call her?

src: I know it well. What must I call her?
trg: Madam.

src: Madam.
trg: Al'ce madam, or Joan madam?

src: Al'ce madam, or Joan madam?
trg: 'Madam,' and nothing else: so lords call ladies.

src: 'Madam,' and nothing else: so lords call ladies.
trg: Madam wife, they say that I have dream'd And slept above some fifteen year or more.

src: Madam wife, they say that I have dream'd And slept above some fifteen year or more.
trg: Ay, and the time seems thirty unto me, Being all this time abandon'd from your bed.

src: Ay, and the time seems thirty unto me, Being all this time abandon'd from your bed.
trg: 'Tis much. Servants, leave me and her alone. Madam, undress you and come now to bed.

src: 'Tis much. Servants, leave me and her alone. Madam, undress you and come now to bed.
trg: Thrice noble lord, let me entreat of you To pardon me yet for a night or two, Or, if not so, until the sun be set: For your physicians have expressly charged, In peril to incur your former malady, That I should yet absent me from your bed: I hope this reason stands for my excuse.

src: Thrice noble lord, let me entreat of you To pardon me yet for a night or two, Or, if not so, until the sun be set: For your physicians have expressly charged, In peril to incur your former malady, That I should yet absent me from your bed: I hope this reason stands for my excuse.
trg: Ay, it stands so that I may hardly tarry so long. But I would be loath to fall into my dreams again: I will therefore tarry in despite of the flesh and the blood.

src: Ay, it stands so that I may hardly tarry so long. But I would be loath to fall into my dreams again: I will therefore tarry in despite of the flesh and the blood.
trg: Your honour's players, heating your amendment, Are come to play a pleasant comedy; For so your doctors hold it very meet, Seeing too much sadness hath congeal'd your blood, And melancholy is the nurse of frenzy: Therefore they thought it good you hear a play And frame your mind to mirth and merriment, Which bars a thousand harms and lengthens life.

src: Your honour's players, heating your amendment, Are come to play a pleasant comedy; For so your doctors hold it very meet, Seeing too much sadness hath congeal'd your blood, And melancholy is the nurse of frenzy: Therefore they thought it good you hear a play And frame your mind to mirth and merriment, Which bars a thousand harms and lengthens life.
trg: Marry, I will, let them play it. Is not a comondy a Christmas gambold or a tumbling-trick?

src: Marry, I will, let them play it. Is not a comondy a Christmas gambold or a tumbling-trick?
trg: No, my good lord; it is more pleasing stuff.

src: No, my good lord; it is more pleasing stuff.
trg: What, household stuff?

src: What, household stuff?
trg: It is a kind of history.

src: It is a kind of history.
trg: Well, well see't. Come, madam wife, sit by my side and let the world slip: we shall ne'er be younger.

src: Well, well see't. Come, madam wife, sit by my side and let the world slip: we shall ne'er be younger.
trg: Tranio, since for the great desire I had To see fair Padua, nursery of arts, I am arrived for fruitful Lombardy, The pleasant garden of great Italy; And by my father's love and leave am arm'd With his good will and thy good company, My trusty servant, well approved in all, Here let us breathe and haply institute A course of learning and ingenious studies. Pisa renown'd for grave citizens Gave me my being and my father first, A merchant of great traffic through the world, Vincetino come of Bentivolii. Vincetino's son brought up in Florence It shall become to serve all hopes conceived, To deck his fortune with his virtuous deeds: And therefore, Tranio, for the time I study, Virtue and that part of philosophy Will I apply that treats of happiness By virtue specially to be achieved. Tell me thy mind; for I have Pisa left And am to Padua come, as he that leaves A shallow plash to plunge him in the deep And with satiety seeks to quench his thirst.

src: Tranio, since for the great desire I had To see fair Padua, nursery of arts, I am arrived for fruitful Lombardy, The pleasant garden of great Italy; And by my father's love and leave am arm'd With his good will and thy good company, My trusty servant, well approved in all, Here let us breathe and haply institute A course of learning and ingenious studies. Pisa renown'd for grave citizens Gave me my being and my father first, A merchant of great traffic through the world, Vincetino come of Bentivolii. Vincetino's son brought up in Florence It shall become to serve all hopes conceived, To deck his fortune with his virtuous deeds: And therefore, Tranio, for the time I study, Virtue and that part of philosophy Will I apply that treats of happiness By virtue specially to be achieved. Tell me thy mind; for I have Pisa left And am to Padua come, as he that leaves A shallow plash to plunge him in the deep And with satiety seeks to quench his thirst.
trg: Mi perdonato, gentle master mine, I am in all affected as yourself; Glad that you thus continue your resolve To suck the sweets of sweet philosophy. Only, good master, while we do admire This virtue and this moral discipline, Let's be no stoics nor no stocks, I pray; Or so devote to Aristotle's cheques As Ovid be an outcast quite abjured: Balk logic with acquaintance that you have And practise rhetoric in your common talk; Music and poesy use to quicken you; The mathematics and the metaphysics, Fall to them as you find your stomach serves you; No profit grows where is no pleasure ta'en: In brief, sir, study what you most affect.

src: Mi perdonato, gentle master mine, I am in all affected as yourself; Glad that you thus continue your resolve To suck the sweets of sweet philosophy. Only, good master, while we do admire This virtue and this moral discipline, Let's be no stoics nor no stocks, I pray; Or so devote to Aristotle's cheques As Ovid be an outcast quite abjured: Balk logic with acquaintance that you have And practise rhetoric in your common talk; Music and poesy use to quicken you; The mathematics and the metaphysics, Fall to them as you find your stomach serves you; No profit grows where is no pleasure ta'en: In brief, sir, study what you most affect.
trg: Gramercies, Tranio, well dost thou advise. If, Biondello, thou wert come ashore, We could at once put us in readiness, And take a lodging fit to entertain Such friends as time in Padua shall beget. But stay a while: what company is this?

src: Gramercies, Tranio, well dost thou advise. If, Biondello, thou wert come ashore, We could at once put us in readiness, And take a lodging fit to entertain Such friends as time in Padua shall beget. But stay a while: what company is this?
trg: Master, some show to welcome us to town.

src: Master, some show to welcome us to town.
trg: Gentlemen, importune me no farther, For how I firmly am resolved you know; That is, not bestow my youngest daughter Before I have a husband for the elder: If either of you both love Katharina, Because I know you well and love you well, Leave shall you have to court her at your pleasure.

src: Gentlemen, importune me no farther, For how I firmly am resolved you know; That is, not bestow my youngest daughter Before I have a husband for the elder: If either of you both love Katharina, Because I know you well and love you well, Leave shall you have to court her at your pleasure.

trg: I pray you, sir, is it your will To make a stale of me amongst these mates?

src: I pray you, sir, is it your will To make a stale of me amongst these mates?
trg: Mates, maid! how mean you that? no mates for you, Unless you were of gentler, milder mould.

src: Mates, maid! how mean you that? no mates for you, Unless you were of gentler, milder mould.
trg: I'faith, sir, you shall never need to fear: I wis it is not half way to her heart; But if it were, doubt not her care should be To comb your noddle with a three-legg'd stool And paint your face and use you like a fool.

src: I'faith, sir, you shall never need to fear: I wis it is not half way to her heart; But if it were, doubt not her care should be To comb your noddle with a three-legg'd stool And paint your face and use you like a fool.
trg: From all such devils, good Lord deliver us!

src: From all such devils, good Lord deliver us!
trg: And me too, good Lord!

src: And me too, good Lord!
trg: Hush, master! here's some good pastime toward: That wench is stark mad or wonderful froward.

src: Hush, master! here's some good pastime toward: That wench is stark mad or wonderful froward.
trg: But in the other's silence do I see Maid's mild behavior and sobriety. Peace, Tranio!

src: But in the other's silence do I see Maid's mild behavior and sobriety. Peace, Tranio!
trg: Well said, master; mum! and gaze your fill.

src: Well said, master; mum! and gaze your fill.
trg: Gentlemen, that I may soon make good What I have said, Bianca, get you in: And let it not displease thee, good Bianca, For I will love thee ne'er the less, my girl.

src: Gentlemen, that I may soon make good What I have said, Bianca, get you in: And let it not displease thee, good Bianca, For I will love thee ne'er the less, my girl.
trg: A pretty peat! it is best Put finger in the eye, an she knew why.

src: A pretty peat! it is best Put finger in the eye, an she knew why.
trg: Sister, content you in my discontent. Sir, to your pleasure humbly I subscribe: My books and instruments shall be my company, On them to took and practise by myself.

src: Sister, content you in my discontent. Sir, to your pleasure humbly I subscribe: My books and instruments shall be my company, On them to took and practise by myself.
trg: Hark, Tranio! thou may'st hear Minerva speak.

src: Hark, Tranio! thou may'st hear Minerva speak.
trg: Signior Baptista, will you be so strange? Sorry am I that our good will effects Bianca's grief.

src: Signior Baptista, will you be so strange? Sorry am I that our good will effects Bianca's grief.
trg: Why will you mew her up, Signior Baptista, for this fiend of hell, And make her bear the penance of her tongue?

src: Why will you mew her up, Signior Baptista, for this fiend of hell, And make her bear the penance of her tongue?
trg: Gentlemen, content ye; I am resolved: Go in, Bianca: And for I know she taketh most delight In music, instruments and poetry, Schoolmasters will I keep within my house, Fit to instruct her youth. If you, Hortensio, Or Signior Gremio, you, know any such, Prefer them hither; for to cunning men I will be very kind, and liberal To mine own children in good bringing up: And so farewell. Katharina, you may stay; For I have more to commune with Bianca.

src: Gentlemen, content ye; I am resolved: Go in, Bianca: And for I know she taketh most delight In music, instruments and poetry, Schoolmasters will I keep within my house, Fit to instruct her youth. If you, Hortensio, Or Signior Gremio, you, know any such, Prefer them hither; for to cunning men I will be very kind, and liberal To mine own children in good bringing up: And so farewell. Katharina, you may stay; For I have more to commune with Bianca.
trg: Why, and I trust I may go too, may I not? What, shall I be appointed hours; as though, belike, I knew not what to take and what to leave, ha?

src: Why, and I trust I may go too, may I not? What, shall I be appointed hours; as though, belike, I knew not what to take and what to leave, ha?
trg: You may go to the devil's dam: your gifts are so good, here's none will hold you. Their love is not so great, Hortensio, but we may blow our nails together, and fast it fairly out: our cakes dough on both sides. Farewell: yet for the love I bear my sweet Bianca, if I can by any means light on a fit man to teach her that wherein she delights, I will wish him to her father.

src: You may go to the devil's dam: your gifts are so good, here's none will hold you. Their love is not so great, Hortensio, but we may blow our nails together, and fast it fairly out: our cakes dough on both sides. Farewell: yet for the love I bear my sweet Bianca, if I can by any means light on a fit man to teach her that wherein she delights, I will wish him to her father.
trg: So will I, Signior Gremio: but a word, I pray. Though the nature of our quarrel yet never brooked parle, know now, upon advice, it toucheth us both, that we may yet again have access to our fair mistress and be happy rivals in Bianco's love, to labour and effect one thing specially.

src: So will I, Signior Gremio: but a word, I pray. Though the nature of our quarrel yet never brooked parle, know now, upon advice, it toucheth us both, that we may yet again have access to our fair mistress and be happy rivals in Bianco's love, to labour and effect one thing specially.
trg: What's that, I pray?

src: What's that, I pray?
trg: Marry, sir, to get a husband for her sister.

src: Marry, sir, to get a husband for her sister.
trg: A husband! a devil.

src: A husband! a devil.
trg: I say, a husband.

src: I say, a husband.
trg: I say, a devil. Thinkest thou, Hortensio, though her father be very rich, any man is so very a fool to be married to hell?

src: I say, a devil. Thinkest thou, Hortensio, though her father be very rich, any man is so very a fool to be married to hell?
trg: Tush, Gremio, though it pass your patience and mine to endure her loud alarums, why, man, there be good fellows in the world, an a man could light on them, would take her with all faults, and money enough.

src: Tush, Gremio, though it pass your patience and mine to endure her loud alarums, why, man, there be good fellows in the world, an a man could light on them, would take her with all faults, and money enough.
trg: I cannot tell; but I had as lief take her dowry with this condition, to be whipped at the high cross every morning.

src: I cannot tell; but I had as lief take her dowry with this condition, to be whipped at the high cross every morning.
trg: Faith, as you say, there's small choice in rotten apples. But come; since this bar in law makes us friends, it shall be so far forth friendly maintained all by helping Baptista's eldest daughter to a husband we set his youngest free for a husband, and then have to't a fresh. Sweet Bianca! Happy man be his dole! He that runs fastest gets the ring. How say you, Signior Gremio?

src: Faith, as you say, there's small choice in rotten apples. But come; since this bar in law makes us friends, it shall be so far forth friendly maintained all by helping Baptista's eldest daughter to a husband we set his youngest free for a husband, and then have to't a fresh. Sweet Bianca! Happy man be his dole! He that runs fastest gets the ring. How say you, Signior Gremio?
trg: I am agreed; and would I had given him the best horse in Padua to begin his wooing that would thoroughly woo her, wed her and bed her and rid the house of her! Come on.

src: I am agreed; and would I had given him the best horse in Padua to begin his wooing that would thoroughly woo her, wed her and bed her and rid the house of her! Come on.
trg: I pray, sir, tell me, is it possible That love should of a sudden take such hold?

src: I pray, sir, tell me, is it possible That love should of a sudden take such hold?
trg: O Tranio, till I found it to be true, I never thought it possible or likely; But see, while idly I stood looking on, I found the effect of love in idleness: And now in plainness do confess to thee, That art to me as secret and as dear As Anna to the queen of Carthage was, Tranio, I burn, I pine, I perish, Tranio, If I achieve not this young modest girl. Counsel me, Tranio, for I know thou canst; Assist me, Tranio, for I know thou wilt.

src: O Tranio, till I found it to be true, I never thought it possible or likely; But see, while idly I stood looking on, I found the effect of love in idleness: And now in plainness do confess to thee, That art to me as secret and as dear As Anna to the queen of Carthage was, Tranio, I burn, I pine, I perish, Tranio, If I achieve not this young modest girl. Counsel me, Tranio, for I know thou canst; Assist me, Tranio, for I know thou wilt.
trg: Master, it is no time to chide you now; Affection is not rated from the heart: If love have touch'd you, nought remains but so, 'Redime te captum quam queas minimo.'

src: Master, it is no time to chide you now; Affection is not rated from the heart: If love have touch'd you, nought remains but so, 'Redime te captum quam queas minimo.'
trg: Gramercies, lad, go forward; this contents: The rest will comfort, for thy counsel's sound.

src: Gramercies, lad, go forward; this contents: The rest will comfort, for thy counsel's sound.
trg: Master, you look'd so longly on the maid, Perhaps you mark'd not what's the pith of all.

src: Master, you look'd so longly on the maid, Perhaps you mark'd not what's the pith of all.
trg: O yes, I saw sweet beauty in her face, Such as the daughter of Agenor had, That made great Jove to humble him to her hand. When with his knees he kiss'd the Cretan strand.

src: O yes, I saw sweet beauty in her face, Such as the daughter of Agenor had, That made great Jove to humble him to her hand. When with his knees he kiss'd the Cretan strand.
trg: Saw you no more? mark'd you not how her sister Began to scold and raise up such a storm That mortal ears might hardly endure the din?

src: Saw you no more? mark'd you not how her sister Began to scold and raise up such a storm That mortal ears might hardly endure the din?
trg: Tranio, I saw her coral lips to move And with her breath she did perfume the air: Sacred and sweet was all I saw in her.

src: Tranio, I saw her coral lips to move And with her breath she did perfume the air: Sacred and sweet was all I saw in her.
trg: Nay, then, 'tis time to stir him from his trance. I pray, awake, sir: if you love the maid, Bend thoughts and wits to achieve her. Thus it stands: Her eldest sister is so curst and shrewd That till the father rid his hands of her, Master, your love must live a maid at home; And therefore has he closely mew'd her up, Because she will not be annoy'd with suitors.

src: Nay, then, 'tis time to stir him from his trance. I pray, awake, sir: if you love the maid, Bend thoughts and wits to achieve her. Thus it stands: Her eldest sister is so curst and shrewd That till the father rid his hands of her, Master, your love must live a maid at home; And therefore has he closely mew'd her up, Because she will not be annoy'd with suitors.
trg: Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father's he! But art thou not advised, he took some care To get her cunning schoolmasters to instruct her?

src: Ah, Tranio, what a cruel father's he! But art thou not advised, he took some care To get her cunning schoolmasters to instruct her?
trg: Ay, marry, am I, sir; and now 'tis plotted.

src: Ay, marry, am I, sir; and now 'tis plotted.
trg: I have it, Tranio.

src: I have it, Tranio.
trg: Master, for my hand, Both our inventions meet and jump in one.

src: Master, for my hand, Both our inventions meet and jump in one.
trg: Tell me thine first.

src: Tell me thine first.
trg: You will be schoolmaster And undertake the teaching of the maid: That's your device.

src: You will be schoolmaster And undertake the teaching of the maid: That's your device.
trg: It is: may it be done?

src: It is: may it be done?
trg: Not possible; for who shall bear your part, And be in Padua here Vincentio's son, Keep house and ply his book, welcome his friends, Visit his countrymen and banquet them?

src: Not possible; for who shall bear your part, And be in Padua here Vincentio's son, Keep house and ply his book, welcome his friends, Visit his countrymen and banquet them?
trg: Basta; content thee, for I have it full. We have not yet been seen in any house, Nor can we lie distinguish'd by our faces For man or master; then it follows thus; Thou shalt be master, Tranio, in my stead, Keep house and port and servants as I should: I will some other be, some Florentine, Some Neapolitan, or meaner man of Pisa. 'Tis hatch'd and shall be so: Tranio, at once Uncase thee; take my colour'd hat and cloak: When Biondello comes, he waits on thee; But I will charm him first to keep his tongue.

src: Basta; content thee, for I have it full. We have not yet been seen in any house, Nor can we lie distinguish'd by our faces For man or master; then it follows thus; Thou shalt be master, Tranio, in my stead, Keep house and port and servants as I should: I will some other be, some Florentine, Some Neapolitan, or meaner man of Pisa. 'Tis hatch'd and shall be so: Tranio, at once Uncase thee; take my colour'd hat and cloak: When Biondello comes, he waits on thee; But I will charm him first to keep his tongue.
trg: So had you need. In brief, sir, sith it your pleasure is, And I am tied to be obedient; For so your father charged me at our parting, 'Be serviceable to my son,' quoth he, Although I think 'twas in another sense; I am content to be Lucentio, Because so well I love Lucentio.

src: So had you need. In brief, sir, sith it your pleasure is, And I am tied to be obedient; For so your father charged me at our parting, 'Be serviceable to my son,' quoth he, Although I think 'twas in another sense; I am content to be Lucentio, Because so well I love Lucentio.
trg: Tranio, be so, because Lucentio loves: And let me be a slave, to achieve that maid Whose sudden sight hath thrall'd my wounded eye. Here comes the rogue. Sirrah, where have you been?

src: Tranio, be so, because Lucentio loves: And let me be a slave, to achieve that maid Whose sudden sight hath thrall'd my wounded eye. Here comes the rogue. Sirrah, where have you been?
trg: Where have I been! Nay, how now! where are you? Master, has my fellow Tranio stolen your clothes? Or you stolen his? or both? pray, what's the news?

src: Where have I been! Nay, how now! where are you? Master, has my fellow Tranio stolen your clothes? Or you stolen his? or both? pray, what's the news?
trg: Sirrah, come hither: 'tis no time to jest, And therefore frame your manners to the time. Your fellow Tranio here, to save my life, Puts my apparel and my countenance on, And I for my escape have put on his; For in a quarrel since I came ashore I kill'd a man and fear I was descried: Wait you on him, I charge you, as becomes, While I make way from hence to save my life: You understand me?

src: Sirrah, come hither: 'tis no time to jest, And therefore frame your manners to the time. Your fellow Tranio here, to save my life, Puts my apparel and my countenance on, And I for my escape have put on his; For in a quarrel since I came ashore I kill'd a man and fear I was descried: Wait you on him, I charge you, as becomes, While I make way from hence to save my life: You understand me?
trg: I, sir! ne'er a whit.

src: I, sir! ne'er a whit.
trg: And not a jot of Tranio in your mouth: Tranio is changed into Lucentio.

src: And not a jot of Tranio in your mouth: Tranio is changed into Lucentio.
trg: The better for him: would I were so too!

src: The better for him: would I were so too!
trg: So could I, faith, boy, to have the next wish after, That Lucentio indeed had Baptista's youngest daughter. But, sirrah, not for my sake, but your master's, I advise You use your manners discreetly in all kind of companies: When I am alone, why, then I am Tranio; But in all places else your master Lucentio.

src: So could I, faith, boy, to have the next wish after, That Lucentio indeed had Baptista's youngest daughter. But, sirrah, not for my sake, but your master's, I advise You use your manners discreetly in all kind of companies: When I am alone, why, then I am Tranio; But in all places else your master Lucentio.
trg: Tranio, let's go: one thing more rests, that thyself execute, to make one among these wooers: if thou ask me why, sufficeth, my reasons are both good and weighty.

src: Tranio, let's go: one thing more rests, that thyself execute, to make one among these wooers: if thou ask me why, sufficeth, my reasons are both good and weighty.
trg: My lord, you nod; you do not mind the play.

src: My lord, you nod; you do not mind the play.
trg: Yes, by Saint Anne, do I. A good matter, surely: comes there any more of it?

src: Yes, by Saint Anne, do I. A good matter, surely: comes there any more of it?
trg: My lord, 'tis but begun.

src: My lord, 'tis but begun.
trg: 'Tis a very excellent piece of work, madam lady: would 'twere done!

src: 'Tis a very excellent piece of work, madam lady: would 'twere done!
trg: Verona, for a while I take my leave, To see my friends in Padua, but of all My best beloved and approved friend, Hortensio; and I trow this is his house. Here, sirrah Grumio; knock, I say.

src: Verona, for a while I take my leave, To see my friends in Padua, but of all My best beloved and approved friend, Hortensio; and I trow this is his house. Here, sirrah Grumio; knock, I say.
trg: Knock, sir! whom should I knock? is there man has rebused your worship?

src: Knock, sir! whom should I knock? is there man has rebused your worship?
trg: Villain, I say, knock me here soundly.

src: Villain, I say, knock me here soundly.
trg: Knock you here, sir! why, sir, what am I, sir, that I should knock you here, sir?

src: Knock you here, sir! why, sir, what am I, sir, that I should knock you here, sir?
trg: Villain, I say, knock me at this gate And rap me well, or I'll knock your knave's pate.

src: Villain, I say, knock me at this gate And rap me well, or I'll knock your knave's pate.
trg: My master is grown quarrelsome. I should knock you first, And then I know after who comes by the worst.

src: My master is grown quarrelsome. I should knock you first, And then I know after who comes by the worst.
trg: Will it not be? Faith, sirrah, an you'll not knock, I'll ring it; I'll try how you can sol, fa, and sing it.

src: Will it not be? Faith, sirrah, an you'll not knock, I'll ring it; I'll try how you can sol, fa, and sing it.
trg: Help, masters, help! my master is mad.

src: Help, masters, help! my master is mad.
trg: Now, knock when I bid you, sirrah villain!

src: Now, knock when I bid you, sirrah villain!
trg: How now! what's the matter? My old friend Grumio! and my good friend Petruchio! How do you all at Verona?

src: How now! what's the matter? My old friend Grumio! and my good friend Petruchio! How do you all at Verona?
trg: Signior Hortensio, come you to part the fray? 'Con tutto il cuore, ben trovato,' may I say.

src: Signior Hortensio, come you to part the fray? 'Con tutto il cuore, ben trovato,' may I say.
trg: 'Alla nostra casa ben venuto, molto honorato signor mio Petruchio.' Rise, Grumio, rise: we will compound this quarrel.

src: 'Alla nostra casa ben venuto, molto honorato signor mio Petruchio.' Rise, Grumio, rise: we will compound this quarrel.
trg: Nay, 'tis no matter, sir, what he 'leges in Latin. if this be not a lawful case for me to leave his service, look you, sir, he bid me knock him and rap him soundly, sir: well, was it fit for a servant to use his master so, being perhaps, for aught I see, two and thirty, a pip out? Whom would to God I had well knock'd at first, Then had not Grumio come by the worst.

src: Nay, 'tis no matter, sir, what he 'leges in Latin. if this be not a lawful case for me to leave his service, look you, sir, he bid me knock him and rap him soundly, sir: well, was it fit for a servant to use his master so, being perhaps, for aught I see, two and thirty, a pip out? Whom would to God I had well knock'd at first, Then had not Grumio come by the worst.
trg: A senseless villain! Good Hortensio, I bade the rascal knock upon your gate And could not get him for my heart to do it.

src: A senseless villain! Good Hortensio, I bade the rascal knock upon your gate And could not get him for my heart to do it.
trg: Knock at the gate! O heavens! Spake you not these words plain, 'Sirrah, knock me here, rap me here, knock me well, and knock me soundly'? And come you now with, 'knocking at the gate'?

src: Knock at the gate! O heavens! Spake you not these words plain, 'Sirrah, knock me here, rap me here, knock me well, and knock me soundly'? And come you now with, 'knocking at the gate'?
trg: Sirrah, be gone, or talk not, I advise you.

src: Sirrah, be gone, or talk not, I advise you.
trg: Petruchio, patience; I am Grumio's pledge: Why, this's a heavy chance 'twixt him and you, Your ancient, trusty, pleasant servant Grumio. And tell me now, sweet friend, what happy gale Blows you to Padua here from old Verona?

src: Petruchio, patience; I am Grumio's pledge: Why, this's a heavy chance 'twixt him and you, Your ancient, trusty, pleasant servant Grumio. And tell me now, sweet friend, what happy gale Blows you to Padua here from old Verona?
trg: Such wind as scatters young men through the world, To seek their fortunes farther than at home Where small experience grows. But in a few, Signior Hortensio, thus it stands with me: Antonio, my father, is deceased; And I have thrust myself into this maze, Haply to wive and thrive as best I may: Crowns in my purse I have and goods at home, And so am come abroad to see the world.

src: Such wind as scatters young men through the world, To seek their fortunes farther than at home Where small experience grows. But in a few, Signior Hortensio, thus it stands with me: Antonio, my father, is deceased; And I have thrust myself into this maze, Haply to wive and thrive as best I may: Crowns in my purse I have and goods at home, And so am come abroad to see the world.
trg: Petruchio, shall I then come roundly to thee And wish thee to a shrewd ill-favour'd wife? Thou'ldst thank me but a little for my counsel: And yet I'll promise thee she shall be rich And very rich: but thou'rt too much my friend, And I'll not wish thee to her.

src: Petruchio, shall I then come roundly to thee And wish thee to a shrewd ill-favour'd wife? Thou'ldst thank me but a little for my counsel: And yet I'll promise thee she shall be rich And very rich: but thou'rt too much my friend, And I'll not wish thee to her.
trg: Signior Hortensio, 'twixt such friends as we Few words suffice; and therefore, if thou know One rich enough to be Petruchio's wife, As wealth is burden of my wooing dance, Be she as foul as was Florentius' love, As old as Sibyl and as curst and shrewd As Socrates' Xanthippe, or a worse, She moves me not, or not removes, at least, Affection's edge in me, were she as rough As are the swelling Adriatic seas: I come to wive it wealthily in Padua; If wealthily, then happily in Padua.

src: Signior Hortensio, 'twixt such friends as we Few words suffice; and therefore, if thou know One rich enough to be Petruchio's wife, As wealth is burden of my wooing dance, Be she as foul as was Florentius' love, As old as Sibyl and as curst and shrewd As Socrates' Xanthippe, or a worse, She moves me not, or not removes, at least, Affection's edge in me, were she as rough As are the swelling Adriatic seas: I come to wive it wealthily in Padua; If wealthily, then happily in Padua.
trg: Nay, look you, sir, he tells you flatly what his mind is: Why give him gold enough and marry him to a puppet or an aglet-baby; or an old trot with ne'er a tooth in her head, though she have as many diseases as two and fifty horses: why, nothing comes amiss, so money comes withal.

src: Nay, look you, sir, he tells you flatly what his mind is: Why give him gold enough and marry him to a puppet or an aglet-baby; or an old trot with ne'er a tooth in her head, though she have as many diseases as two and fifty horses: why, nothing comes amiss, so money comes withal.
trg: Petruchio, since we are stepp'd thus far in, I will continue that I broach'd in jest. I can, Petruchio, help thee to a wife With wealth enough and young and beauteous, Brought up as best becomes a gentlewoman: Her only fault, and that is faults enough, Is that she is intolerable curst And shrewd and froward, so beyond all measure That, were my state far worser than it is, I would not wed her for a mine of gold.

src: Petruchio, since we are stepp'd thus far in, I will continue that I broach'd in jest. I can, Petruchio, help thee to a wife With wealth enough and young and beauteous, Brought up as best becomes a gentlewoman: Her only fault, and that is faults enough, Is that she is intolerable curst And shrewd and froward, so beyond all measure That, were my state far worser than it is, I would not wed her for a mine of gold.
trg: Hortensio, peace! thou know'st not gold's effect: Tell me her father's name and 'tis enough; For I will board her, though she chide as loud As thunder when the clouds in autumn crack.

src: Hortensio, peace! thou know'st not gold's effect: Tell me her father's name and 'tis enough; For I will board her, though she chide as loud As thunder when the clouds in autumn crack.
trg: Her father is Baptista Minola, An affable and courteous gentleman: Her name is Katharina Minola, Renown'd in Padua for her scolding tongue.

src: Her father is Baptista Minola, An affable and courteous gentleman: Her name is Katharina Minola, Renown'd in Padua for her scolding tongue.
trg: I know her father, though I know not her; And he knew my deceased father well. I will not sleep, Hortensio, till I see her; And therefore let me be thus bold with you To give you over at this first encounter, Unless you will accompany me thither.

src: I know her father, though I know not her; And he knew my deceased father well. I will not sleep, Hortensio, till I see her; And therefore let me be thus bold with you To give you over at this first encounter, Unless you will accompany me thither.
trg: I pray you, sir, let him go while the humour lasts. O' my word, an she knew him as well as I do, she would think scolding would do little good upon him: she may perhaps call him half a score knaves or so: why, that's nothing; an he begin once, he'll rail in his rope-tricks. I'll tell you what sir, an she stand him but a little, he will throw a figure in her face and so disfigure her with it that she shall have no more eyes to see withal than a cat. You know him not, sir.

src: I pray you, sir, let him go while the humour lasts. O' my word, an she knew him as well as I do, she would think scolding would do little good upon him: she may perhaps call him half a score knaves or so: why, that's nothing; an he begin once, he'll rail in his rope-tricks. I'll tell you what sir, an she stand him but a little, he will throw a figure in her face and so disfigure her with it that she shall have no more eyes to see withal than a cat. You know him not, sir.
trg: Tarry, Petruchio, I must go with thee, For in Baptista's keep my treasure is: He hath the jewel of my life in hold, His youngest daughter, beautiful Binaca, And her withholds from me and other more, Suitors to her and rivals in my love, Supposing it a thing impossible, For those defects I have before rehearsed, That ever Katharina will be woo'd; Therefore this order hath Baptista ta'en, That none shall have access unto Bianca Till Katharina the curst have got a husband.

src: Tarry, Petruchio, I must go with thee, For in Baptista's keep my treasure is: He hath the jewel of my life in hold, His youngest daughter, beautiful Binaca, And her withholds from me and other more, Suitors to her and rivals in my love, Supposing it a thing impossible, For those defects I have before rehearsed, That ever Katharina will be woo'd; Therefore this order hath Baptista ta'en, That none shall have access unto Bianca Till Katharina the curst have got a husband.
trg: Katharina the curst! A title for a maid of all titles the worst.

src: Katharina the curst! A title for a maid of all titles the worst.
trg: Now shall my friend Petruchio do me grace, And offer me disguised in sober robes To old Baptista as a schoolmaster Well seen in music, to instruct Bianca; That so I may, by this device, at least Have leave and leisure to make love to her And unsuspected court her by herself.

src: Now shall my friend Petruchio do me grace, And offer me disguised in sober robes To old Baptista as a schoolmaster Well seen in music, to instruct Bianca; That so I may, by this device, at least Have leave and leisure to make love to her And unsuspected court her by herself.
trg: Here's no knavery! See, to beguile the old folks, how the young folks lay their heads together! Master, master, look about you: who goes there, ha?

src: Here's no knavery! See, to beguile the old folks, how the young folks lay their heads together! Master, master, look about you: who goes there, ha?
trg: Peace, Grumio! it is the rival of my love. Petruchio, stand by a while.

src: Peace, Grumio! it is the rival of my love. Petruchio, stand by a while.
trg: A proper stripling and an amorous!

src: A proper stripling and an amorous!
trg: O, very well; I have perused the note. Hark you, sir: I'll have them very fairly bound: All books of love, see that at any hand; And see you read no other lectures to her: You understand me: over and beside Signior Baptista's liberality, I'll mend it with a largess. Take your paper too, And let me have them very well perfumed For she is sweeter than perfume itself To whom they go to. What will you read to her?

src: O, very well; I have perused the note. Hark you, sir: I'll have them very fairly bound: All books of love, see that at any hand; And see you read no other lectures to her: You understand me: over and beside Signior Baptista's liberality, I'll mend it with a largess. Take your paper too, And let me have them very well perfumed For she is sweeter than perfume itself To whom they go to. What will you read to her?
trg: Whate'er I read to her, I'll plead for you As for my patron, stand you so assured, As firmly as yourself were still in place: Yea, and perhaps with more successful words Than you, unless you were a scholar, sir.

src: Whate'er I read to her, I'll plead for you As for my patron, stand you so assured, As firmly as yourself were still in place: Yea, and perhaps with more successful words Than you, unless you were a scholar, sir.
trg: O this learning, what a thing it is!

src: O this learning, what a thing it is!
trg: O this woodcock, what an ass it is!

src: O this woodcock, what an ass it is!
trg: Peace, sirrah!

src: Peace, sirrah!
trg: Grumio, mum! God save you, Signior Gremio.

src: Grumio, mum! God save you, Signior Gremio.
trg: And you are well met, Signior Hortensio. Trow you whither I am going? To Baptista Minola. I promised to inquire carefully About a schoolmaster for the fair Bianca: And by good fortune I have lighted well On this young man, for learning and behavior Fit for her turn, well read in poetry And other books, good ones, I warrant ye.

src: And you are well met, Signior Hortensio. Trow you whither I am going? To Baptista Minola. I promised to inquire carefully About a schoolmaster for the fair Bianca: And by good fortune I have lighted well On this young man, for learning and behavior Fit for her turn, well read in poetry And other books, good ones, I warrant ye.
trg: 'Tis well; and I have met a gentleman Hath promised me to help me to another, A fine musician to instruct our mistress; So shall I no whit be behind in duty To fair Bianca, so beloved of me.

src: 'Tis well; and I have met a gentleman Hath promised me to help me to another, A fine musician to instruct our mistress; So shall I no whit be behind in duty To fair Bianca, so beloved of me.
trg: Beloved of me; and that my deeds shall prove.

src: Beloved of me; and that my deeds shall prove.
trg: And that his bags shall prove.

src: And that his bags shall prove.
trg: Gremio, 'tis now no time to vent our love: Listen to me, and if you speak me fair, I'll tell you news indifferent good for either. Here is a gentleman whom by chance I met, Upon agreement from us to his liking, Will undertake to woo curst Katharina, Yea, and to marry her, if her dowry please.

src: Gremio, 'tis now no time to vent our love: Listen to me, and if you speak me fair, I'll tell you news indifferent good for either. Here is a gentleman whom by chance I met, Upon agreement from us to his liking, Will undertake to woo curst Katharina, Yea, and to marry her, if her dowry please.
trg: So said, so done, is well. Hortensio, have you told him all her faults?

src: So said, so done, is well. Hortensio, have you told him all her faults?
trg: I know she is an irksome brawling scold: If that be all, masters, I hear no harm.

src: I know she is an irksome brawling scold: If that be all, masters, I hear no harm.
trg: No, say'st me so, friend? What countryman?

src: No, say'st me so, friend? What countryman?
trg: Born in Verona, old Antonio's son: My father dead, my fortune lives for me; And I do hope good days and long to see.

src: Born in Verona, old Antonio's son: My father dead, my fortune lives for me; And I do hope good days and long to see.
trg: O sir, such a life, with such a wife, were strange! But if you have a stomach, to't i' God's name: You shall have me assisting you in all. But will you woo this wild-cat?

src: O sir, such a life, with such a wife, were strange! But if you have a stomach, to't i' God's name: You shall have me assisting you in all. But will you woo this wild-cat?
trg: Will I live?

src: Will I live?
trg: Will he woo her? ay, or I'll hang her.

src: Will he woo her? ay, or I'll hang her.
trg: Why came I hither but to that intent? Think you a little din can daunt mine ears? Have I not in my time heard lions roar? Have I not heard the sea puff'd up with winds Rage like an angry boar chafed with sweat? Have I not heard great ordnance in the field, And heaven's artillery thunder in the skies? Have I not in a pitched battle heard Loud 'larums, neighing steeds, and trumpets' clang? And do you tell me of a woman's tongue, That gives not half so great a blow to hear As will a chestnut in a farmer's fire? Tush, tush! fear boys with bugs.

src: Why came I hither but to that intent? Think you a little din can daunt mine ears? Have I not in my time heard lions roar? Have I not heard the sea puff'd up with winds Rage like an angry boar chafed with sweat? Have I not heard great ordnance in the field, And heaven's artillery thunder in the skies? Have I not in a pitched battle heard Loud 'larums, neighing steeds, and trumpets' clang? And do you tell me of a woman's tongue, That gives not half so great a blow to hear As will a chestnut in a farmer's fire? Tush, tush! fear boys with bugs.
trg: For he fears none.

src: For he fears none.
trg: Hortensio, hark: This gentleman is happily arrived, My mind presumes, for his own good and ours.

src: Hortensio, hark: This gentleman is happily arrived, My mind presumes, for his own good and ours.
trg: I promised we would be contributors And bear his charging of wooing, whatsoe'er.

src: I promised we would be contributors And bear his charging of wooing, whatsoe'er.
trg: And so we will, provided that he win her.

src: And so we will, provided that he win her.
trg: I would I were as sure of a good dinner.

src: I would I were as sure of a good dinner.
trg: Gentlemen, God save you. If I may be bold, Tell me, I beseech you, which is the readiest way To the house of Signior Baptista Minola?

src: Gentlemen, God save you. If I may be bold, Tell me, I beseech you, which is the readiest way To the house of Signior Baptista Minola?
trg: He that has the two fair daughters: is't he you mean?

src: He that has the two fair daughters: is't he you mean?
trg: Even he, Biondello.

src: Even he, Biondello.
trg: Hark you, sir; you mean not her to--

src: Hark you, sir; you mean not her to--
trg: Perhaps, him and her, sir: what have you to do?

src: Perhaps, him and her, sir: what have you to do?
trg: Not her that chides, sir, at any hand, I pray.

src: Not her that chides, sir, at any hand, I pray.
trg: I love no chiders, sir. Biondello, let's away.

src: I love no chiders, sir. Biondello, let's away.
trg: Well begun, Tranio.

src: Well begun, Tranio.
trg: Sir, a word ere you go; Are you a suitor to the maid you talk of, yea or no?

src: Sir, a word ere you go; Are you a suitor to the maid you talk of, yea or no?
trg: And if I be, sir, is it any offence?

src: And if I be, sir, is it any offence?
trg: No; if without more words you will get you hence.

src: No; if without more words you will get you hence.
trg: Why, sir, I pray, are not the streets as free For me as for you?

src: Why, sir, I pray, are not the streets as free For me as for you?
trg: But so is not she.

src: But so is not she.
trg: For what reason, I beseech you?

src: For what reason, I beseech you?
trg: For this reason, if you'll know, That she's the choice love of Signior Gremio.

src: For this reason, if you'll know, That she's the choice love of Signior Gremio.
trg: That she's the chosen of Signior Hortensio.

src: That she's the chosen of Signior Hortensio.
trg: Softly, my masters! if you be gentlemen, Do me this right; hear me with patience. Baptista is a noble gentleman, To whom my father is not all unknown; And were his daughter fairer than she is, She may more suitors have and me for one. Fair Leda's daughter had a thousand wooers; Then well one more may fair Bianca have: And so she shall; Lucentio shall make one, Though Paris came in hope to speed alone.

src: Softly, my masters! if you be gentlemen, Do me this right; hear me with patience. Baptista is a noble gentleman, To whom my father is not all unknown; And were his daughter fairer than she is, She may more suitors have and me for one. Fair Leda's daughter had a thousand wooers; Then well one more may fair Bianca have: And so she shall; Lucentio shall make one, Though Paris came in hope to speed alone.
trg: What! this gentleman will out-talk us all.

src: What! this gentleman will out-talk us all.
trg: Sir, give him head: I know he'll prove a jade.

src: Sir, give him head: I know he'll prove a jade.
trg: Hortensio, to what end are all these words?

src: Hortensio, to what end are all these words?
trg: Sir, let me be so bold as ask you, Did you yet ever see Baptista's daughter?

src: Sir, let me be so bold as ask you, Did you yet ever see Baptista's daughter?
trg: No, sir; but hear I do that he hath two, The one as famous for a scolding tongue As is the other for beauteous modesty.

src: No, sir; but hear I do that he hath two, The one as famous for a scolding tongue As is the other for beauteous modesty.
trg: Sir, sir, the first's for me; let her go by.

src: Sir, sir, the first's for me; let her go by.
trg: Yea, leave that labour to great Hercules; And let it be more than Alcides' twelve.

src: Yea, leave that labour to great Hercules; And let it be more than Alcides' twelve.
trg: Sir, understand you this of me in sooth: The youngest daughter whom you hearken for Her father keeps from all access of suitors, And will not promise her to any man Until the elder sister first be wed: The younger then is free and not before.

src: Sir, understand you this of me in sooth: The youngest daughter whom you hearken for Her father keeps from all access of suitors, And will not promise her to any man Until the elder sister first be wed: The younger then is free and not before.
trg: If it be so, sir, that you are the man Must stead us all and me amongst the rest, And if you break the ice and do this feat, Achieve the elder, set the younger free For our access, whose hap shall be to have her Will not so graceless be to be ingrate.

src: If it be so, sir, that you are the man Must stead us all and me amongst the rest, And if you break the ice and do this feat, Achieve the elder, set the younger free For our access, whose hap shall be to have her Will not so graceless be to be ingrate.
trg: Sir, you say well and well you do conceive; And since you do profess to be a suitor, You must, as we do, gratify this gentleman, To whom we all rest generally beholding.

src: Sir, you say well and well you do conceive; And since you do profess to be a suitor, You must, as we do, gratify this gentleman, To whom we all rest generally beholding.
trg: Sir, I shall not be slack: in sign whereof, Please ye we may contrive this afternoon, And quaff carouses to our mistress' health, And do as adversaries do in law, Strive mightily, but eat and drink as friends.

src: Sir, I shall not be slack: in sign whereof, Please ye we may contrive this afternoon, And quaff carouses to our mistress' health, And do as adversaries do in law, Strive mightily, but eat and drink as friends.
trg: O excellent motion! Fellows, let's be gone.

src: O excellent motion! Fellows, let's be gone.
trg: The motion's good indeed and be it so, Petruchio, I shall be your ben venuto.

src: The motion's good indeed and be it so, Petruchio, I shall be your ben venuto.
trg: Good sister, wrong me not, nor wrong yourself, To make a bondmaid and a slave of me; That I disdain: but for these other gawds, Unbind my hands, I'll pull them off myself, Yea, all my raiment, to my petticoat; Or what you will command me will I do, So well I know my duty to my elders.

src: Good sister, wrong me not, nor wrong yourself, To make a bondmaid and a slave of me; That I disdain: but for these other gawds, Unbind my hands, I'll pull them off myself, Yea, all my raiment, to my petticoat; Or what you will command me will I do, So well I know my duty to my elders.
trg: Of all thy suitors, here I charge thee, tell Whom thou lovest best: see thou dissemble not.

src: Of all thy suitors, here I charge thee, tell Whom thou lovest best: see thou dissemble not.
trg: Believe me, sister, of all the men alive I never yet beheld that special face Which I could fancy more than any other.

src: Believe me, sister, of all the men alive I never yet beheld that special face Which I could fancy more than any other.
trg: Minion, thou liest. Is't not Hortensio?

src: Minion, thou liest. Is't not Hortensio?
trg: If you affect him, sister, here I swear I'll plead for you myself, but you shall have him.

src: If you affect him, sister, here I swear I'll plead for you myself, but you shall have him.
trg: O then, belike, you fancy riches more: You will have Gremio to keep you fair.

src: O then, belike, you fancy riches more: You will have Gremio to keep you fair.
trg: Is it for him you do envy me so? Nay then you jest, and now I well perceive You have but jested with me all this while: I prithee, sister Kate, untie my hands.

src: Is it for him you do envy me so? Nay then you jest, and now I well perceive You have but jested with me all this while: I prithee, sister Kate, untie my hands.
trg: If that be jest, then all the rest was so.

src: If that be jest, then all the rest was so.
trg: Why, how now, dame! whence grows this insolence? Bianca, stand aside. Poor girl! she weeps. Go ply thy needle; meddle not with her. For shame, thou helding of a devilish spirit, Why dost thou wrong her that did ne'er wrong thee? When did she cross thee with a bitter word?

src: Why, how now, dame! whence grows this insolence? Bianca, stand aside. Poor girl! she weeps. Go ply thy needle; meddle not with her. For shame, thou helding of a devilish spirit, Why dost thou wrong her that did ne'er wrong thee? When did she cross thee with a bitter word?
trg: Her silence flouts me, and I'll be revenged.

src: Her silence flouts me, and I'll be revenged.
trg: What, in my sight? Bianca, get thee in.

src: What, in my sight? Bianca, get thee in.
trg: What, will you not suffer me? Nay, now I see She is your treasure, she must have a husband; I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day And for your love to her lead apes in hell. Talk not to me: I will go sit and weep Till I can find occasion of revenge.

src: What, will you not suffer me? Nay, now I see She is your treasure, she must have a husband; I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day And for your love to her lead apes in hell. Talk not to me: I will go sit and weep Till I can find occasion of revenge.
trg: Was ever gentleman thus grieved as I? But who comes here?

src: Was ever gentleman thus grieved as I? But who comes here?
trg: Good morrow, neighbour Baptista.

src: Good morrow, neighbour Baptista.
trg: Good morrow, neighbour Gremio. God save you, gentlemen!

src: Good morrow, neighbour Gremio. God save you, gentlemen!
trg: And you, good sir! Pray, have you not a daughter Call'd Katharina, fair and virtuous?

src: And you, good sir! Pray, have you not a daughter Call'd Katharina, fair and virtuous?
trg: I have a daughter, sir, called Katharina.

src: I have a daughter, sir, called Katharina.
trg: You are too blunt: go to it orderly.

src: You are too blunt: go to it orderly.
trg: You wrong me, Signior Gremio: give me leave. I am a gentleman of Verona, sir, That, hearing of her beauty and her wit, Her affability and bashful modesty, Her wondrous qualities and mild behavior, Am bold to show myself a forward guest Within your house, to make mine eye the witness Of that report which I so oft have heard. And, for an entrance to my entertainment, I do present you with a man of mine, Cunning in music and the mathematics, To instruct her fully in those sciences, Whereof I know she is not ignorant: Accept of him, or else you do me wrong: His name is Licio, born in Mantua.

src: You wrong me, Signior Gremio: give me leave. I am a gentleman of Verona, sir, That, hearing of her beauty and her wit, Her affability and bashful modesty, Her wondrous qualities and mild behavior, Am bold to show myself a forward guest Within your house, to make mine eye the witness Of that report which I so oft have heard. And, for an entrance to my entertainment, I do present you with a man of mine, Cunning in music and the mathematics, To instruct her fully in those sciences, Whereof I know she is not ignorant: Accept of him, or else you do me wrong: His name is Licio, born in Mantua.
trg: You're welcome, sir; and he, for your good sake. But for my daughter Katharina, this I know, She is not for your turn, the more my grief.

src: You're welcome, sir; and he, for your good sake. But for my daughter Katharina, this I know, She is not for your turn, the more my grief.
trg: I see you do not mean to part with her, Or else you like not of my company.

src: I see you do not mean to part with her, Or else you like not of my company.
trg: Mistake me not; I speak but as I find. Whence are you, sir? what may I call your name?

src: Mistake me not; I speak but as I find. Whence are you, sir? what may I call your name?
trg: Petruchio is my name; Antonio's son, A man well known throughout all Italy.

src: Petruchio is my name; Antonio's son, A man well known throughout all Italy.
trg: I know him well: you are welcome for his sake.

src: I know him well: you are welcome for his sake.
trg: Saving your tale, Petruchio, I pray, Let us, that are poor petitioners, speak too: Baccare! you are marvellous forward.

src: Saving your tale, Petruchio, I pray, Let us, that are poor petitioners, speak too: Baccare! you are marvellous forward.
trg: O, pardon me, Signior Gremio; I would fain be doing.

src: O, pardon me, Signior Gremio; I would fain be doing.
trg: I doubt it not, sir; but you will curse your wooing. Neighbour, this is a gift very grateful, I am sure of it. To express the like kindness, myself, that have been more kindly beholding to you than any, freely give unto you this young scholar, that hath been long studying at Rheims; as cunning in Greek, Latin, and other languages, as the other in music and mathematics: his name is Cambio; pray, accept his service.

src: I doubt it not, sir; but you will curse your wooing. Neighbour, this is a gift very grateful, I am sure of it. To express the like kindness, myself, that have been more kindly beholding to you than any, freely give unto you this young scholar, that hath been long studying at Rheims; as cunning in Greek, Latin, and other languages, as the other in music and mathematics: his name is Cambio; pray, accept his service.
trg: A thousand thanks, Signior Gremio. Welcome, good Cambio. But, gentle sir, methinks you walk like a stranger: may I be so bold to know the cause of your coming?

src: A thousand thanks, Signior Gremio. Welcome, good Cambio. But, gentle sir, methinks you walk like a stranger: may I be so bold to know the cause of your coming?
trg: Pardon me, sir, the boldness is mine own, That, being a stranger in this city here, Do make myself a suitor to your daughter, Unto Bianca, fair and virtuous. Nor is your firm resolve unknown to me, In the preferment of the eldest sister. This liberty is all that I request, That, upon knowledge of my parentage, I may have welcome 'mongst the rest that woo And free access and favour as the rest: And, toward the education of your daughters, I here bestow a simple instrument, And this small packet of Greek and Latin books: If you accept them, then their worth is great.

src: Pardon me, sir, the boldness is mine own, That, being a stranger in this city here, Do make myself a suitor to your daughter, Unto Bianca, fair and virtuous. Nor is your firm resolve unknown to me, In the preferment of the eldest sister. This liberty is all that I request, That, upon knowledge of my parentage, I may have welcome 'mongst the rest that woo And free access and favour as the rest: And, toward the education of your daughters, I here bestow a simple instrument, And this small packet of Greek and Latin books: If you accept them, then their worth is great.
trg: Lucentio is your name; of whence, I pray?

src: Lucentio is your name; of whence, I pray?
trg: Of Pisa, sir; son to Vincentio.

src: Of Pisa, sir; son to Vincentio.
trg: A mighty man of Pisa; by report I know him well: you are very welcome, sir, Take you the lute, and you the set of books; You shall go see your pupils presently. Holla, within! Sirrah, lead these gentlemen To my daughters; and tell them both, These are their tutors: bid them use them well. We will go walk a little in the orchard, And then to dinner. You are passing welcome, And so I pray you all to think yourselves.

src: A mighty man of Pisa; by report I know him well: you are very welcome, sir, Take you the lute, and you the set of books; You shall go see your pupils presently. Holla, within! Sirrah, lead these gentlemen To my daughters; and tell them both, These are their tutors: bid them use them well. We will go walk a little in the orchard, And then to dinner. You are passing welcome, And so I pray you all to think yourselves.
trg: Signior Baptista, my business asketh haste, And every day I cannot come to woo. You knew my father well, and in him me, Left solely heir to all his lands and goods, Which I have better'd rather than decreased: Then tell me, if I get your daughter's love, What dowry shall I have with her to wife?

src: Signior Baptista, my business asketh haste, And every day I cannot come to woo. You knew my father well, and in him me, Left solely heir to all his lands and goods, Which I have better'd rather than decreased: Then tell me, if I get your daughter's love, What dowry shall I have with her to wife?
trg: After my death the one half of my lands, And in possession twenty thousand crowns.

src: After my death the one half of my lands, And in possession twenty thousand crowns.
trg: And, for that dowry, I'll assure her of Her widowhood, be it that she survive me, In all my lands and leases whatsoever: Let specialties be therefore drawn between us, That covenants may be kept on either hand.

src: And, for that dowry, I'll assure her of Her widowhood, be it that she survive me, In all my lands and leases whatsoever: Let specialties be therefore drawn between us, That covenants may be kept on either hand.
trg: Ay, when the special thing is well obtain'd, That is, her love; for that is all in all.

src: Ay, when the special thing is well obtain'd, That is, her love; for that is all in all.
trg: Why, that is nothing: for I tell you, father, I am as peremptory as she proud-minded; And where two raging fires meet together They do consume the thing that feeds their fury: Though little fire grows great with little wind, Yet extreme gusts will blow out fire and all: So I to her and so she yields to me; For I am rough and woo not like a babe.

src: Why, that is nothing: for I tell you, father, I am as peremptory as she proud-minded; And where two raging fires meet together They do consume the thing that feeds their fury: Though little fire grows great with little wind, Yet extreme gusts will blow out fire and all: So I to her and so she yields to me; For I am rough and woo not like a babe.
trg: Well mayst thou woo, and happy be thy speed! But be thou arm'd for some unhappy words.

src: Well mayst thou woo, and happy be thy speed! But be thou arm'd for some unhappy words.
trg: Ay, to the proof; as mountains are for winds, That shake not, though they blow perpetually.

src: Ay, to the proof; as mountains are for winds, That shake not, though they blow perpetually.
trg: How now, my friend! why dost thou look so pale?

src: How now, my friend! why dost thou look so pale?
trg: For fear, I promise you, if I look pale.

src: For fear, I promise you, if I look pale.
trg: What, will my daughter prove a good musician?

src: What, will my daughter prove a good musician?
trg: I think she'll sooner prove a soldier Iron may hold with her, but never lutes.

src: I think she'll sooner prove a soldier Iron may hold with her, but never lutes.
trg: Why, then thou canst not break her to the lute?

src: Why, then thou canst not break her to the lute?
trg: Why, no; for she hath broke the lute to me. I did but tell her she mistook her frets, And bow'd her hand to teach her fingering; When, with a most impatient devilish spirit, 'Frets, call you these?' quoth she; 'I'll fume with them:' And, with that word, she struck me on the head, And through the instrument my pate made way; And there I stood amazed for a while, As on a pillory, looking through the lute; While she did call me rascal fiddler And twangling Jack; with twenty such vile terms, As had she studied to misuse me so.

src: Why, no; for she hath broke the lute to me. I did but tell her she mistook her frets, And bow'd her hand to teach her fingering; When, with a most impatient devilish spirit, 'Frets, call you these?' quoth she; 'I'll fume with them:' And, with that word, she struck me on the head, And through the instrument my pate made way; And there I stood amazed for a while, As on a pillory, looking through the lute; While she did call me rascal fiddler And twangling Jack; with twenty such vile terms, As had she studied to misuse me so.
trg: Now, by the world, it is a lusty wench; I love her ten times more than e'er I did: O, how I long to have some chat with her!

src: Now, by the world, it is a lusty wench; I love her ten times more than e'er I did: O, how I long to have some chat with her!
trg: Well, go with me and be not so discomfited: Proceed in practise with my younger daughter; She's apt to learn and thankful for good turns. Signior Petruchio, will you go with us, Or shall I send my daughter Kate to you?

src: Well, go with me and be not so discomfited: Proceed in practise with my younger daughter; She's apt to learn and thankful for good turns. Signior Petruchio, will you go with us, Or shall I send my daughter Kate to you?
trg: I pray you do. I will attend her here, And woo her with some spirit when she comes. Say that she rail; why then I'll tell her plain She sings as sweetly as a nightingale: Say that she frown, I'll say she looks as clear As morning roses newly wash'd with dew: Say she be mute and will not speak a word; Then I'll commend her volubility, And say she uttereth piercing eloquence: If she do bid me pack, I'll give her thanks, As though she bid me stay by her a week: If she deny to wed, I'll crave the day When I shall ask the banns and when be married. But here she comes; and now, Petruchio, speak. Good morrow, Kate; for that's your name, I hear.

src: I pray you do. I will attend her here, And woo her with some spirit when she comes. Say that she rail; why then I'll tell her plain She sings as sweetly as a nightingale: Say that she frown, I'll say she looks as clear As morning roses newly wash'd with dew: Say she be mute and will not speak a word; Then I'll commend her volubility, And say she uttereth piercing eloquence: If she do bid me pack, I'll give her thanks, As though she bid me stay by her a week: If she deny to wed, I'll crave the day When I shall ask the banns and when be married. But here she comes; and now, Petruchio, speak. Good morrow, Kate; for that's your name, I hear.
trg: Well have you heard, but something hard of hearing: They call me Katharina that do talk of me.

src: Well have you heard, but something hard of hearing: They call me Katharina that do talk of me.
trg: You lie, in faith; for you are call'd plain Kate, And bonny Kate and sometimes Kate the curst; But Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendom Kate of Kate Hall, my super-dainty Kate, For dainties are all Kates, and therefore, Kate, Take this of me, Kate of my consolation; Hearing thy mildness praised in every town, Thy virtues spoke of, and thy beauty sounded, Yet not so deeply as to thee belongs, Myself am moved to woo thee for my wife.

src: You lie, in faith; for you are call'd plain Kate, And bonny Kate and sometimes Kate the curst; But Kate, the prettiest Kate in Christendom Kate of Kate Hall, my super-dainty Kate, For dainties are all Kates, and therefore, Kate, Take this of me, Kate of my consolation; Hearing thy mildness praised in every town, Thy virtues spoke of, and thy beauty sounded, Yet not so deeply as to thee belongs, Myself am moved to woo thee for my wife.
trg: Moved! in good time: let him that moved you hither Remove you hence: I knew you at the first You were a moveable.

src: Moved! in good time: let him that moved you hither Remove you hence: I knew you at the first You were a moveable.
trg: Why, what's a moveable?

src: Why, what's a moveable?
trg: A join'd-stool.

src: A join'd-stool.
trg: Thou hast hit it: come, sit on me.

src: Thou hast hit it: come, sit on me.
trg: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.

src: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.
trg: Women are made to bear, and so are you.

src: Women are made to bear, and so are you.
trg: No such jade as you, if me you mean.

src: No such jade as you, if me you mean.
trg: Alas! good Kate, I will not burden thee; For, knowing thee to be but young and light--

src: Alas! good Kate, I will not burden thee; For, knowing thee to be but young and light--
trg: Too light for such a swain as you to catch; And yet as heavy as my weight should be.

src: Too light for such a swain as you to catch; And yet as heavy as my weight should be.
trg: Should be! should--buzz!

src: Should be! should--buzz!
trg: Well ta'en, and like a buzzard.

src: Well ta'en, and like a buzzard.
trg: O slow-wing'd turtle! shall a buzzard take thee?

src: O slow-wing'd turtle! shall a buzzard take thee?
trg: Ay, for a turtle, as he takes a buzzard.

src: Ay, for a turtle, as he takes a buzzard.
trg: Come, come, you wasp; i' faith, you are too angry.

src: Come, come, you wasp; i' faith, you are too angry.
trg: If I be waspish, best beware my sting.

src: If I be waspish, best beware my sting.
trg: My remedy is then, to pluck it out.

src: My remedy is then, to pluck it out.
trg: Ay, if the fool could find it where it lies,

src: Ay, if the fool could find it where it lies,
trg: Who knows not where a wasp does wear his sting? In his tail.

src: Who knows not where a wasp does wear his sting? In his tail.
trg: In his tongue.

src: In his tongue.
trg: Whose tongue?

src: Whose tongue?
trg: Yours, if you talk of tails: and so farewell.

src: Yours, if you talk of tails: and so farewell.
trg: What, with my tongue in your tail? nay, come again, Good Kate; I am a gentleman.

src: What, with my tongue in your tail? nay, come again, Good Kate; I am a gentleman.
trg: That I'll try.

src: That I'll try.
trg: I swear I'll cuff you, if you strike again.

src: I swear I'll cuff you, if you strike again.
trg: So may you lose your arms: If you strike me, you are no gentleman; And if no gentleman, why then no arms.

src: So may you lose your arms: If you strike me, you are no gentleman; And if no gentleman, why then no arms.
trg: A herald, Kate? O, put me in thy books!

src: A herald, Kate? O, put me in thy books!
trg: What is your crest? a coxcomb?

src: What is your crest? a coxcomb?
trg: A combless cock, so Kate will be my hen.

src: A combless cock, so Kate will be my hen.
trg: No cock of mine; you crow too like a craven.

src: No cock of mine; you crow too like a craven.
trg: Nay, come, Kate, come; you must not look so sour.

src: Nay, come, Kate, come; you must not look so sour.
trg: It is my fashion, when I see a crab.

src: It is my fashion, when I see a crab.
trg: Why, here's no crab; and therefore look not sour.

src: Why, here's no crab; and therefore look not sour.
trg: There is, there is.

src: There is, there is.
trg: Then show it me.

src: Then show it me.
trg: Had I a glass, I would.

src: Had I a glass, I would.
trg: What, you mean my face?

src: What, you mean my face?
trg: Well aim'd of such a young one.

src: Well aim'd of such a young one.
trg: Now, by Saint George, I am too young for you.

src: Now, by Saint George, I am too young for you.
trg: Yet you are wither'd.

src: Yet you are wither'd.
trg: 'Tis with cares.

src: 'Tis with cares.
trg: I care not.

src: I care not.
trg: Nay, hear you, Kate: in sooth you scape not so.

src: Nay, hear you, Kate: in sooth you scape not so.
trg: I chafe you, if I tarry: let me go.

src: I chafe you, if I tarry: let me go.
trg: No, not a whit: I find you passing gentle. 'Twas told me you were rough and coy and sullen, And now I find report a very liar; For thou are pleasant, gamesome, passing courteous, But slow in speech, yet sweet as spring-time flowers: Thou canst not frown, thou canst not look askance, Nor bite the lip, as angry wenches will, Nor hast thou pleasure to be cross in talk, But thou with mildness entertain'st thy wooers, With gentle conference, soft and affable. Why does the world report that Kate doth limp? O slanderous world! Kate like the hazel-twig Is straight and slender and as brown in hue As hazel nuts and sweeter than the kernels. O, let me see thee walk: thou dost not halt.

src: No, not a whit: I find you passing gentle. trg: Go, fool, and whom thou keep'st command.

src: Go, fool, and whom thou keep'st command.
trg: Did ever Dian so become a grove As Kate this chamber with her princely gait? O, be thou Dian, and let her be Kate; And then let Kate be chaste and Dian sportful!

src: Did ever Dian so become a grove As Kate this chamber with her princely gait? O, be thou Dian, and let her be Kate; And then let Kate be chaste and Dian sportful!
trg: Where did you study all this goodly speech?

src: Where did you study all this goodly speech?
trg: It is extempore, from my mother-wit.

src: It is extempore, from my mother-wit.
trg: A witty mother! witless else her son.

src: A witty mother! witless else her son.
trg: Am I not wise?

src: Am I not wise?
trg: Yes; keep you warm.

src: Yes; keep you warm.
trg: Marry, so I mean, sweet Katharina, in thy bed: And therefore, setting all this chat aside, Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented That you shall be my wife; your dowry 'greed on; And, Will you, nill you, I will marry you. Now, Kate, I am a husband for your turn; For, by this light, whereby I see thy beauty, Thy beauty, that doth make me like thee well, Thou must be married to no man but me; For I am he am born to tame you Kate, And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate Conformable as other household Kates. Here comes your father: never make denial; I must and will have Katharina to my wife.

src: Marry, so I mean, sweet Katharina, in thy bed: And therefore, setting all this chat aside, Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented That you shall be my wife; your dowry 'greed on; And, Will you, nill you, I will marry you. Now, Kate, I am a husband for your turn; For, by this light, whereby I see thy beauty, Thy beauty, that doth make me like thee well, Thou must be married to no man but me; For I am he am born to tame you Kate, And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate Conformable as other household Kates.
