trg: Now, Signior Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?

src: Now, Signior Petruchio, how speed you with my daughter?
trg: How but well, sir? how but well? It were impossible I should speed amiss.

src: How but well, sir? how but well? It were impossible I should speed amiss.
trg: Why, how now, daughter Katharina! in your dumps?

src: Why, how now, daughter Katharina! in your dumps?
trg: Call you me daughter? now, I promise you You have show'd a tender fatherly regard, To wish me wed to one half lunatic; A mad-cup ruffian and a swearing Jack, That thinks with oaths to face the matter out.

src: Call you me daughter? now, I promise you You have show'd a tender fatherly regard, To wish me wed to one half lunatic; A mad-cup ruffian and a swearing Jack, That thinks with oaths to face the matter out.
trg: Father, 'tis thus: yourself and all the world, That talk'd of her, have talk'd amiss of her: If she be curst, it is for policy, For she's not froward, but modest as the dove; She is not hot, but temperate as the morn; For patience she will prove a second Grissel, And Roman Lucrece for her chastity: And to conclude, we have 'greed so well together, That upon Sunday is the wedding-day.

src: Father, 'tis thus: yourself and all the world, That talk'd of her, have talk'd amiss of her: If she be curst, it is for policy, For she's not froward, but modest as the dove; She is not hot, but temperate as the morn; For patience she will prove a second Grissel, And Roman Lucrece for her chastity: And to conclude, we have 'greed so well together, That upon Sunday is the wedding-day.
trg: I'll see thee hang'd on Sunday first.

src: I'll see thee hang'd on Sunday first.
trg: Hark, Petruchio; she says she'll see thee hang'd first.

src: Hark, Petruchio; she says she'll see thee hang'd first.
trg: Is this your speeding? nay, then, good night our part!

src: Is this your speeding? nay, then, good night our part!
trg: Be patient, gentlemen; I choose her for myself: If she and I be pleased, what's that to you? 'Tis bargain'd 'twixt us twain, being alone, That she shall still be curst in company. I tell you, 'tis incredible to believe How much she loves me: O, the kindest Kate! She hung about my neck; and kiss on kiss She vied so fast, protesting oath on oath, That in a twink she won me to her love. O, you are novices! 'tis a world to see, How tame, when men and women are alone, A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew. Give me thy hand, Kate: I will unto Venice, To buy apparel 'gainst the wedding-day. Provide the feast, father, and bid the guests; I will be sure my Katharina shall be fine.

src: Be patient, gentlemen; I choose her for myself: If she and I be pleased, what's that to you? 'Tis bargain'd 'twixt us twain, being alone, That she shall still be curst in company. I tell you, 'tis incredible to believe How much she loves me: O, the kindest Kate! She hung about my neck; and kiss on kiss She vied so fast, protesting oath on oath, That in a twink she won me to her love. O, you are novices! 'tis a world to see, How tame, when men and women are alone, A meacock wretch can make the curstest shrew. Give me thy hand, Kate: I will unto Venice, To buy apparel 'gainst the wedding-day. Provide the feast, father, and bid the guests; I will be sure my Katharina shall be fine.
trg: I know not what to say: but give me your hands; God send you joy, Petruchio! 'tis a match.

src: I know not what to say: but give me your hands; God send you joy, Petruchio! 'tis a match.
trg: Amen, say we: we will be witnesses.

src: Amen, say we: we will be witnesses.
trg: Father, and wife, and gentlemen, adieu; I will to Venice; Sunday comes apace: We will have rings and things and fine array; And kiss me, Kate, we will be married o'Sunday.

src: Father, and wife, and gentlemen, adieu; I will to Venice; Sunday comes apace: We will have rings and things and fine array; And kiss me, Kate, we will be married o'Sunday.
trg: Was ever match clapp'd up so suddenly?

src: Was ever match clapp'd up so suddenly?
trg: Faith, gentlemen, now I play a merchant's part, And venture madly on a desperate mart.

src: Faith, gentlemen, now I play a merchant's part, And venture madly on a desperate mart.
trg: 'Twas a commodity lay fretting by you: 'Twill bring you gain, or perish on the seas.

src: 'Twas a commodity lay fretting by you: 'Twill bring you gain, or perish on the seas.
trg: The gain I seek is, quiet in the match.

src: The gain I seek is, quiet in the match.
trg: No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch. But now, Baptists, to your younger daughter: Now is the day we long have looked for: I am your neighbour, and was suitor first.

src: No doubt but he hath got a quiet catch. But now, Baptists, to your younger daughter: Now is the day we long have looked for: I am your neighbour, and was suitor first.
trg: And I am one that love Bianca more Than words can witness, or your thoughts can guess.

src: And I am one that love Bianca more Than words can witness, or your thoughts can guess.
trg: Youngling, thou canst not love so dear as I.

src: Youngling, thou canst not love so dear as I.
trg: Graybeard, thy love doth freeze.

src: Graybeard, thy love doth freeze.
trg: But thine doth fry. Skipper, stand back: 'tis age that nourisheth.

src: But thine doth fry. Skipper, stand back: 'tis age that nourisheth.
trg: But youth in ladies' eyes that flourisheth.

src: But youth in ladies' eyes that flourisheth.
trg: Content you, gentlemen: I will compound this strife: 'Tis deeds must win the prize; and he of both That can assure my daughter greatest dower Shall have my Bianca's love. Say, Signior Gremio, What can you assure her?

src: Content you, gentlemen: I will compound this strife: 'Tis deeds must win the prize; and he of both That can assure my daughter greatest dower Shall have my Bianca's love. Say, Signior Gremio, What can you assure her?
trg: First, as you know, my house within the city Is richly furnished with plate and gold; Basins and ewers to lave her dainty hands; My hangings all of Tyrian tapestry; In ivory coffers I have stuff'd my crowns; In cypress chests my arras counterpoints, Costly apparel, tents, and canopies, Fine linen, Turkey cushions boss'd with pearl, Valance of Venice gold in needlework, Pewter and brass and all things that belong To house or housekeeping: then, at my farm I have a hundred milch-kine to the pail, Sixscore fat oxen standing in my stalls, And all things answerable to this portion. Myself am struck in years, I must confess; And if I die to-morrow, this is hers, If whilst I live she will be only mine.

src: First, as you know, my house within the city Is richly furnished with plate and gold; Basins and ewers to lave her dainty hands; My hangings all of Tyrian tapestry; In ivory coffers I have stuff'd my crowns; In cypress chests my arras counterpoints, Costly apparel, tents, and canopies, Fine linen, Turkey cushions boss'd with pearl, Valance of Venice gold in needlework, Pewter and brass and all things that belong To house or housekeeping: then, at my farm I have a hundred milch-kine to the pail, Sixscore fat oxen standing in my stalls, And all things answerable to this portion. Myself am struck in years, I must confess; And if I die to-morrow, this is hers, If whilst I live she will be only mine.
trg: That 'only' came well in. Sir, list to me: I am my father's heir and only son: If I may have your daughter to my wife, I'll leave her houses three or four as good, Within rich Pisa walls, as any one Old Signior Gremio has in Padua; Besides two thousand ducats by the year Of fruitful land, all which shall be her jointure. What, have I pinch'd you, Signior Gremio?

src: That 'only' came well in. Sir, list to me: I am my father's heir and only son: If I may have your daughter to my wife, I'll leave her houses three or four as good, Within rich Pisa walls, as any one Old Signior Gremio has in Padua; Besides two thousand ducats by the year Of fruitful land, all which shall be her jointure. What, have I pinch'd you, Signior Gremio?
trg: Two thousand ducats by the year of land! My land amounts not to so much in all: That she shall have; besides an argosy That now is lying in Marseilles' road. What, have I choked you with an argosy?

src: Two thousand ducats by the year of land! My land amounts not to so much in all: That she shall have; besides an argosy That now is lying in Marseilles' road. What, have I choked you with an argosy?
trg: Gremio, 'tis known my father hath no less Than three great argosies; besides two galliases, And twelve tight galleys: these I will assure her, And twice as much, whate'er thou offer'st next.

src: Gremio, 'tis known my father hath no less Than three great argosies; besides two galliases, And twelve tight galleys: these I will assure her, And twice as much, whate'er thou offer'st next.
trg: Nay, I have offer'd all, I have no more; And she can have no more than all I have: If you like me, she shall have me and mine.

src: Nay, I have offer'd all, I have no more; And she can have no more than all I have: If you like me, she shall have me and mine.
trg: Why, then the maid is mine from all the world, By your firm promise: Gremio is out-vied.

src: Why, then the maid is mine from all the world, By your firm promise: Gremio is out-vied.
trg: I must confess your offer is the best; And, let your father make her the assurance, She is your own; else, you must pardon me, if you should die before him, where's her dower?

src: I must confess your offer is the best; And, let your father make her the assurance, She is your own; else, you must pardon me, if you should die before him, where's her dower?
trg: That's but a cavil: he is old, I young.

src: That's but a cavil: he is old, I young.
trg: And may not young men die, as well as old?

src: And may not young men die, as well as old?
trg: Well, gentlemen, I am thus resolved: on Sunday next you know My daughter Katharina is to be married: Now, on the Sunday following, shall Bianca Be bride to you, if you this assurance; If not, Signior Gremio: And so, I take my leave, and thank you both.

src: Well, gentlemen, I am thus resolved: on Sunday next you know My daughter Katharina is to be married: Now, on the Sunday following, shall Bianca Be bride to you, if you this assurance; If not, Signior Gremio: And so, I take my leave, and thank you both.
trg: Adieu, good neighbour. Now I fear thee not: Sirrah young gamester, your father were a fool To give thee all, and in his waning age Set foot under thy table: tut, a toy! An old Italian fox is not so kind, my boy.

src: Adieu, good neighbour. Now I fear thee not: Sirrah young gamester, your father were a fool To give thee all, and in his waning age Set foot under thy table: tut, a toy! An old Italian fox is not so kind, my boy.
trg: A vengeance on your crafty wither'd hide! Yet I have faced it with a card of ten. 'Tis in my head to do my master good: I see no reason but supposed Lucentio Must get a father, call'd 'supposed Vincentio;' And that's a wonder: fathers commonly Do get their children; but in this case of wooing, A child shall get a sire, if I fail not of my cunning.

src: A vengeance on your crafty wither'd hide! Yet I have faced it with a card of ten. 'Tis in my head to do my master good: I see no reason but supposed Lucentio Must get a father, call'd 'supposed Vincentio;' And that's a wonder: fathers commonly Do get their children; but in this case of wooing, A child shall get a sire, if I fail not of my cunning.
trg: Fiddler, forbear; you grow too forward, sir: Have you so soon forgot the entertainment Her sister Katharina welcomed you withal?

src: Fiddler, forbear; you grow too forward, sir: Have you so soon forgot the entertainment Her sister Katharina welcomed you withal?
trg: But, wrangling pedant, this is The patroness of heavenly harmony: Then give me leave to have prerogative; And when in music we have spent an hour, Your lecture shall have leisure for as much.

src: But, wrangling pedant, this is The patroness of heavenly harmony: Then give me leave to have prerogative; And when in music we have spent an hour, Your lecture shall have leisure for as much.
trg: Preposterous ass, that never read so far To know the cause why music was ordain'd! Was it not to refresh the mind of man After his studies or his usual pain? Then give me leave to read philosophy, And while I pause, serve in your harmony.

src: Preposterous ass, that never read so far To know the cause why music was ordain'd! Was it not to refresh the mind of man After his studies or his usual pain? Then give me leave to read philosophy, And while I pause, serve in your harmony.
trg: Sirrah, I will not bear these braves of thine.

src: Sirrah, I will not bear these braves of thine.
trg: Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong, To strive for that which resteth in my choice: I am no breeching scholar in the schools; I'll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times, But learn my lessons as I please myself. And, to cut off all strife, here sit we down: Take you your instrument, play you the whiles; His lecture will be done ere you have tuned.

src: Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong, To strive for that which resteth in my choice: I am no breeching scholar in the schools; I'll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times, But learn my lessons as I please myself. And, to cut off all strife, here sit we down: Take you your instrument, play you the whiles; His lecture will be done ere you have tuned.
trg: You'll leave his lecture when I am in tune?

src: You'll leave his lecture when I am in tune?
trg: That will be never: tune your instrument.

src: That will be never: tune your instrument.
trg: Where left we last?

src: Where left we last?
trg: Here, madam: 'Hic ibat Simois; hic est Sigeia tellus; Hic steterat Priami regia celsa senis.'

src: Here, madam: 'Hic ibat Simois; hic est Sigeia tellus; Hic steterat Priami regia celsa senis.'
trg: Construe them.

src: Construe them.
trg: 'Hic ibat,' as I told you before, 'Simois,' I am Lucentio, 'hic est,' son unto Vincentio of Pisa, 'Sigeia tellus,' disguised thus to get your love; 'Hic steterat,' and that Lucentio that comes a-wooing, 'Priami,' is my man Tranio, 'regia,' bearing my port, 'celsa senis,' that we might beguile the old pantaloon.

src: 'Hic ibat,' as I told you before, 'Simois,' I am Lucentio, 'hic est,' son unto Vincentio of Pisa, 'Sigeia tellus,' disguised thus to get your love; 'Hic steterat,' and that Lucentio that comes a-wooing, 'Priami,' is my man Tranio, 'regia,' bearing my port, 'celsa senis,' that we might beguile the old pantaloon.
trg: Madam, my instrument's in tune.

src: Madam, my instrument's in tune.
trg: Let's hear. O fie! the treble jars.

src: Let's hear. O fie! the treble jars.
trg: Spit in the hole, man, and tune again.

src: Spit in the hole, man, and tune again.
trg: Now let me see if I can construe it: 'Hic ibat Simois,' I know you not, 'hic est Sigeia tellus,' I trust you not; 'Hic steterat Priami,' take heed he hear us not, 'regia,' presume not, 'celsa senis,' despair not.

src: Now let me see if I can construe it: 'Hic ibat Simois,' I know you not, 'hic est Sigeia tellus,' I trust you not; 'Hic steterat Priami,' take heed he hear us not, 'regia,' presume not, 'celsa senis,' despair not.
trg: Madam, 'tis now in tune.

src: Madam, 'tis now in tune.
trg: All but the base.

src: All but the base.
trg: The base is right; 'tis the base knave that jars. How fiery and forward our pedant is! Now, for my life, the knave doth court my love: Pedascule, I'll watch you better yet.

src: The base is right; 'tis the base knave that jars. How fiery and forward our pedant is! Now, for my life, the knave doth court my love: Pedascule, I'll watch you better yet.
trg: In time I may believe, yet I mistrust.

src: In time I may believe, yet I mistrust.
trg: Mistrust it not: for, sure, AEacides Was Ajax, call'd so from his grandfather.

src: Mistrust it not: for, sure, AEacides Was Ajax, call'd so from his grandfather.
trg: I must believe my master; else, I promise you, I should be arguing still upon that doubt: But let it rest. Now, Licio, to you: Good masters, take it not unkindly, pray, That I have been thus pleasant with you both.

src: I must believe my master; else, I promise you, I should be arguing still upon that doubt: But let it rest. Now, Licio, to you: Good masters, take it not unkindly, pray, That I have been thus pleasant with you both.
trg: You may go walk, and give me leave a while: My lessons make no music in three parts.

src: You may go walk, and give me leave a while: My lessons make no music in three parts.
trg: Are you so formal, sir? well, I must wait, And watch withal; for, but I be deceived, Our fine musician groweth amorous.

src: Are you so formal, sir? well, I must wait, And watch withal; for, but I be deceived, Our fine musician groweth amorous.
trg: Madam, before you touch the instrument, To learn the order of my fingering, I must begin with rudiments of art; To teach you gamut in a briefer sort, More pleasant, pithy and effectual, Than hath been taught by any of my trade: And there it is in writing, fairly drawn.

src: Madam, before you touch the instrument, To learn the order of my fingering, I must begin with rudiments of art; To teach you gamut in a briefer sort, More pleasant, pithy and effectual, Than hath been taught by any of my trade: And there it is in writing, fairly drawn.
trg: Why, I am past my gamut long ago.

src: Why, I am past my gamut long ago.
trg: Yet read the gamut of Hortensio.

src: Yet read the gamut of Hortensio.

trg: Mistress, your father prays you leave your books And help to dress your sister's chamber up: You know to-morrow is the wedding-day.

src: Mistress, your father prays you leave your books And help to dress your sister's chamber up: You know to-morrow is the wedding-day.
trg: Farewell, sweet masters both; I must be gone.

src: Farewell, sweet masters both; I must be gone.
trg: Faith, mistress, then I have no cause to stay.

src: Faith, mistress, then I have no cause to stay.
trg: But I have cause to pry into this pedant: Methinks he looks as though he were in love: Yet if thy thoughts, Bianca, be so humble To cast thy wandering eyes on every stale, Seize thee that list: if once I find thee ranging, Hortensio will be quit with thee by changing.

src: But I have cause to pry into this pedant: Methinks he looks as though he were in love: Yet if thy thoughts, Bianca, be so humble To cast thy wandering eyes on every stale, Seize thee that list: if once I find thee ranging, Hortensio will be quit with thee by changing.

trg: No shame but mine: I must, forsooth, be forced To give my hand opposed against my heart Unto a mad-brain rudesby full of spleen; Who woo'd in haste and means to wed at leisure. I told you, I, he was a frantic fool, Hiding his bitter jests in blunt behavior: And, to be noted for a merry man, He'll woo a thousand, 'point the day of marriage, Make feasts, invite friends, and proclaim the banns; Yet never means to wed where he hath woo'd. Now must the world point at poor Katharina, And say, 'Lo, there is mad Petruchio's wife, If it would please him come and marry her!'

src: No shame but mine: I must, forsooth, be forced To give my hand opposed against my heart Unto a mad-brain rudesby full of spleen; Who woo'd in haste and means to wed at leisure. I told you, I, he was a frantic fool, Hiding his bitter jests in blunt behavior: And, to be noted for a merry man, He'll woo a thousand, 'point the day of marriage, Make feasts, invite friends, and proclaim the banns; Yet never means to wed where he hath woo'd. Now must the world point at poor Katharina, And say, 'Lo, there is mad Petruchio's wife, If it would please him come and marry her!'
trg: Patience, good Katharina, and Baptista too. Upon my life, Petruchio means but well, Whatever fortune stays him from his word: Though he be blunt, I know him passing wise; Though he be merry, yet withal he's honest.

src: Patience, good Katharina, and Baptista too. Upon my life, Petruchio means but well, Whatever fortune stays him from his word: Though he be blunt, I know him passing wise; Though he be merry, yet withal he's honest.
trg: Would Katharina had never seen him though!

src: Would Katharina had never seen him though!
trg: Go, girl; I cannot blame thee now to weep; For such an injury would vex a very saint, Much more a shrew of thy impatient humour.

src: Go, girl; I cannot blame thee now to weep; For such an injury would vex a very saint, Much more a shrew of thy impatient humour.
trg: Master, master! news, old news, and such news as you never heard of!

src: Master, master! news, old news, and such news as you never heard of!
trg: Is it new and old too? how may that be?

src: Is it new and old too? how may that be?
trg: Why, is it not news, to hear of Petruchio's coming?

src: Why, is it not news, to hear of Petruchio's coming?
trg: Is he come?

src: Is he come?
trg: Why, no, sir.

src: Why, no, sir.
trg: What then?

src: What then?
trg: He is coming.

src: He is coming.
trg: When will he be here?

src: When will he be here?
trg: When he stands where I am and sees you there.

src: When he stands where I am and sees you there.
trg: But say, what to thine old news?

src: But say, what to thine old news?
trg: Why, Petruchio is coming in a new hat and an old jerkin, a pair of old breeches thrice turned, a pair of boots that have been candle-cases, one buckled, another laced, an old rusty sword ta'en out of the town-armory, with a broken hilt, and chapeless; with two broken points: his horse hipped with an old mothy saddle and stirrups of no kindred; besides, possessed with the glanders and like to mose in the chine; troubled with the lampass, infected with the fashions, full of wingdalls, sped with spavins, rayed with yellows, past cure of the fives, stark spoiled with the staggers, begnawn with the bots, swayed in the back and shoulder-shotten; near-legged before and with, a half-chequed bit and a head-stall of sheeps leather which, being restrained to keep him from stumbling, hath been often burst and now repaired with knots; one girth six time pieced and a woman's crupper of velure, which hath two letters for her name fairly set down in studs, and here and there pieced with packthread.

src: Why, Petruchio is coming in a new hat and an old jerkin, a pair of old breeches thrice turned, a pair of boots that have been candle-cases, one buckled, another laced, an old rusty sword ta'en out of the town-armory, with a broken hilt, and chapeless; with two broken points: his horse hipped with an old mothy saddle and stirrups of no kindred; besides, possessed with the glanders and like to mose in the chine; troubled with the lampass, infected with the fashions, full of wingdalls, sped with spavins, rayed with yellows, past cure of the fives, stark spoiled with the staggers, begnawn with the bots, swayed in the back and shoulder-shotten; near-legged before and with, a half-chequed bit and a head-stall of sheeps leather which, being restrained to keep him from stumbling, hath been often burst and now repaired with knots; one girth six time pieced and a woman's crupper of velure, which hath two letters for her name fairly set down in studs, and here and there pieced with packthread.
trg: Who comes with him?

src: Who comes with him?
trg: O, sir, his lackey, for all the world caparisoned like the horse; with a linen stock on one leg and a kersey boot-hose on the other, gartered with a red and blue list; an old hat and 'the humour of forty fancies' pricked in't for a feather: a monster, a very monster in apparel, and not like a Christian footboy or a gentleman's lackey.

src: O, sir, his lackey, for all the world caparisoned like the horse; with a linen stock on one leg and a kersey boot-hose on the other, gartered with a red and blue list; an old hat and 'the humour of forty fancies' pricked in't for a feather: a monster, a very monster in apparel, and not like a Christian footboy or a gentleman's lackey.
trg: 'Tis some odd humour pricks him to this fashion; Yet oftentimes he goes but mean-apparell'd.

src: 'Tis some odd humour pricks him to this fashion; Yet oftentimes he goes but mean-apparell'd.
trg: I am glad he's come, howsoe'er he comes.

src: I am glad he's come, howsoe'er he comes.
trg: Why, sir, he comes not.

src: Why, sir, he comes not.
trg: Didst thou not say he comes?

src: Didst thou not say he comes?
trg: Who? that Petruchio came?

src: Who? that Petruchio came?
trg: Ay, that Petruchio came.

src: Ay, that Petruchio came.
trg: No, sir, I say his horse comes, with him on his back.

src: No, sir, I say his horse comes, with him on his back.
trg: Why, that's all one.

src: Why, that's all one.
trg: Nay, by Saint Jamy, I hold you a penny, A horse and a man Is more than one, And yet not many.

src: Nay, by Saint Jamy, I hold you a penny, A horse and a man Is more than one, And yet not many.
trg: Come, where be these gallants? who's at home?

src: Come, where be these gallants? who's at home?
trg: You are welcome, sir.

src: You are welcome, sir.
trg: And yet I come not well.

src: And yet I come not well.
trg: And yet you halt not.

src: And yet you halt not.
trg: Not so well apparell'd As I wish you were.

src: Not so well apparell'd As I wish you were.
trg: Were it better, I should rush in thus. But where is Kate? where is my lovely bride? How does my father? Gentles, methinks you frown: And wherefore gaze this goodly company, As if they saw some wondrous monument, Some comet or unusual prodigy?

src: Were it better, I should rush in thus. But where is Kate? where is my lovely bride? How does my father? Gentles, methinks you frown: And wherefore gaze this goodly company, As if they saw some wondrous monument, Some comet or unusual prodigy?
trg: Why, sir, you know this is your wedding-day: First were we sad, fearing you would not come; Now sadder, that you come so unprovided. Fie, doff this habit, shame to your estate, An eye-sore to our solemn festival!

src: Why, sir, you know this is your wedding-day: First were we sad, fearing you would not come; Now sadder, that you come so unprovided. Fie, doff this habit, shame to your estate, An eye-sore to our solemn festival!
trg: And tells us, what occasion of import Hath all so long detain'd you from your wife, And sent you hither so unlike yourself?

src: And tells us, what occasion of import Hath all so long detain'd you from your wife, And sent you hither so unlike yourself?
trg: Tedious it were to tell, and harsh to hear: Sufficeth I am come to keep my word, Though in some part enforced to digress; Which, at more leisure, I will so excuse As you shall well be satisfied withal. But where is Kate? I stay too long from her: The morning wears, 'tis time we were at church.

src: Tedious it were to tell, and harsh to hear: Sufficeth I am come to keep my word, Though in some part enforced to digress; Which, at more leisure, I will so excuse As you shall well be satisfied withal. But where is Kate? I stay too long from her: The morning wears, 'tis time we were at church.
trg: See not your bride in these unreverent robes: Go to my chamber; Put on clothes of mine.

src: See not your bride in these unreverent robes: Go to my chamber; Put on clothes of mine.
trg: Not I, believe me: thus I'll visit her.

src: Not I, believe me: thus I'll visit her.
trg: But thus, I trust, you will not marry her.

src: But thus, I trust, you will not marry her.
trg: Good sooth, even thus; therefore ha' done with words: To me she's married, not unto my clothes: Could I repair what she will wear in me, As I can change these poor accoutrements, 'Twere well for Kate and better for myself. But what a fool am I to chat with you, When I should bid good morrow to my bride, And seal the title with a lovely kiss!

src: Good sooth, even thus; therefore ha' done with words: To me she's married, not unto my clothes: Could I repair what she will wear in me, As I can change these poor accoutrements, 'Twere well for Kate and better for myself. trg: Trembled and shook; for why, he stamp'd and swore, As if the vicar meant to cozen him. But after many ceremonies done, He calls for wine: 'A health!' quoth he, as if He had been aboard, carousing to his mates After a storm; quaff'd off the muscadel And threw the sops all in the sexton's face; Having no other reason But that his beard grew thin and hungerly And seem'd to ask him sops as he was drinking. This done, he took the bride about the neck And kiss'd her lips with such a clamorous smack That at the parting all the church did echo: And I seeing this came thence for very shame; And after me, I know, the rout is coming. Such a mad marriage never was before: Hark, hark! I hear the minstrels play.

trg: They shall go forward, Kate, at thy command. trg: Thus have I politicly begun my reign, And 'tis my hope to end successfully. My falcon now is sharp and passing empty; And till she stoop she must not be full-gorged, For then she never looks upon her lure. Another way I have to man my haggard, To make her come and know her keeper's call, That is, to watch her, as we watch these kites That bate and beat and will not be obedient. She eat no meat to-day, nor none shall eat; Last night she slept not, nor to-night she shall not; As with the meat, some undeserved fault I'll find about the making of the bed; And here I'll fling the pillow, there the bolster, This way the coverlet, another way the sheets: Ay, and amid this hurly I intend That all is done in reverend care of her; And in conclusion she shall watch all night: And if she chance to nod I'll rail and brawl And with the clamour keep her still awake. This is a way to kill a wife with kindness; And thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour. He that knows better how to tame a shrew, Now let him speak: 'tis charity to show.

src: Thus have I politicly begun my reign, And 'tis my hope to end successfully. My falcon now is sharp and passing empty; And till she stoop she must not be full-gorged, For then she never looks upon her lure. src: Signior Hortensio, I have often heard Of your entire affection to Bianca; And since mine eyes are witness of her lightness, I will with you, if you be so contented, Forswear Bianca and her love for ever.
trg: See, how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio, Here is my hand, and here I firmly vow Never to woo her no more, but do forswear her, As one unworthy all the former favours That I have fondly flatter'd her withal.

src: See, how they kiss and court! Signior Lucentio, Here is my hand, and here I firmly vow Never to woo her no more, but do forswear her, As one unworthy all the former favours That I have fondly flatter'd her withal.

src: And here I take the unfeigned oath, Never to marry with her though she would entreat: Fie on her! see, how beastly she doth court him!
trg: Would all the world but he had quite forsworn! For me, that I may surely keep mine oath, I will be married to a wealthy widow, Ere three days pass, which hath as long loved me As I have loved this proud disdainful haggard. And so farewell, Signior Lucentio. Kindness in women, not their beauteous looks, Shall win my love: and so I take my leave, In resolution as I swore before.

src: And what of him, Tranio?

Your ships are stay'd at Venice, and the duke, For private quarrel 'twixt your duke and him, Hath publish'd and proclaim'd it openly: 'Tis, marvel, but that you are but newly come, You might have heard it else proclaim'd about.

src: Well, sir, to do you courtesy, This will I do, and this I will advise you: First, tell me, have you ever been at Pisa?
trg: Ay, sir, in Pisa have I often been, Pisa renowned for grave citizens.

src: Among them know you one Vincentio?
trg: I know him not, but I have heard of him; A merchant of incomparable wealth.

src: I know him not, but I have heard of him; A merchant of incomparable wealth.

src: He is my father, sir; and, sooth to say, In countenance somewhat doth resemble you.

trg: To save your life in this extremity, This favour will I do you for his sake; And think it not the worst of an your fortunes That you are like to Sir Vincentio. His name and credit shall you undertake, And in my house you shall be friendly lodged: Look that you take upon you as you should; You understand me, sir: so shall you stay Till you have done your business in the city: If this be courtesy, sir, accept of it.

src: To save your life in this extremity, This favour will I do you for his sake; And think it not the worst of an your fortunes That you are like to Sir Vincentio. src: O sir, I do; and will repute you ever The patron of my life and liberty.
trg: Then go with me to make the matter good. This, by the way, I let you understand; my father is here look'd for every day, To pass assurance of a dower in marriage 'Twixt me and one Baptista's daughter here: In all these circumstances I'll instruct you: Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.

src: Then go with me to make the matter good. This, by the way, I let you understand; my father is here look'd for every day, To pass assurance of a dower in marriage 'Twixt me and one Baptista's daughter here: In all these circumstances I'll instruct you: Go with me to clothe you as becomes you.
trg: No, no, forsooth; I dare not for my life.

src: No, no, forsooth; I dare not for my life.
trg: The more my wrong, the more his spite appears: What, did he marry me to famish me? Beggars, that come unto my father's door, Upon entreaty have a present aims; If not, elsewhere they meet with charity: But I, who never knew how to entreat, Nor never needed that I should entreat, Am starved for meat, giddy for lack of sleep, With oath kept waking and with brawling fed: And that which spites me more than all these wants, He does it under name of perfect love; As who should say, if I should sleep or eat, 'Twere deadly sickness or else present death. I prithee go and get me some repast; I care not what, so it be wholesome food.

src: The more my wrong, the more his spite appears: What, did he marry me to famish me? trg: What say you to a neat's foot?

src: What say you to a neat's foot?

src: 'Tis passing good: I prithee let me have it.

src: I fear it is too choleric a meat. How say you to a fat tripe finely broil'd?
trg: I like it well: good Grumio, fetch it me.

src: I like it well: good Grumio, fetch it me.
trg: I cannot tell; I fear 'tis choleric. What say you to a piece of beef and mustard?

src: I cannot tell; I fear 'tis choleric. What say you to a piece of beef and mustard?
trg: A dish that I do love to feed upon.

src: A dish that I do love to feed upon.
trg: Ay, but the mustard is too hot a little.

src: Ay, but the mustard is too hot a little.
trg: Why then, the beef, and let the mustard rest.

src: Why then, the beef, and let the mustard rest.
trg: Nay then, I will not: you shall have the mustard, Or else you get no beef of Grumio.

src: Nay then, I will not: you shall have the mustard, Or else you get no beef of Grumio.

src: Then both, or one, or any thing thou wilt.

src: Why then, the mustard without the beef.
trg: Go, get thee gone, thou false deluding slave, That feed'st me with the very name of meat: Sorrow on thee and all the pack of you, That triumph thus upon my misery! Go, get thee gone, I say.

src: Go, get thee gone, thou false deluding slave, That feed'st me with the very name of meat: Sorrow on thee and all the pack of you, That triumph thus upon my misery! Go, get thee gone, I say.
trg: How fares my Kate? What, sweeting, all amort?

src: How fares my Kate? What, sweeting, all amort?

src: Mistress, what cheer?

src: Faith, as cold as can be.

What, not a word? Nay, then thou lovest it not; And all my pains is sorted to no proof. Here, take away this dish.

src: I pray you, let it stand.

src: The poorest service is repaid with thanks; And so shall mine, before you touch the meat.

src: I thank you, sir.

src: Signior Petruchio, fie! you are to blame. Come, mistress Kate, I'll bear you company.

src: Here is the cap your worship did bespeak.
trg: Why, this was moulded on a porringer; A velvet dish: fie, fie! 'tis lewd and filthy: Why, 'tis a cockle or a walnut-shell, A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby's cap: Away with it! come, let me have a bigger.

src: Why, this was moulded on a porringer; A velvet dish: fie, fie! 'tis lewd and filthy: Why, 'tis a cockle or a walnut-shell, A knack, a toy, a trick, a baby's cap: Away with it! come, let me have a bigger.
trg: I'll have no bigger: this doth fit the time, And gentlewomen wear such caps as these

src: I'll have no bigger: this doth fit the time, And gentlewomen wear such caps as these
trg: When you are gentle, you shall have one too, And not till then.

src: When you are gentle, you shall have one too, And not till then.

trg: Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak; And speak I will; I am no child, no babe: Your betters have endured me say my mind, And if you cannot, best you stop your ears. My tongue will tell the anger of my heart, Or else my heart concealing it will break, And rather than it shall, I will be free Even to the uttermost, as I please, in words.

trg: Why, thou say'st true; it is a paltry cap, A custard-coffin, a bauble, a silken pie: I love thee well, in that thou likest it not.

src: Why, thou say'st true; it is a paltry cap, A custard-coffin, a bauble, a silken pie: I love thee well, in that thou likest it not.

src: Love me or love me not, I like the cap; And it I will have, or I will have none.
trg: Thy gown? why, ay: come, tailor, let us see't. O mercy, God! what masquing stuff is here? What's this? a sleeve? 'tis like a demi-cannon: What, up and down, carved like an apple-tart? Here's snip and nip and cut and slish and slash, Like to a censer in a barber's shop: Why, what, i' devil's name, tailor, call'st thou this?

src: Thy gown? why, ay: come, tailor, let us see't. O mercy, God! what masquing stuff is here? What's this? a sleeve? 'tis like a demi-cannon: What, up and down, carved like an apple-tart? src: You bid me make it orderly and well, According to the fashion and the time.
trg: Marry, and did; but if you be remember'd, I did not bid you mar it to the time. Go, hop me over every kennel home, For you shall hop without my custom, sir: I'll none of it: hence! make your best of it.

src: Marry, and did; but if you be remember'd, I did not bid you mar it to the time. Go, hop me over every kennel home, For you shall hop without my custom, sir: I'll none of it: hence! make your best of it.

src: I never saw a better-fashion'd gown, More quaint, more pleasing, nor more commendable: Belike you mean to make a puppet of me.

src: She says your worship means to make a puppet of her.

I tell thee, I, that thou hast marr'd her gown.

src: O monstrous arrogance! Thou liest, thou thread, thou thimble, Thou yard, three-quarters, half-yard, quarter, nail! Thou flea, thou nit, thou winter-cricket thou! src: But how did you desire it should be made?
trg: Marry, sir, with needle and thread.

src: Marry, sir, with needle and thread.

src: But did you not request to have it cut?
trg: Thou hast faced many things.

src: Thou hast faced many things.
trg: I have.

src: I have.
trg: Face not me: thou hast braved many men; brave not me; I will neither be faced nor braved. I say unto thee, I bid thy master cut out the gown; but I did not bid him cut it to pieces: ergo, thou liest.

src: Face not me: thou hast braved many men; brave not me; I will neither be faced nor braved. I say unto thee, I bid thy master cut out the gown; but I did not bid him cut it to pieces: ergo, thou liest.

src: Why, here is the note of the fashion to testify

src: The note lies in's throat, if he say I said so.

src: Proceed.

src: I confess the cape.

src: I confess two sleeves.

src: Error i' the bill, sir; error i' the bill. I commanded the sleeves should be cut out and sewed up again; and that I'll prove upon thee, though thy little finger be armed in a thimble.
trg: This is true that I say: an I had thee in place where, thou shouldst know it.

src: This is true that I say: an I had thee in place where, thou shouldst know it.
trg: I am for thee straight: take thou the bill, give me thy mete-yard, and spare not me.

src: I am for thee straight: take thou the bill, give me thy mete-yard, and spare not me.

src: God-a-mercy, Grumio! then he shall have no odds.
trg: Well, sir, in brief, the gown is not for me.

src: Well, sir, in brief, the gown is not for me.

src: You are i' the right, sir: 'tis for my mistress.
trg: Go, take it up unto thy master's use.

src: Go, take it up unto thy master's use.
trg: Villain, not for thy life: take up my mistress' gown for thy master's use!

src: Villain, not for thy life: take up my mistress' gown for thy master's use!

src: Why, sir, what's your conceit in that?
trg: O, sir, the conceit is deeper than you think for: Take up my mistress' gown to his master's use! O, fie, fie, fie!

src: O, sir, the conceit is deeper than you think for: Take up my mistress' gown to his master's use! O, fie, fie, fie!

src: Tailor, I'll pay thee for thy gown tomorrow: Take no unkindness of his hasty words: Away! I say; commend me to thy master.
trg: Well, come, my Kate; we will unto your father's Even in these honest mean habiliments: Our purses shall be proud, our garments poor; For 'tis the mind that makes the body rich; And as the sun breaks through the darkest clouds, So honour peereth in the meanest habit. What is the jay more precious than the lark, Because his fathers are more beautiful? Or is the adder better than the eel, Because his painted skin contents the eye? O, no, good Kate; neither art thou the worse For this poor furniture and mean array. if thou account'st it shame. lay it on me; And therefore frolic: we will hence forthwith, To feast and sport us at thy father's house. Go, call my men, and let us straight to him; And bring our horses unto Long-lane end; There will we mount, and thither walk on foot Let's see; I think 'tis now some seven o'clock, And well we may come there by dinner-time.

src: It shall be seven ere I go to horse: Look, what I speak, or do, or think to do, You are still crossing it. Sirs, let't alone: I will not go to-day; and ere I do, It shall be what o'clock I say it is.

trg: Sir, this is the house: please it you that I call?

src: Sir, this is the house: please it you that I call?
trg: Ay, what else? and but I be deceived Signior Baptista may remember me, Near twenty years ago, in Genoa, Where we were lodgers at the Pegasus.

src: Ay, what else? and but I be deceived Signior Baptista may remember me, Near twenty years ago, in Genoa, Where we were lodgers at the Pegasus.
trg: 'Tis well; and hold your own, in any case, With such austerity as 'longeth to a father.

src: 'Tis well; and hold your own, in any case, With such austerity as 'longeth to a father.
trg: I warrant you. But, sir, here comes your boy; 'Twere good he were school'd.

src: I warrant you. But, sir, here comes your boy; 'Twere good he were school'd.
trg: Fear you not him. Sirrah Biondello, Now do your duty throughly, I advise you: Imagine 'twere the right Vincentio.

src: Fear you not him. Sirrah Biondello, Now do your duty throughly, I advise you: Imagine 'twere the right Vincentio.
trg: Tut, fear not me.

src: Tut, fear not me.
trg: But hast thou done thy errand to Baptista?

src: But hast thou done thy errand to Baptista?
trg: I told him that your father was at Venice, And that you look'd for him this day in Padua.

src: I told him that your father was at Venice, And that you look'd for him this day in Padua.
trg: Thou'rt a tall fellow: hold thee that to drink. Here comes Baptista: set your countenance, sir. Signior Baptista, you are happily met. Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of: I pray you stand good father to me now, Give me Bianca for my patrimony.

src: Thou'rt a tall fellow: hold thee that to drink. Here comes Baptista: set your countenance, sir. Signior Baptista, you are happily met. Sir, this is the gentleman I told you of: I pray you stand good father to me now, Give me Bianca for my patrimony.
trg: Soft son! Sir, by your leave: having come to Padua To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio Made me acquainted with a weighty cause Of love between your daughter and himself: And, for the good report I hear of you And for the love he beareth to your daughter And she to him, to stay him not too long, I am content, in a good father's care, To have him match'd; and if you please to like No worse than I, upon some agreement Me shall you find ready and willing With one consent to have her so bestow'd; For curious I cannot be with you, Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so well.

src: Soft son! Sir, by your leave: having come to Padua To gather in some debts, my son Lucentio Made me acquainted with a weighty cause Of love between your daughter and himself: And, for the good report I hear of you And for the love he beareth to your daughter And she to him, to stay him not too long, I am content, in a good father's care, To have him match'd; and if you please to like No worse than I, upon some agreement Me shall you find ready and willing With one consent to have her so bestow'd; For curious I cannot be with you, Signior Baptista, of whom I hear so well.
trg: Sir, pardon me in what I have to say: Your plainness and your shortness please me well. Right true it is, your son Lucentio here Doth love my daughter and she loveth him, Or both dissemble deeply their affections: And therefore, if you say no more than this, That like a father you will deal with him And pass my daughter a sufficient dower, The match is made, and all is done: Your son shall have my daughter with consent.

src: Sir, pardon me in what I have to say: Your plainness and your shortness please me well. Right true it is, your son Lucentio here Doth love my daughter and she loveth him, Or both dissemble deeply their affections: And therefore, if you say no more than this, That like a father you will deal with him And pass my daughter a sufficient dower, The match is made, and all is done: Your son shall have my daughter with consent.
trg: I thank you, sir. Where then do you know best We be affied and such assurance ta'en As shall with either part's agreement stand?

src: I thank you, sir. Where then do you know best We be affied and such assurance ta'en As shall with either part's agreement stand?
trg: Not in my house, Lucentio; for, you know, Pitchers have ears, and I have many servants: Besides, old Gremio is hearkening still; And happily we might be interrupted.

src: Not in my house, Lucentio; for, you know, Pitchers have ears, and I have many servants: Besides, old Gremio is hearkening still; And happily we might be interrupted.
trg: Then at my lodging, an it like you: There doth my father lie; and there, this night, We'll pass the business privately and well. Send for your daughter by your servant here: My boy shall fetch the scrivener presently. The worst is this, that, at so slender warning, You are like to have a thin and slender pittance.

src: Then at my lodging, an it like you: There doth my father lie; and there, this night, We'll pass the business privately and well. Send for your daughter by your servant here: My boy shall fetch the scrivener presently. The worst is this, that, at so slender warning, You are like to have a thin and slender pittance.
trg: It likes me well. Biondello, hie you home, And bid Bianca make her ready straight; And, if you will, tell what hath happened, Lucentio's father is arrived in Padua, And how she's like to be Lucentio's wife.

src: It likes me well. Biondello, hie you home, And bid Bianca make her ready straight; And, if you will, tell what hath happened, Lucentio's father is arrived in Padua, And how she's like to be Lucentio's wife.
trg: I pray the gods she may with all my heart!

src: I pray the gods she may with all my heart!
trg: Dally not with the gods, but get thee gone. Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way? Welcome! one mess is like to be your cheer: Come, sir; we will better it in Pisa.

src: Dally not with the gods, but get thee gone. Signior Baptista, shall I lead the way? Welcome! one mess is like to be your cheer: Come, sir; we will better it in Pisa.
trg: I follow you.

src: I follow you.
trg: Cambio!

src: Cambio!
trg: What sayest thou, Biondello?

src: What sayest thou, Biondello?
trg: You saw my master wink and laugh upon you?

src: You saw my master wink and laugh upon you?
trg: Biondello, what of that?

src: Biondello, what of that?
trg: Faith, nothing; but has left me here behind, to expound the meaning or moral of his signs and tokens.

src: Faith, nothing; but has left me here behind, to expound the meaning or moral of his signs and tokens.
trg: I pray thee, moralize them.

src: I pray thee, moralize them.
trg: Then thus. Baptista is safe, talking with the deceiving father of a deceitful son.

src: Then thus. Baptista is safe, talking with the deceiving father of a deceitful son.
trg: And what of him?

src: And what of him?
trg: His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.

src: His daughter is to be brought by you to the supper.
trg: And then?

src: And then?
trg: The old priest of Saint Luke's church is at your command at all hours.

src: The old priest of Saint Luke's church is at your command at all hours.
trg: And what of all this?

src: And what of all this?
trg: I cannot tell; expect they are busied about a counterfeit assurance: take you assurance of her, 'cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum:' to the church; take the priest, clerk, and some sufficient honest witnesses: If this be not that you look for, I have no more to say, But bid Bianca farewell for ever and a day.

src: I cannot tell; expect they are busied about a counterfeit assurance: take you assurance of her, 'cum privilegio ad imprimendum solum:' to the church; take the priest, clerk, and some sufficient honest witnesses: If this be not that you look for, I have no more to say, But bid Bianca farewell for ever and a day.
trg: Hearest thou, Biondello?

src: Hearest thou, Biondello?
trg: I cannot tarry: I knew a wench married in an afternoon as she went to the garden for parsley to stuff a rabbit; and so may you, sir: and so, adieu, sir. My master hath appointed me to go to Saint Luke's, to bid the priest be ready to come against you come with your appendix.

src: I cannot tarry: I knew a wench married in an afternoon as she went to the garden for parsley to stuff a rabbit; and so may you, sir: and so, adieu, sir. My master hath appointed me to go to Saint Luke's, to bid the priest be ready to come against you come with your appendix.
trg: I may, and will, if she be so contented: She will be pleased; then wherefore should I doubt? Hap what hap may, I'll roundly go about her: It shall go hard if Cambio go without her.

src: I may, and will, if she be so contented: She will be pleased; then wherefore should I doubt? Hap what hap may, I'll roundly go about her: It shall go hard if Cambio go without her.
trg: Come on, i' God's name; once more toward our father's. Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!

src: Come on, i' God's name; once more toward our father's. Good Lord, how bright and goodly shines the moon!
trg: The moon! the sun: it is not moonlight now.

src: The moon! the sun: it is not moonlight now.
trg: I say it is the moon that shines so bright.

src: I say it is the moon that shines so bright.
trg: I know it is the sun that shines so bright.

src: I know it is the sun that shines so bright.
trg: Now, by my mother's son, and that's myself, It shall be moon, or star, or what I list, Or ere I journey to your father's house. Go on, and fetch our horses back again. Evermore cross'd and cross'd; nothing but cross'd!

src: Now, by my mother's son, and that's myself, It shall be moon, or star, or what I list, Or ere I journey to your father's house. Go on, and fetch our horses back again. Evermore cross'd and cross'd; nothing but cross'd!
trg: Say as he says, or we shall never go.

src: Say as he says, or we shall never go.
trg: Forward, I pray, since we have come so far, And be it moon, or sun, or what you please: An if you please to call it a rush-candle, Henceforth I vow it shall be so for me.

src: Forward, I pray, since we have come so far, And be it moon, or sun, or what you please: An if you please to call it a rush-candle, Henceforth I vow it shall be so for me.
trg: I say it is the moon.

src: I say it is the moon.
trg: I know it is the moon.

src: I know it is the moon.
trg: Nay, then you lie: it is the blessed sun.

src: Nay, then you lie: it is the blessed sun.
trg: Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun: But sun it is not, when you say it is not; And the moon changes even as your mind. What you will have it named, even that it is; And so it shall be so for Katharina.

src: Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun: But sun it is not, when you say it is not; And the moon changes even as your mind. What you will have it named, even that it is; And so it shall be so for Katharina.
trg: Petruchio, go thy ways; the field is won.

src: Petruchio, go thy ways; the field is won.
trg: Well, forward, forward! thus the bowl should run, And not unluckily against the bias. But, soft! company is coming here. Good morrow, gentle mistress: where away? Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly too, Hast thou beheld a fresher gentlewoman? Such war of white and red within her cheeks! What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty, As those two eyes become that heavenly face? Fair lovely maid, once more good day to thee. Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty's sake.

src: Well, forward, forward! thus the bowl should run, And not unluckily against the bias. But, soft! company is coming here. Good morrow, gentle mistress: where away? Tell me, sweet Kate, and tell me truly too, Hast thou beheld a fresher gentlewoman? Such war of white and red within her cheeks! What stars do spangle heaven with such beauty, As those two eyes become that heavenly face? Fair lovely maid, once more good day to thee. Sweet Kate, embrace her for her beauty's sake.
trg: A' will make the man mad, to make a woman of him.

src: A' will make the man mad, to make a woman of him.
trg: Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet, Whither away, or where is thy abode? Happy the parents of so fair a child; Happier the man, whom favourable stars Allot thee for his lovely bed-fellow!

src: Young budding virgin, fair and fresh and sweet, Whither away, or where is thy abode? Happy the parents of so fair a child; Happier the man, whom favourable stars Allot thee for his lovely bed-fellow!
trg: Why, how now, Kate! I hope thou art not mad: This is a man, old, wrinkled, faded, wither'd, And not a maiden, as thou say'st he is.

src: Why, how now, Kate! I hope thou art not mad: This is a man, old, wrinkled, faded, wither'd, And not a maiden, as thou say'st he is.
trg: Pardon, old father, my mistaking eyes, That have been so bedazzled with the sun That everything I look on seemeth green: Now I perceive thou art a reverend father; Pardon, I pray thee, for my mad mistaking.

src: Pardon, old father, my mistaking eyes, That have been so bedazzled with the sun That everything I look on seemeth green: Now I perceive thou art a reverend father; Pardon, I pray thee, for my mad mistaking.
trg: Do, good old grandsire; and withal make known Which way thou travellest: if along with us, We shall be joyful of thy company.

src: Do, good old grandsire; and withal make known Which way thou travellest: if along with us, We shall be joyful of thy company.
trg: Fair sir, and you my merry mistress, That with your strange encounter much amazed me, My name is call'd Vincentio; my dwelling Pisa; And bound I am to Padua; there to visit A son of mine, which long I have not seen.

src: Fair sir, and you my merry mistress, That with your strange encounter much amazed me, My name is call'd Vincentio; my dwelling Pisa; And bound I am to Padua; there to visit A son of mine, which long I have not seen.
trg: What is his name?

src: What is his name?
trg: Lucentio, gentle sir.

src: Lucentio, gentle sir.
trg: Happily we met; the happier for thy son. And now by law, as well as reverend age, I may entitle thee my loving father: The sister to my wife, this gentlewoman, Thy son by this hath married. Wonder not, Nor be grieved: she is of good esteem, Her dowery wealthy, and of worthy birth; Beside, so qualified as may beseem The spouse of any noble gentleman. Let me embrace with old Vincentio, And wander we to see thy honest son, Who will of thy arrival be full joyous.

src: Happily we met; the happier for thy son. And now by law, as well as reverend age, I may entitle thee my loving father: The sister to my wife, this gentlewoman, Thy son by this hath married. Wonder not, Nor be grieved: she is of good esteem, Her dowery wealthy, and of worthy birth; Beside, so qualified as may beseem The spouse of any noble gentleman. Let me embrace with old Vincentio, And wander we to see thy honest son, Who will of thy arrival be full joyous.
trg: But is it true? or else is it your pleasure, Like pleasant travellers, to break a jest Upon the company you overtake?

src: But is it true? or else is it your pleasure, Like pleasant travellers, to break a jest Upon the company you overtake?
trg: I do assure thee, father, so it is.

src: I do assure thee, father, so it is.
trg: Come, go along, and see the truth hereof; For our first merriment hath made thee jealous.

src: Come, go along, and see the truth hereof; For our first merriment hath made thee jealous.
trg: Well, Petruchio, this has put me in heart. Have to my widow! and if she be froward, Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward.

src: Well, Petruchio, this has put me in heart. Have to my widow! and if she be froward, Then hast thou taught Hortensio to be untoward.
trg: Softly and swiftly, sir; for the priest is ready.

src: Softly and swiftly, sir; for the priest is ready.
trg: I fly, Biondello: but they may chance to need thee at home; therefore leave us.

src: I fly, Biondello: but they may chance to need thee at home; therefore leave us.
trg: Nay, faith, I'll see the church o' your back; and then come back to my master's as soon as I can.

src: Nay, faith, I'll see the church o' your back; and then come back to my master's as soon as I can.
trg: I marvel Cambio comes not all this while.

src: I marvel Cambio comes not all this while.
trg: Sir, here's the door, this is Lucentio's house: My father's bears more toward the market-place; Thither must I, and here I leave you, sir.

src: Sir, here's the door, this is Lucentio's house: My father's bears more toward the market-place; Thither must I, and here I leave you, sir.
trg: You shall not choose but drink before you go: I think I shall command your welcome here, And, by all likelihood, some cheer is toward.

src: You shall not choose but drink before you go: I think I shall command your welcome here, And, by all likelihood, some cheer is toward.
trg: They're busy within; you were best knock louder.

src: They're busy within; you were best knock louder.
trg: What's he that knocks as he would beat down the gate?

src: What's he that knocks as he would beat down the gate?
trg: Is Signior Lucentio within, sir?

src: Is Signior Lucentio within, sir?
trg: He's within, sir, but not to be spoken withal.

src: He's within, sir, but not to be spoken withal.
trg: What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two, to make merry withal?

src: What if a man bring him a hundred pound or two, to make merry withal?
trg: Keep your hundred pounds to yourself: he shall need none, so long as I live.

src: Keep your hundred pounds to yourself: he shall need none, so long as I live.
trg: Nay, I told you your son was well beloved in Padua. Do you hear, sir? To leave frivolous circumstances, I pray you, tell Signior Lucentio that his father is come from Pisa, and is here at the door to speak with him.

src: Nay, I told you your son was well beloved in Padua. Do you hear, sir? To leave frivolous circumstances, I pray you, tell Signior Lucentio that his father is come from Pisa, and is here at the door to speak with him.
trg: Thou liest: his father is come from Padua and here looking out at the window.

src: Thou liest: his father is come from Padua and here looking out at the window.
trg: Art thou his father?

src: Art thou his father?
trg: Ay, sir; so his mother says, if I may believe her.

src: Ay, sir; so his mother says, if I may believe her.

trg: Lay hands on the villain: I believe a' means to cozen somebody in this city under my countenance.

src: Lay hands on the villain: I believe a' means to cozen somebody in this city under my countenance.
trg: I have seen them in the church together: God send 'em good shipping! But who is here? mine old master Vincentio! now we are undone and brought to nothing.

src: I have seen them in the church together: God send 'em good shipping! But who is here? mine old master Vincentio! now we are undone and brought to nothing.

trg: Hope I may choose, sir.

src: Hope I may choose, sir.
trg: Come hither, you rogue. What, have you forgot me?

src: Come hither, you rogue. What, have you forgot me?
trg: Forgot you! no, sir: I could not forget you, for I never saw you before in all my life.

src: Forgot you! no, sir: I could not forget you, for I never saw you before in all my life.
trg: What, you notorious villain, didst thou never see thy master's father, Vincentio?

src: What, you notorious villain, didst thou never see thy master's father, Vincentio?
trg: What, my old worshipful old master? yes, marry, sir: see where he looks out of the window.

src: What, my old worshipful old master? yes, marry, sir: see where he looks out of the window.
trg: Is't so, indeed.

src: Is't so, indeed.
trg: Help, help, help! here's a madman will murder me.

src: Help, help, help! here's a madman will murder me.
trg: Help, son! help, Signior Baptista!

src: Help, son! help, Signior Baptista!
trg: Prithee, Kate, let's stand aside and see the end of this controversy.

src: Prithee, Kate, let's stand aside and see the end of this controversy.
trg: Sir, what are you that offer to beat my servant?

src: Sir, what are you that offer to beat my servant?
trg: What am I, sir! nay, what are you, sir? O immortal gods! O fine villain! A silken doublet! a velvet hose! a scarlet cloak! and a copatain hat! O, I am undone! I am undone! while I play the good husband at home, my son and my servant spend all at the university.

src: What am I, sir! nay, what are you, sir? O immortal gods! O fine villain! A silken doublet! a velvet hose! a scarlet cloak! and a copatain hat! O, I am undone! I am undone! while I play the good husband at home, my son and my servant spend all at the university.
trg: How now! what's the matter?

src: How now! what's the matter?
trg: What, is the man lunatic?

src: What, is the man lunatic?
trg: Sir, you seem a sober ancient gentleman by your habit, but your words show you a madman. Why, sir, what 'cerns it you if I wear pearl and gold? I thank my good father, I am able to maintain it.

src: Sir, you seem a sober ancient gentleman by your habit, but your words show you a madman. Why, sir, what 'cerns it you if I wear pearl and gold? I thank my good father, I am able to maintain it.
trg: Thy father! O villain! he is a sailmaker in Bergamo.

src: Thy father! O villain! he is a sailmaker in Bergamo.
trg: You mistake, sir, you mistake, sir. Pray, what do you think is his name?

src: You mistake, sir, you mistake, sir. Pray, what do you think is his name?
trg: His name! as if I knew not his name: I have brought him up ever since he was three years old, and his name is Tranio.

src: His name! as if I knew not his name: I have brought him up ever since he was three years old, and his name is Tranio.
trg: Away, away, mad ass! his name is Lucentio and he is mine only son, and heir to the lands of me, Signior Vincentio.

src: Away, away, mad ass! his name is Lucentio and he is mine only son, and heir to the lands of me, Signior Vincentio.
trg: Lucentio! O, he hath murdered his master! Lay hold on him, I charge you, in the duke's name. O, my son, my son! Tell me, thou villain, where is my son Lucentio?

src: Lucentio! O, he hath murdered his master! Lay hold on him, I charge you, in the duke's name. O, my son, my son! Tell me, thou villain, where is my son Lucentio?
trg: Call forth an officer. Carry this mad knave to the gaol. Father Baptista, I charge you see that he be forthcoming.

src: Call forth an officer. Carry this mad knave to the gaol. Father Baptista, I charge you see that he be forthcoming.
trg: Carry me to the gaol!

src: Carry me to the gaol!
trg: Stay, officer: he shall not go to prison.

src: Stay, officer: he shall not go to prison.
trg: Talk not, Signior Gremio: I say he shall go to prison.

src: Talk not, Signior Gremio: I say he shall go to prison.
trg: Take heed, Signior Baptista, lest you be cony-catched in this business: I dare swear this is the right Vincentio.

src: Take heed, Signior Baptista, lest you be cony-catched in this business: I dare swear this is the right Vincentio.
trg: Swear, if thou darest.

src: Swear, if thou darest.
trg: Nay, I dare not swear it.

src: Nay, I dare not swear it.
trg: Then thou wert best say that I am not Lucentio.

src: Then thou wert best say that I am not Lucentio.
trg: Yes, I know thee to be Signior Lucentio.

src: Yes, I know thee to be Signior Lucentio.
trg: Away with the dotard! to the gaol with him!

src: Away with the dotard! to the gaol with him!
trg: Thus strangers may be hailed and abused: O monstrous villain!

src: Thus strangers may be hailed and abused: O monstrous villain!
trg: O! we are spoiled and--yonder he is: deny him, forswear him, or else we are all undone.

src: O! we are spoiled and--yonder he is: deny him, forswear him, or else we are all undone.

trg: Lives my sweet son?

src: Lives my sweet son?
trg: Pardon, dear father.

src: Pardon, dear father.
trg: How hast thou offended? Where is Lucentio?

src: How hast thou offended? Where is Lucentio?
trg: Here's Lucentio, Right son to the right Vincentio; That have by marriage made thy daughter mine, While counterfeit supposes bleared thine eyne.

src: Here's Lucentio, Right son to the right Vincentio; That have by marriage made thy daughter mine, While counterfeit supposes bleared thine eyne.
trg: Here's packing, with a witness to deceive us all!

src: Here's packing, with a witness to deceive us all!
trg: Where is that damned villain Tranio, That faced and braved me in this matter so?

src: Where is that damned villain Tranio, That faced and braved me in this matter so?
trg: Why, tell me, is not this my Cambio?

src: Why, tell me, is not this my Cambio?
trg: Cambio is changed into Lucentio.

src: Cambio is changed into Lucentio.
trg: Love wrought these miracles. Bianca's love Made me exchange my state with Tranio, While he did bear my countenance in the town; And happily I have arrived at the last Unto the wished haven of my bliss. What Tranio did, myself enforced him to; Then pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.

src: Love wrought these miracles. Bianca's love Made me exchange my state with Tranio, While he did bear my countenance in the town; And happily I have arrived at the last Unto the wished haven of my bliss. What Tranio did, myself enforced him to; Then pardon him, sweet father, for my sake.
trg: I'll slit the villain's nose, that would have sent me to the gaol.

src: I'll slit the villain's nose, that would have sent me to the gaol.
trg: But do you hear, sir? have you married my daughter without asking my good will?

src: But do you hear, sir? have you married my daughter without asking my good will?
trg: Fear not, Baptista; we will content you, go to: but I will in, to be revenged for this villany.

src: Fear not, Baptista; we will content you, go to: but I will in, to be revenged for this villany.
trg: And I, to sound the depth of this knavery.

src: And I, to sound the depth of this knavery.
trg: Look not pale, Bianca; thy father will not frown.

src: Look not pale, Bianca; thy father will not frown.
trg: My cake is dough; but I'll in among the rest, Out of hope of all, but my share of the feast.

src: My cake is dough; but I'll in among the rest, Out of hope of all, but my share of the feast.
trg: Husband, let's follow, to see the end of this ado.

src: Husband, let's follow, to see the end of this ado.
trg: First kiss me, Kate, and we will.

src: First kiss me, Kate, and we will.
trg: What, in the midst of the street?

src: What, in the midst of the street?
trg: What, art thou ashamed of me?

src: What, art thou ashamed of me?
trg: No, sir, God forbid; but ashamed to kiss.

src: No, sir, God forbid; but ashamed to kiss.
trg: Why, then let's home again. Come, sirrah, let's away.

src: Why, then let's home again. Come, sirrah, let's away.
trg: Nay, I will give thee a kiss: now pray thee, love, stay.

src: Nay, I will give thee a kiss: now pray thee, love, stay.
trg: Is not this well? Come, my sweet Kate: Better once than never, for never too late.

src: Is not this well? Come, my sweet Kate: Better once than never, for never too late.
trg: At last, though long, our jarring notes agree: And time it is, when raging war is done, To smile at scapes and perils overblown. My fair Bianca, bid my father welcome, While I with self-same kindness welcome thine. Brother Petruchio, sister Katharina, And thou, Hortensio, with thy loving widow, Feast with the best, and welcome to my house: My banquet is to close our stomachs up, After our great good cheer. trg: Fie, fie! unknit that threatening unkind brow, And dart not scornful glances from those eyes, To wound thy lord, thy king, thy governor: It blots thy beauty as frosts do bite the meads, Confounds thy fame as whirlwinds shake fair buds, And in no sense is meet or amiable. A woman moved is like a fountain troubled, Muddy, ill-seeming, thick, bereft of beauty; And while it is so, none so dry or thirsty Will deign to sip or touch one drop of it. Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper, Thy head, thy sovereign; one that cares for thee, And for thy maintenance commits his body To painful labour both by sea and land, To watch the night in storms, the day in cold, Whilst thou liest warm at home, secure and safe; And craves no other tribute at thy hands But love, fair looks and true obedience; Too little payment for so great a debt. Such duty as the subject owes the prince Even such a woman oweth to her husband; And when she is froward, peevish, sullen, sour, And not obedient to his honest will, What is she but a foul contending rebel And graceless traitor to her loving lord? I am ashamed that women are so simple To offer war where they should kneel for peace; Or seek for rule, supremacy and sway, When they are bound to serve, love and obey. Why are our bodies soft and weak and smooth, Unapt to toil and trouble in the world, But that our soft conditions and our hearts Should well agree with our external parts? Come, come, you froward and unable worms! My mind hath been as big as one of yours, My heart as great, my reason haply more, To bandy word for word and frown for frown; But now I see our lances are but straws, Our strength as weak, our weakness past compare, That seeming to be most which we indeed least are. Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot, And place your hands below your husband's foot: In token of which duty, if he please, My hand is ready; may it do him ease.

src: Thy mother was a piece of virtue, and She said thou wast my daughter; and thy father Was Duke of Milan; and thou his only heir And princess no worse issued.
trg: O the heavens! What foul play had we, that we came from thence? Or blessed was't we did?

src: O the heavens! What foul play had we, that we came from thence? Or blessed was't we did?
trg: Both, both, my girl: By foul play, as thou say'st, were we heaved thence, But blessedly holp hither.

src: Both, both, my girl: By foul play, as thou say'st, were we heaved thence, But blessedly holp hither.
trg: O, my heart bleeds To think o' the teen that I have turn'd you to, Which is from my remembrance! Please you, farther.

src: O, my heart bleeds To think o' the teen that I have turn'd you to, Which is from my remembrance! Please you, farther.
trg: My brother and thy uncle, call'd Antonio-- I pray thee, mark me--that a brother should Be so perfidious!--he whom next thyself Of all the world I loved and to him put The manage of my state; as at that time Through all the signories it was the first And Prospero the prime duke, being so reputed In dignity, and for the liberal arts Without a parallel; those being all my study, The government I cast upon my brother And to my state grew stranger, being transported And rapt in secret studies. Thy false uncle-- Dost thou attend me?

src: My brother and thy uncle, call'd Antonio-- I pray thee, mark me--that a brother should Be so perfidious!--he whom next thyself Of all the world I loved and to him put The manage of my state; as at that time Through all the signories it was the first And Prospero the prime duke, being so reputed In dignity, and for the liberal arts Without a parallel; those being all my study, The government I cast upon my brother And to my state grew stranger, being transported And rapt in secret studies. Thy false uncle-- Dost thou attend me?
trg: Sir, most heedfully.

src: Sir, most heedfully.
trg: Being once perfected how to grant suits, How to deny them, who to advance and who To trash for over-topping, new created The creatures that were mine, I say, or changed 'em, Or else new form'd 'em; having both the key Of officer and office, set all hearts i' the state To what tune pleased his ear; that now he was The ivy which had hid my princely trunk, And suck'd my verdure out on't. Thou attend'st not.

trg: O, good sir, I do.

src: O, good sir, I do.
trg: I pray thee, mark me. I, thus neglecting worldly ends, all dedicated To closeness and the bettering of my mind With that which, but by being so retired, O'er-prized all popular rate, in my false brother Awaked an evil nature; and my trust, Like a good parent, did beget of him A falsehood in its contrary as great As my trust was; which had indeed no limit, A confidence sans bound. He being thus lorded, Not only with what my revenue yielded, But what my power might else exact, like one Who having into truth, by telling of it, Made such a sinner of his memory, To credit his own lie, he did believe He was indeed the duke; out o' the substitution And executing the outward face of royalty, With all prerogative: hence his ambition growing-- Dost thou hear?

src: Your tale, sir, would cure deafness.
trg: To have no screen between this part he play'd And him he play'd it for, he needs will be Absolute Milan. Me, poor man, my library Was dukedom large enough: of temporal royalties He thinks me now incapable; confederates-- So dry he was for sway--wi' the King of Naples To give him annual tribute, do him homage, Subject his coronet to his crown and bend The dukedom yet unbow'd--alas, poor Milan!-- To most ignoble stooping.

trg: Mark his condition and the event; then tell me If this might be a brother.

src: Mark his condition and the event; then tell me If this might be a brother.
trg: I should sin To think but nobly of my grandmother: Good wombs have borne bad sons.

src: I should sin To think but nobly of my grandmother: Good wombs have borne bad sons.
trg: Now the condition. The King of Naples, being an enemy To me inveterate, hearkens my brother's suit; Which was, that he, in lieu o' the premises Of homage and I know not how much tribute, Should presently extirpate me and mine Out of the dukedom and confer fair Milan With all the honours on my brother: whereon, A treacherous army levied, one midnight Fated to the purpose did Antonio open The gates of Milan, and, i' the dead of darkness, The ministers for the purpose hurried thence Me and thy crying self.

trg: Alack, for pity! I, not remembering how I cried out then, Will cry it o'er again: it is a hint That wrings mine eyes to't.

trg: Hear a little further And then I'll bring thee to the present business Which now's upon's; without the which this story Were most impertinent.

src: Hear a little further And then I'll bring thee to the present business Which now's upon's; without the which this story Were most impertinent.
trg: Wherefore did they not That hour destroy us?

src: Wherefore did they not That hour destroy us?
trg: Well demanded, wench: My tale provokes that question. Dear, they durst not, So dear the love my people bore me, nor set A mark so bloody on the business, but With colours fairer painted their foul ends. In few, they hurried us aboard a bark, Bore us some leagues to sea; where they prepared A rotten carcass of a boat, not rigg'd, Nor tackle, sail, nor mast; the very rats Instinctively had quit it: there they hoist us, To cry to the sea that roar'd to us, to sigh To the winds whose pity, sighing back again, Did us but loving wrong.

src: Alack, what trouble Was I then to you!
trg: O, a cherubim Thou wast that did preserve me. Thou didst smile. Infused with a fortitude from heaven, When I have deck'd the sea with drops full salt, Under my burthen groan'd; which raised in me An undergoing stomach, to bear up Against what should ensue.

src: O, a cherubim Thou wast that did preserve me. Thou didst smile. Infused with a fortitude from heaven, When I have deck'd the sea with drops full salt, Under my burthen groan'd; which raised in me An undergoing stomach, to bear up Against what should ensue.
trg: How came we ashore?

src: How came we ashore?
trg: By Providence divine. Some food we had and some fresh water that A noble Neapolitan, Gonzalo, Out of his charity, being then appointed Master of this design, did give us, with Rich garments, linens, stuffs and necessaries, Which since have steaded much; so, of his gentleness, Knowing I loved my books, he furnish'd me From mine own library with volumes that I prize above my dukedom.

trg: Would I might But ever see that man!

src: Would I might But ever see that man!
trg: Now I arise: Sit still, and hear the last of our sea-sorrow. Here in this island we arrived; and here Have I, thy schoolmaster, made thee more profit Than other princesses can that have more time For vainer hours and tutors not so careful.

src: Now I arise: Sit still, and hear the last of our sea-sorrow. Here in this island we arrived; and here Have I, thy schoolmaster, made thee more profit Than other princesses can that have more time For vainer hours and tutors not so careful.
trg: Heavens thank you for't! And now, I pray you, sir, For still 'tis beating in my mind, your reason For raising this sea-storm?

src: Heavens thank you for't! And now, I pray you, sir, For still 'tis beating in my mind, your reason For raising this sea-storm?
trg: Know thus far forth. By accident most strange, bountiful Fortune, Now my dear lady, hath mine enemies Brought to this shore; and by my prescience I find my zenith doth depend upon A most auspicious star, whose influence If now I court not but omit, my fortunes Will ever after droop. Here cease more questions: Thou art inclined to sleep; 'tis a good dulness, And give it way: I know thou canst not choose. Come away, servant, come. I am ready now. Approach, my Ariel, come.
