trg: All hail, great master! grave sir, hail! I come To answer thy best pleasure; be't to fly, To swim, to dive into the fire, to ride On the curl'd clouds, to thy strong bidding task Ariel and all his quality.

src: All hail, great master! grave sir, hail! I come To answer thy best pleasure; be't to fly, To swim, to dive into the fire, to ride On the curl'd clouds, to thy strong bidding task Ariel and all his quality.
trg: Hast thou, spirit, Perform'd to point the tempest that I bade thee?

src: Hast thou, spirit, Perform'd to point the tempest that I bade thee?
trg: To every article. I boarded the king's ship; now on the beak, Now in the waist, the deck, in every cabin, I flamed amazement: sometime I'ld divide, And burn in many places; on the topmast, The yards and bowsprit, would I flame distinctly, Then meet and join. Jove's lightnings, the precursors O' the dreadful thunder-claps, more momentary And sight-outrunning were not; the fire and cracks Of sulphurous roaring the most mighty Neptune Seem to besiege and make his bold waves tremble, Yea, his dread trident shake.

trg: My brave spirit! Who was so firm, so constant, that this coil Would not infect his reason?

src: My brave spirit! Who was so firm, so constant, that this coil Would not infect his reason?
trg: Not a soul But felt a fever of the mad and play'd Some tricks of desperation. All but mariners Plunged in the foaming brine and quit the vessel, Then all afire with me: the king's son, Ferdinand, With hair up-staring,--then like reeds, not hair,-- Was the first man that leap'd; cried, 'Hell is empty And all the devils are here.'

trg: Why that's my spirit! But was not this nigh shore?

src: Why that's my spirit! But was not this nigh shore?
trg: Close by, my master.

src: Close by, my master.
trg: But are they, Ariel, safe?

src: But are they, Ariel, safe?
trg: Not a hair perish'd; On their sustaining garments not a blemish, But fresher than before: and, as thou badest me, In troops I have dispersed them 'bout the isle. The king's son have I landed by himself; Whom I left cooling of the air with sighs In an odd angle of the isle and sitting, His arms in this sad knot.

trg: Of the king's ship The mariners say how thou hast disposed And all the rest o' the fleet.

src: Of the king's ship The mariners say how thou hast disposed And all the rest o' the fleet.
trg: Safely in harbour Is the king's ship; in the deep nook, where once Thou call'dst me up at midnight to fetch dew From the still-vex'd Bermoothes, there she's hid: The mariners all under hatches stow'd; Who, with a charm join'd to their suffer'd labour, I have left asleep; and for the rest o' the fleet Which I dispersed, they all have met again And are upon the Mediterranean flote, Bound sadly home for Naples, Supposing that they saw the king's ship wreck'd And his great person perish.

trg: Ariel, thy charge Exactly is perform'd: but there's more work. What is the time o' the day?

src: Ariel, thy charge Exactly is perform'd: but there's more work. What is the time o' the day?
trg: Past the mid season.

src: Past the mid season.
trg: At least two glasses. The time 'twixt six and now Must by us both be spent most preciously.

src: At least two glasses. The time 'twixt six and now Must by us both be spent most preciously.
trg: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, Let me remember thee what thou hast promised, Which is not yet perform'd me.

src: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, Let me remember thee what thou hast promised, Which is not yet perform'd me.
trg: How now? moody? What is't thou canst demand?

src: How now? moody? What is't thou canst demand?
trg: My liberty.

src: My liberty.
trg: Before the time be out? no more!

src: Before the time be out? no more!
trg: I prithee, Remember I have done thee worthy service; Told thee no lies, made thee no mistakings, served Without or grudge or grumblings: thou didst promise To bate me a full year.

src: I prithee, Remember I have done thee worthy service; Told thee no lies, made thee no mistakings, served Without or grudge or grumblings: thou didst promise To bate me a full year.
trg: Dost thou forget From what a torment I did free thee?

src: Dost thou forget From what a torment I did free thee?
trg: No.

src: No.
trg: Thou dost, and think'st it much to tread the ooze Of the salt deep, To run upon the sharp wind of the north, To do me business in the veins o' the earth When it is baked with frost.

src: Thou dost, and think'st it much to tread the ooze Of the salt deep, To run upon the sharp wind of the north, To do me business in the veins o' the earth When it is baked with frost.
trg: I do not, sir.

src: I do not, sir.
trg: Thou liest, malignant thing! Hast thou forgot The foul witch Sycorax, who with age and envy Was grown into a hoop? hast thou forgot her?

src: Thou liest, malignant thing! Hast thou forgot The foul witch Sycorax, who with age and envy Was grown into a hoop? hast thou forgot her?
trg: No, sir.

src: No, sir.
trg: Thou hast. Where was she born? speak; tell me.

src: Thou hast. Where was she born? speak; tell me.
trg: Sir, in Argier.

src: Sir, in Argier.
trg: O, was she so? I must Once in a month recount what thou hast been, Which thou forget'st. This damn'd witch Sycorax, For mischiefs manifold and sorceries terrible To enter human hearing, from Argier, Thou know'st, was banish'd: for one thing she did They would not take her life. Is not this true?

Is not this true?
trg: Ay, sir.

src: Ay, sir.
trg: This blue-eyed hag was hither brought with child And here was left by the sailors. Thou, my slave, As thou report'st thyself, wast then her servant; And, for thou wast a spirit too delicate To act her earthy and abhorr'd commands, Refusing her grand hests, she did confine thee, By help of her more potent ministers And in her most unmitigable rage, Into a cloven pine; within which rift Imprison'd thou didst painfully remain A dozen years; within which space she died And left thee there; where thou didst vent thy groans As fast as mill-wheels strike. Then was this island-- Save for the son that she did litter here, A freckled whelp hag-born--not honour'd with A human shape.

trg: Yes, Caliban her son.

src: Yes, Caliban her son.
trg: Dull thing, I say so; he, that Caliban Whom now I keep in service. Thou best know'st What torment I did find thee in; thy groans Did make wolves howl and penetrate the breasts Of ever angry bears: it was a torment To lay upon the damn'd, which Sycorax Could not again undo: it was mine art, When I arrived and heard thee, that made gape The pine and let thee out.

trg: I thank thee, master.

src: I thank thee, master.
trg: If thou more murmur'st, I will rend an oak And peg thee in his knotty entrails till Thou hast howl'd away twelve winters.

src: If thou more murmur'st, I will rend an oak And peg thee in his knotty entrails till Thou hast howl'd away twelve winters.
trg: Pardon, master; I will be correspondent to command And do my spiriting gently.

src: Pardon, master; I will be correspondent to command And do my spiriting gently.
trg: Do so, and after two days I will discharge thee.

src: Do so, and after two days I will discharge thee.
trg: That's my noble master! What shall I do? say what; what shall I do?

src: That's my noble master! What shall I do? say what; what shall I do?
trg: Go make thyself like a nymph o' the sea: be subject To no sight but thine and mine, invisible To every eyeball else. Go take this shape And hither come in't: go, hence with diligence! Awake, dear heart, awake! thou hast slept well; Awake!

src: Go make thyself like a nymph o' the sea: be subject To no sight but thine and mine, invisible To every eyeball else. Go take this shape And hither come in't: go, hence with diligence! Awake, dear heart, awake! thou hast slept well; Awake!
trg: The strangeness of your story put Heaviness in me.

src: The strangeness of your story put Heaviness in me.
trg: Shake it off. Come on; We'll visit Caliban my slave, who never Yields us kind answer.

src: Shake it off. Come on; We'll visit Caliban my slave, who never Yields us kind answer.
trg: 'Tis a villain, sir, I do not love to look on.

src: 'Tis a villain, sir, I do not love to look on.
trg: But, as 'tis, We cannot miss him: he does make our fire, Fetch in our wood and serves in offices That profit us. What, ho! slave! Caliban! Thou earth, thou! speak.

src: But, as 'tis, We cannot miss him: he does make our fire, Fetch in our wood and serves in offices That profit us. What, ho! slave! Caliban! Thou earth, thou! speak.

trg: Come forth, I say! there's other business for thee: Come, thou tortoise! when? Fine apparition! My quaint Ariel, Hark in thine ear.

src: Come forth, I say! there's other business for thee: Come, thou tortoise! when? Fine apparition! My quaint Ariel, Hark in thine ear.
trg: My lord it shall be done.

src: My lord it shall be done.
trg: Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil himself Upon thy wicked dam, come forth!

src: Thou poisonous slave, got by the devil himself Upon thy wicked dam, come forth!
trg: As wicked dew as e'er my mother brush'd With raven's feather from unwholesome fen Drop on you both! a south-west blow on ye And blister you all o'er!

src: As wicked dew as e'er my mother brush'd With raven's feather from unwholesome fen Drop on you both! a south-west blow on ye And blister you all o'er!
trg: For this, be sure, to-night thou shalt have cramps, Side-stitches that shall pen thy breath up; urchins Shall, for that vast of night that they may work, All exercise on thee; thou shalt be pinch'd As thick as honeycomb, each pinch more stinging Than bees that made 'em.

src: For this, be sure, to-night thou shalt have cramps, Side-stitches that shall pen thy breath up; urchins Shall, for that vast of night that they may work, All exercise on thee; thou shalt be pinch'd As thick as honeycomb, each pinch more stinging Than bees that made 'em.
trg: I must eat my dinner. This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, Which thou takest from me. When thou camest first, Thou strokedst me and madest much of me, wouldst give me Water with berries in't, and teach me how To name the bigger light, and how the less, That burn by day and night: and then I loved thee And show'd thee all the qualities o' the isle, The fresh springs, brine-pits, barren place and fertile: Cursed be I that did so! All the charms Of Sycorax, toads, beetles, bats, light on you! For I am all the subjects that you have, Which first was mine own king: and here you sty me In this hard rock, whiles you do keep from me The rest o' the island.

trg: Thou most lying slave, Whom stripes may move, not kindness! I have used thee, Filth as thou art, with human care, and lodged thee In mine own cell, till thou didst seek to violate The honour of my child.

trg: O ho, O ho! would't had been done! Thou didst prevent me; I had peopled else This isle with Calibans.

src: O ho, O ho! would't had been done! Thou didst prevent me; I had peopled else This isle with Calibans.
trg: Abhorred slave, Which any print of goodness wilt not take, Being capable of all ill! I pitied thee, Took pains to make thee speak, taught thee each hour One thing or other: when thou didst not, savage, Know thine own meaning, but wouldst gabble like A thing most brutish, I endow'd thy purposes With words that made them known. But thy vile race, Though thou didst learn, had that in't which good natures Could not abide to be with; therefore wast thou Deservedly confined into this rock, Who hadst deserved more than a prison.

trg: Hag-seed, hence! Fetch us in fuel; and be quick, thou'rt best, To answer other business. Shrug'st thou, malice? If thou neglect'st or dost unwillingly What I command, I'll rack thee with old cramps, Fill all thy bones with aches, make thee roar That beasts shall tremble at thy din.

trg: No, pray thee. I must obey: his art is of such power, It would control my dam's god, Setebos, and make a vassal of him.

src: No, pray thee. I must obey: his art is of such power, It would control my dam's god, Setebos, and make a vassal of him.
trg: So, slave; hence! Come unto these yellow sands, And then take hands: Courtsied when you have and kiss'd The wild waves whist, Foot it featly here and there; And, sweet sprites, the burthen bear. Hark, hark!

src: So, slave; hence! Come unto these yellow sands, And then take hands: Courtsied when you have and kiss'd The wild waves whist, Foot it featly here and there; And, sweet sprites, the burthen bear. Hark, hark!
trg: Where should this music be? i' the air or the earth? It sounds no more: and sure, it waits upon Some god o' the island. Sitting on a bank, Weeping again the king my father's wreck, This music crept by me upon the waters, Allaying both their fury and my passion With its sweet air: thence I have follow'd it, Or it hath drawn me rather. But 'tis gone. No, it begins again. Full fathom five thy father lies; Of his bones are coral made; Those are pearls that were his eyes: Nothing of him that doth fade But doth suffer a sea-change Into something rich and strange. Sea-nymphs hourly ring his knell Hark! now I hear them,--Ding-dong, bell.

trg: The ditty does remember my drown'd father. This is no mortal business, nor no sound That the earth owes. I hear it now above me.

src: The ditty does remember my drown'd father. This is no mortal business, nor no sound That the earth owes. I hear it now above me.
trg: The fringed curtains of thine eye advance And say what thou seest yond.

src: The fringed curtains of thine eye advance And say what thou seest yond.
trg: What is't? a spirit? Lord, how it looks about! Believe me, sir, It carries a brave form. But 'tis a spirit.

src: What is't? a spirit? Lord, how it looks about! Believe me, sir, It carries a brave form. But 'tis a spirit.
trg: No, wench; it eats and sleeps and hath such senses As we have, such. This gallant which thou seest Was in the wreck; and, but he's something stain'd With grief that's beauty's canker, thou mightst call him A goodly person: he hath lost his fellows And strays about to find 'em.

src: No, wench; it eats and sleeps and hath such senses As we have, such. This gallant which thou seest Was in the wreck; and, but he's something stain'd With grief that's beauty's canker, thou mightst call him A goodly person: he hath lost his fellows And strays about to find 'em.
trg: I might call him A thing divine, for nothing natural I ever saw so noble.

src: I might call him A thing divine, for nothing natural I ever saw so noble.

trg: Most sure, the goddess On whom these airs attend! Vouchsafe my prayer May know if you remain upon this island; And that you will some good instruction give How I may bear me here: my prime request, Which I do last pronounce, is, O you wonder! If you be maid or no?

src: Most sure, the goddess On whom these airs attend! Vouchsafe my prayer May know if you remain upon this island; And that you will some good instruction give How I may bear me here: my prime request, Which I do last pronounce, is, O you wonder! If you be maid or no?

src: No wonder, sir; But certainly a maid.
trg: My language! heavens! I am the best of them that speak this speech, Were I but where 'tis spoken.

src: My language! heavens! I am the best of them that speak this speech, Were I but where 'tis spoken.
trg: How? the best? What wert thou, if the King of Naples heard thee?

src: How? the best? What wert thou, if the King of Naples heard thee?
trg: A single thing, as I am now, that wonders To hear thee speak of Naples. He does hear me; And that he does I weep: myself am Naples, Who with mine eyes, never since at ebb, beheld The king my father wreck'd.

src: A single thing, as I am now, that wonders To hear thee speak of Naples. He does hear me; And that he does I weep: myself am Naples, Who with mine eyes, never since at ebb, beheld The king my father wreck'd.
trg: Alack, for mercy!

src: Alack, for mercy!
trg: Yes, faith, and all his lords; the Duke of Milan And his brave son being twain.

src: Yes, faith, and all his lords; the Duke of Milan And his brave son being twain.

trg: Why speaks my father so ungently? This Is the third man that e'er I saw, the first That e'er I sigh'd for: pity move my father To be inclined my way!

src: Why speaks my father so ungently? This Is the third man that e'er I saw, the first That e'er I sigh'd for: pity move my father To be inclined my way!
trg: O, if a virgin, And your affection not gone forth, I'll make you The queen of Naples.

src: O, if a virgin, And your affection not gone forth, I'll make you The queen of Naples.
trg: Soft, sir! one word more. They are both in either's powers; but this swift business I must uneasy make, lest too light winning Make the prize light. One word more; I charge thee That thou attend me: thou dost here usurp The name thou owest not; and hast put thyself Upon this island as a spy, to win it From me, the lord on't.

src: No, as I am a man.

trg: Follow me. Speak not you for him; he's a traitor. Come; I'll manacle thy neck and feet together: Sea-water shalt thou drink; thy food shall be The fresh-brook muscles, wither'd roots and husks Wherein the acorn cradled. Follow.

src: Follow me. Speak not you for him; he's a traitor. Come; I'll manacle thy neck and feet together: Sea-water shalt thou drink; thy food shall be The fresh-brook muscles, wither'd roots and husks Wherein the acorn cradled. Follow.

src: No; I will resist such entertainment till Mine enemy has more power.
trg: O dear father, Make not too rash a trial of him, for He's gentle and not fearful.

src: O dear father, Make not too rash a trial of him, for He's gentle and not fearful.
trg: What? I say, My foot my tutor? Put thy sword up, traitor; Who makest a show but darest not strike, thy conscience Is so possess'd with guilt: come from thy ward, For I can here disarm thee with this stick And make thy weapon drop.

src: What? I say, My foot my tutor? Put thy sword up, traitor; Who makest a show but darest not strike, thy conscience Is so possess'd with guilt: come from thy ward, For I can here disarm thee with this stick And make thy weapon drop.

src: Beseech you, father.

src: Hence! hang not on my garments.
trg: Sir, have pity; I'll be his surety.

src: Sir, have pity; I'll be his surety.
trg: Silence! one word more Shall make me chide thee, if not hate thee. What! An advocate for an imposter! hush! Thou think'st there is no more such shapes as he, Having seen but him and Caliban: foolish wench! To the most of men this is a Caliban And they to him are angels.

src: Silence! one word more Shall make me chide thee, if not hate thee. What! An advocate for an imposter! hush! Thou think'st there is no more such shapes as he, Having seen but him and Caliban: foolish wench! To the most of men this is a Caliban And they to him are angels.
trg: My affections Are then most humble; I have no ambition To see a goodlier man.

src: My affections Are then most humble; I have no ambition To see a goodlier man.
trg: Come on; obey: Thy nerves are in their infancy again And have no vigour in them.

src: Come on; obey: Thy nerves are in their infancy again And have no vigour in them.
trg: So they are; My spirits, as in a dream, are all bound up. My father's loss, the weakness which I feel, The wreck of all my friends, nor this man's threats, To whom I am subdued, are but light to me, Might I but through my prison once a day Behold this maid: all corners else o' the earth Let liberty make use of; space enough Have I in such a prison.

src: So they are; My spirits, as in a dream, are all bound up. My father's loss, the weakness which I feel, The wreck of all my friends, nor this man's threats, To whom I am subdued, are but light to me, Might I but through my prison once a day Behold this maid: all corners else o' the earth Let liberty make use of; space enough Have I in such a prison.

trg: Be of comfort; My father's of a better nature, sir, Than he appears by speech: this is unwonted Which now came from him.

src: Be of comfort; My father's of a better nature, sir, Than he appears by speech: this is unwonted Which now came from him.
trg: Thou shalt be free As mountain winds: but then exactly do All points of my command.

src: Thou shalt be free As mountain winds: but then exactly do All points of my command.
trg: To the syllable.

src: To the syllable.
trg: Come, follow. Speak not for him.

src: Come, follow. Speak not for him.
trg: Beseech you, sir, be merry; you have cause, So have we all, of joy; for our escape Is much beyond our loss. Our hint of woe Is common; every day some sailor's wife, The masters of some merchant and the merchant Have just our theme of woe; but for the miracle, I mean our preservation, few in millions Can speak like us: then wisely, good sir, weigh Our sorrow with our comfort.

src: I assure you, Carthage.

src: His word is more than the miraculous harp; he hath raised the wall and houses too.

src: What impossible matter will he make easy next?

src: I think he will carry this island home in his pocket and give it his son for an apple.

src: Ay.

src: Why, in good time.

src: Sir, we were talking that our garments seem now as fresh as when we were at Tunis at the marriage of your daughter, who is now queen.

src: And the rarest that e'er came there.
trg: Bate, I beseech you, widow Dido.

src: Bate, I beseech you, widow Dido.
trg: O, widow Dido! ay, widow Dido.

src: O, widow Dido! ay, widow Dido.
trg: Is not, sir, my doublet as fresh as the first day I wore it? I mean, in a sort.

src: Is not, sir, my doublet as fresh as the first day I wore it? I mean, in a sort.
trg: That sort was well fished for.

src: That sort was well fished for.
trg: When I wore it at your daughter's marriage?

src: When I wore it at your daughter's marriage?
trg: You cram these words into mine ears against The stomach of my sense. Would I had never Married my daughter there! for, coming thence, My son is lost and, in my rate, she too, Who is so far from Italy removed I ne'er again shall see her. O thou mine heir Of Naples and of Milan, what strange fish Hath made his meal on thee?

trg: Sir, he may live: I saw him beat the surges under him, And ride upon their backs; he trod the water, Whose enmity he flung aside, and breasted The surge most swoln that met him; his bold head 'Bove the contentious waves he kept, and oar'd Himself with his good arms in lusty stroke To the shore, that o'er his wave-worn basis bow'd, As stooping to relieve him: I not doubt He came alive to land.

src: No, no, he's gone.
trg: Sir, you may thank yourself for this great loss, That would not bless our Europe with your daughter, But rather lose her to an African; Where she at least is banish'd from your eye, Who hath cause to wet the grief on't.

src: Prithee, peace.
trg: You were kneel'd to and importuned otherwise By all of us, and the fair soul herself Weigh'd between loathness and obedience, at Which end o' the beam should bow. We have lost your son, I fear, for ever: Milan and Naples have More widows in them of this business' making Than we bring men to comfort them: The fault's your own.

src: You were kneel'd to and importuned otherwise By all of us, and the fair soul herself Weigh'd between loathness and obedience, at Which end o' the beam should bow. src: Very well.
trg: And most chirurgeonly.

src: And most chirurgeonly.

src: Had I plantation of this isle, my lord,--

src: And were the king on't, what would I do?

src: 'Scape being drunk for want of wine.
trg: I' the commonwealth I would by contraries Execute all things; for no kind of traffic Would I admit; no name of magistrate; Letters should not be known; riches, poverty, And use of service, none; contract, succession, Bourn, bound of land, tilth, vineyard, none; No use of metal, corn, or wine, or oil; No occupation; all men idle, all; And women too, but innocent and pure; No sovereignty;--

src: No marrying 'mong his subjects?

src: I would with such perfection govern, sir, To excel the golden age.

src: God save his majesty!
trg: Long live Gonzalo!

src: Long live Gonzalo!

src: And,--do you mark me, sir?
trg: Prithee, no more: thou dost talk nothing to me.

src: Prithee, no more: thou dost talk nothing to me.
trg: I do well believe your highness; and did it to minister occasion to these gentlemen, who are of such sensible and nimble lungs that they always use to laugh at nothing.

src: I do well believe your highness; and did it to minister occasion to these gentlemen, who are of such sensible and nimble lungs that they always use to laugh at nothing.

src: 'Twas you we laughed at.
trg: Who in this kind of merry fooling am nothing to you: so you may continue and laugh at nothing still.

src: Who in this kind of merry fooling am nothing to you: so you may continue and laugh at nothing still.

src: What a blow was there given!
trg: An it had not fallen flat-long.

src: An it had not fallen flat-long.

src: You are gentlemen of brave metal; you would lift the moon out of her sphere, if she would continue in it five weeks without changing.

src: We would so, and then go a bat-fowling.
trg: Nay, good my lord, be not angry.

src: Nay, good my lord, be not angry.

src: No, I warrant you; I will not adventure my discretion so weakly. Will you laugh me asleep, for I am very heavy?

src: Go sleep, and hear us.

src: What, all so soon asleep! I wish mine eyes Would, with themselves, shut up my thoughts: I find They are inclined to do so.

trg: We two, my lord, Will guard your person while you take your rest, And watch your safety.

src: We two, my lord, Will guard your person while you take your rest, And watch your safety.

src: Thank you. Wondrous heavy.

src: It is the quality o' the climate.

src: Do you not hear me speak?
trg: I do; and surely It is a sleepy language and thou speak'st Out of thy sleep. What is it thou didst say? This is a strange repose, to be asleep With eyes wide open; standing, speaking, moving, And yet so fast asleep.
